Débats de la Chambre des communes

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act

PersonSpeaking.Affiliation: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada, Lib.)

Content.ProceduralText: Bill C-41. Introduction and first reading
Content.ParaText: moved for leave to introduce Bill C-41, An Act to amend the Criminal Code and An Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying) and to make related amendments to other Acts.
Content.ProceduralText: (Motions deemed adopted, bill read the first time and printed)

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Public Safety and National Security regarding Bill C‑236, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Corrections and Conditional Release Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
Pursuant to Standing Order 97.1, the committee requests a 30-day extension to consider the bill.

Pursuant to Standing Order 97.1(3)(a), a motion to concur in the report is deemed moved, the question deemed put and a recorded division deemed demanded and deferred until Wednesday, October 28, at the expiry of the time provided for Oral Questions.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the eighth report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, entitled “Monitoring of the Rehabilitation Services Contract Awarded to PCVRS by Veterans Affairs Canada”.
Pursuant to Standing Order 109, the committee requests that the government table a comprehensive response to this report.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to rise to table a petition signed by coastal British Columbians. They highlight that fish in Canadian waters are a public resource and should provide lasting economic, social and cultural benefits for Canadians, first nations and coastal communities; that the current Pacific licensing and quota system has weakened British Columbia's independent fishing fleet, reduced employment security and created barriers for new entrants in intergenerational succession; and that rising licence and quota prices, excessive lease costs, corporate concentration and speculative investment have made it increasingly difficult for active harvesters to earn a sustainable livelihood, with some paying lease fees of up to 80% of the value of their catch.

They highlight that Canada does not maintain a public registry identifying the beneficial ownership of commercial fishing licenses and quota, and places no restrictions on future foreign beneficial ownership in the Pacific region. They also highlight that FOPO recommended reforms to improve the sharing of risks and benefits in Pacific fisheries.

The petitioners call on the government to, first, implement a made-in-British Columbia owner-operator and fleet separation framework where appropriate; second, establish a public registry disclosing the beneficial ownership of commercial fishing licenses and quota; third, prohibit future foreign ownership and foreign beneficial ownership of commercial fishing licenses and quota in the Pacific region; fourth, limit excessive corporate concentration, support fair transition measures and improve access to capital for independent fish harvesters, first nations and new entrants; and, last, implement long-overdue licensing reforms that strengthen independent fish harvesters, coastal communities and the long-term sustainability of Pacific fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise to table a petition from almost 3,000 people from across Canada and Saskatchewan with regard to endometriosis. This petition came about because of a meeting with a constituent named Tina and her health care providers in my office.

Almost two million Canadians are affected by endometriosis. Endometriosis has a significantly negative impact on the well-being and health of Canadians suffering from the condition. There are severe existing gaps in diagnosing and treating endometriosis, including long wait times to see health care providers, the need for increased awareness of the condition and the slow progress of endometriosis research in Canada.

The petitioners call upon the Government of Canada to adopt the following recommendations from the Standing Committee on Health's report entitled “Women's Health in Canada”. First, it should increase funding for research that supports innovation and discovery with respect to the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. Second, it should develop a national action plan on endometriosis in collaboration with related governing and administrative bodies, as well as people living with endometriosis, clinicians and researchers, to address gaps and barriers that hinder awareness, diagnosis and treatment.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Unless we want to change the Standing Orders to enable members to read petitions, I suggest that we enforce the rule that says members cannot read a petition. If you review the petitions from today so far or yesterday's petitions, you will see that more and more members are reading petitions.
I will keep an eye out for that.
Presenting petitions, the hon. member for Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola.
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people of Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola.

I have a petition for all of British Columbia, but with a focus on Merritt, in my riding, which is part of the West Coast Corridor Resiliency Partnership. We had floods in Merritt in 2021. The government promised that it would have British Columbians' backs in Merritt, and it has contributed next to nothing despite those promises.
I stand with the good people of Merritt, who want the infrastructure that is required for flood mitigation.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to rise to present two petitions this morning.

The first petition is about the memorial grant for first responders. The petitioners note that first responders put their lives on the line to protect Canadians and that their families may face significant financial hardship when tragedy strikes. They call upon the Government of Canada to increase the memorial grant to reflect inflation and ensure that it is indexed annually. They believe that the families of first responders who make the ultimate sacrifice deserve the support that reflects the rising cost of living.
An hon. member: He's reading too.
Sometimes it is hard to understand if a person is reading the petition or reading a summary of the petition.
There is still quite a bit of time left for the segment.
Mr. Speaker, for first responders, we can and must do better.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition concerns the temporary special measures introduced for Turkish and Syrian nationals following the major earthquake of February 2023. The petitioners note that many families that benefited from these measures have permits that have expired or will expire by the end of 2026. Many of them established themselves in Canada, contributing to our economy and raising children who now attend Canadian schools.
The petitioners—
An hon. member: We have readers.

When it comes to petitions, there is always a bit of an introduction and then a summary that sometimes sounds like the petition. It is difficult sometimes to gauge, but as long as it is of reasonable length and is not clearly being read, then it is acceptable.
The hon. member can continue.

Mr. Speaker, the petitioners are asking the Government of Canada to extend temporary resident status by 36 months and to provide work permits, where applicable. They also want applicants to be allowed to work in Canada while waiting for a decision and want to ensure that the best interests of affected children are taken into consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the people of Richmond Hill South. It is a real honour to present this petition.

The petitioners are concerned that the Prime Minister has welcomed the European Commission president's proposal for Canada to join the EU as an associate member. The petitioners are concerned that Canadians have endured years of Liberal immigration mismanagement and do not want EU-style, open-border policies imposed on Canada or Canadian taxpayer dollars to be used to directly or indirectly fund EU programs. They believe that Canadian laws, borders and taxes must be controlled by Canadians, not EU politicians and bureaucrats, and that Canada is a sovereign nation and will never be the EU's 28th member state.

Therefore, the petitioners are calling upon the Government of Canada to, number one, immediately disclose all discussions and proposals concerning Canada's potential associate membership to the EU; number two, reject any agreement that would surrender Canadian sovereignty or impose EU immigration policies, laws, taxes or regulations on Canadians; and, number three, guarantee that Canada will not become a member of the EU.
Mr. Speaker, I rise this morning to present a petition on behalf of my constituents and those living in the riding of my hon. colleague, the member for Vancouver Quadra.

This petition is signed by a group of scientists and academic experts on the west coast who are concerned about legislative proposals put forward by the government. They encourage the government, in particular, to ensure the highest standards of environmental assessment and review for all legislation, including Bill C-39. The petitioners call for the highest standards of governance to be ensured so that protections and safeguards for Canada's democratic processes and decision-making will be preserved in the future. The petitioners, as experts on the natural environment and our economy, also call on the government to reject any false distinction between supporting the economy and the environment, because both can be done at once.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would ask that all questions be allowed to stand.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.
[For text of questions and responses, see Written Questions website]

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Opposition Motion—Appearance of the Prime Minister before the Standing Committee on Finance

Content.ParaText: moved:

Quote.QuotePara: That, given that,
(i) the cost of government is driving up the cost of living,
(ii) the Parliamentary Budget Officer reports that this government's fastest-growing cost is interest on the national debt which has more than doubled since 2021,
(iii) this Liberal government now spends more on debt interest than the Canada Health Transfer,
(iv) an average family of four will pay nearly $6,000 in federal taxes toward interest on the national debt this year, based on numbers from the Parliamentary Budget Officer,
(v) the Prime Minister promised that he would reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio and deficit-to-GDP ratio,
the House call on the Prime Minister to appear as a witness before the Standing Committee on Finance to testify on saving Canadians money by cutting deficit spending, debt interest and taxes.

Content.ParaText: He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Wellington—Halton Hills North.

I rise today to speak to my opposition day motion. The motion calls on the Prime Minister to appear before the Standing Committee on Finance to explain how his government plans to cut deficit spending, debt interest and the tax burden on Canadians. Behind the billions of dollars we discuss here in Ottawa lies a reality we must never lose sight of: that of hard-working families, retirees counting every dollar, entrepreneurs trying to keep their businesses afloat and young people dreaming of owning a home.

In my riding of Richmond—Arthabaska—des‑Sources, I meet people who get up early, work long hours and do everything they can to provide a good life for their families. These are farmers, manufacturing workers, business owners, young families and seniors who have contributed to our society throughout their lives. These people are not asking for the moon. They want to be able to cover the cost of groceries, the mortgage, home heating and other bills without constantly worrying about their finances. Above all, they want to know that the tax dollars they hand over to the federal government are being used responsibly.

Public finances are not merely a matter of figures. They have a very real impact on the lives of Canadians. On October 20, the Parliamentary Budget Officer published her latest economic and fiscal outlook, and those figures should give us all pause for thought. According to this report, Canada's real economic growth is expected to reach just 0.9% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. These are modest growth rates for a country blessed with such abundant natural resources, such talented people and such significant economic potential. For Conservatives and for me, that is simply not good enough. Surely, we can be more ambitious.

Meanwhile, federal deficits are projected to total more than $333 billion over the next five years. That is not all. According to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the federal deficit is expected to reach $63 billion this year, before rising to $70 billion in 2027-28. Even in 2030-31, the government is projected to run a deficit of nearly $68 billion. In other words, these forecasts do not point to a return to a balanced budget at any point during the period under review.

I want to call attention to another very alarming item in the report. Public debt charges now make up the fastest-growing category of federal expenditures. In 2021‑22, they amounted to $24.5 billion. This year, they are expected to reach $60 billion. By 2030-31, the cost of debt charges alone could reach $83 billion. These funds are not going to be used to build hospitals, hire nurses, improve our roads and highways or give Canadians a break on their grocery bills. They will be used to meet financial obligations racked up the government.

Of course, all governments have to be able to borrow. Debt can be useful for funding necessary and productive investments. However, the government has to be able to show that the borrowed funds will produce tangible results and that public finances will remain manageable. This is exactly why we are requesting today that the Prime Minister come and explain himself before the finance committee. We are seeing no results on the ground. In fact, daily life is growing worse for our people.
I would now like to focus this debate on a reality that I am very familiar with, the reality of Richmond—Arthabaska—des-Sources.

In my region, we are fortunate to have innovative entrepreneurs, passionate farmers, manufacturers and community organizations that do outstanding work. However, behind this economic vitality, there are also people facing significant financial hardship. The recent statistics on food assistance are particularly telling.

According to Moisson Mauricie—Centre-du-Québec's 2026 hunger report, the network of 61 member organizations are now responding to over 137,000 requests for food assistance every month. That is an increase of 23% in just one year and an increase of 60% in five years. I repeat: Requests for food assistance have increased by 60% in five years. What is even more worrisome is that nearly 13% of the households assisted by this network have employment income. They have an income, but they are still struggling to make ends meet. That means that people are working, getting paid and yet still have to ask for help to put food on the table. That is what is happening.

The report also indicates that over 17% of the households that receive assistance rely mainly on an old age pension or retirement pension. Let us think about these seniors who worked for 30, 40 or 50 years. These are people who paid their taxes, raised their children and families and contributed to the development of our community. Today, some of them have to turn to food banks to make ends meet. That is what is happening right now. This situation deserves our full attention.

I want to take this opportunity to thank the volunteers and community organizations in our regions that meet these needs every day. Their work is essential. However, we should be asking ourselves why so many Canadians need their services. Our collective goal should be to allow people to live with dignity from their work and their retirement income.

In a country as rich as ours, both in terms of resources and opportunities, we need to find a way to make the essentials more affordable. That means a more productive economy, investments that create wealth and the sound management of public finances. We need to put an end to the Liberal culture of reckless spending. This Liberal culture is all about reckless spending.

I am also thinking about the farmers in my riding. In Richmond—Arthabaska—des-Sources, agriculture plays a significant role in our economy and our regional identity. Our producers have to contend with the cost of fuel, machinery, equipment, fertilizers and transportation. When a farmer's expenses rise, they cannot always incorporate those costs into the selling price of their products. They often have to absorb the increase at the expense of their profitability. When production and transportation costs rise throughout the food chain, this inevitably affects the price paid at the grocery store. That is why economic decisions made here in Ottawa have to take into account the impact on businesses and families in our regions.

The same goes for our manufacturing companies. When a company needs to invest more to modernize, hire workers, or break into new markets, it needs a predictable economic environment. As a former entrepreneur, I know that what people need is predictability. Businesses need to have confidence in the future. They need a government capable of distinguishing between investments that truly foster growth and spending that simply burdens public finances. Prosperity cannot be decreed. It is built through hard work, innovation, investment, and entrepreneurship.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's report also raises a fundamental question about the government's financial commitments. The Prime Minister promised to reduce the deficit-to-GDP ratio. However, according to projections published on October 20, that target is unlikely to be consistently met. The Prime Minister has to be able to defend his choices to the representatives of the people of Canada.
I want to close by calling to mind once again the people of my riding. A family in Victoriaville will have to make choices when revising its budget, because the cost of essentials continues to rise.
The Prime Minister also has to make choices. We expect him to appear before the Standing Committee on Finance to answer our questions and those of concerned Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to hear our colleague talk about the importance of volunteering in his riding. Many organizations in his riding, including the Breakfast Club, provide meals to thousands of children. The problem is that his leader described the work of the Breakfast Club as bureaucratic. He has said that helping to ensure that kids go to school with full bellies is bureaucratic.
I would like to know if the member agrees with his leader.
Madam Speaker, once again, I want to thank the people and volunteers getting involved in our communities.

In my riding, a group of men founded Clan Destins, which supports the Boîtes à lunch program. These individuals have dedicated themselves to the cause and are raising funds because the government is currently unable to support them. I thank them for that. What we need right now is for people to be able to make ends meet. That is the ultimate goal.

Madam Speaker, my colleague spoke at length about businesses and economic matters, but he did not say a word about the loss of purchasing power among seniors. He knows very well that seniors aged 65 to 74 have not received an increase in their old age security pension. They have lost their purchasing power.
Does my colleague intend to support Bill C‑261, which I am sponsoring, so that this injustice and inequity between seniors can finally be eliminated?

Madam Speaker, with all due respect to my colleague, I think she must have been absent during my speech, in which I spoke about our seniors who worked for 30, 40 or 50 years and paid taxes all their lives. That is exactly what I said in the speech I delivered a few minutes ago.
Madam Speaker, I would first like to congratulate former NDP MP Olivia Chow on her re-election and for receiving the greatest vote count by any mayor in Canadian history last night.

My colleague, in his speech, talked a lot about small and medium-sized businesses and the pressures they are facing. Right now, we are seeing record profits for big oil, big banks, big grocery and big telecommunications companies. Does he agree that there should be an excess profit tax on those posting obscene amounts of profits?

That could then reduce taxes for small and medium-sized businesses so some of the pressure can be taken off them. The big corporations are eating their lunch right now and it is time we provide relief for them.

Madam Speaker, the Conservative Party is the party that wants to lower taxes. We need to cut red tape in Ottawa, reduce the size of government and put money back in the pockets of all Canadians. That is what the next Conservative government will do.
Madam Speaker, according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the interest on the national debt is the fastest-growing category of government expenditures, outpacing health care transfers.
How does my colleague think the government could reduce spending and put the budget back on a more responsible path?

Madam Speaker, it is unbelievable. We are paying more for interest on the debt than we are investing in health care, as my colleague just said. Has anyone thought about everything that could be done with that money? The problem is the current Liberal culture; the Liberals spend recklessly without achieving any results.

I often talk about a real-life example involving the lease of a parcel of land in Nova Scotia. A private company leases land for $13,500 and is leasing it back to the Liberal government for $20 million a year for 10 years. That comes to $200 million. That is how the government spends its money. We need sound management, and the culture of reckless spending must end.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, the government's economic plan is not working. We now have enough data coming in over the last 18 months of the Prime Minister's tenure to know that its plan is not working. That is confirmed by the most recent report from the Parliamentary Budget Officer of October 20, which warns that the federal debt is growing at two times the pace of the federal deficit. That is because the government is capitalizing the borrowing it is doing and putting it on the balance sheet through the use of arm's-length entities like Crown corporations rather than expensing it on the profit and loss statement, on the budget. This accounting is in some ways hiding the pace of the growth of the federal debt. As a result, the PBO projects that the federal debt will increase this year from 41% of GDP to 43% of GDP by decade's end, going from $1.3 trillion to $1.67 trillion, an increase of some $367 billion. This is despite the fact that the Liberal Party and the Prime Minister promised in the last election to ensure, “debt-to-GDP declines over the budget horizon.” Clearly, the government is not abiding by its commitment in its last platform.

This massive growth in the federal debt is having real consequences. As a result of this acceleration of the growth in the federal debt, two times the pace of the deficit, interest on the national debt is now starting to grow at an alarming pace. Just several years ago, interest on the national debt cost six cents for every tax dollar of revenue. Today, it is 10.5¢ for every tax dollar of revenue. By decade's end, in a mere just over three years, it is going to be almost 14¢ of every tax dollar, which is projected to be approximately $83 billion a year. That is almost one and a half times what the federal government spends in cash transfers on public health care.

For those who say that that amount is not nearly as high as the crisis we faced in the 1980s and 1990s, I looked at the interest expense ratio charts the government produces. When the interest on the national debt started to accelerate in the late 1970s, if I recall correctly, in 1977 it was a mere 14¢ of every tax dollar. A short six or seven years later, it had skyrocketed well beyond 20¢, hitting 30¢ per tax dollar in less than a decade, leading to the fiscal crisis of the mid-1990s. This growth in interest on the national debt is concerning. It is an alarm that has been raised by many of the folks who helped get Canada on the right fiscal track in the late 1990s, like Don Drummond, who has been saying that the government should abide by its fiscal anchors and keep the debt-to-GDP ratio on a declining track, and that we are putting the very hard-earned gains of the 1990s at risk. Those hard-earned gains led to a much lower cost of capital for this country relative to other economic peers such as the United States. That is being put at risk with the government's reckless spending.

Even though the government is borrowing at twice the pace and is spending way more than the previous Trudeau government, with deficits double that of the last budget of Minister Chrystia Freeland at almost 2% rather than 1% of GDP, and is spending tons of money and borrowing even more money, the economy is not doing well. In fact, economic growth is being downgraded. The PBO downgraded economic growth for this year to 0.9%.

That follows on the heels of other economic projections, which have downgraded growth over the last couple of months. The Bank of Canada has downgraded growth, and bank economists have downgraded growth. We are now in a situation where growth has been downgraded to less than 1% this year, effectively zero, all while affordability and inflation continue to be a problem. In fact, the markets are projecting that the Bank of Canada is going to hike interest rates. We have somewhat of a stagflationary environment here, again, proof that the government's economic plan is not working.

I would like to finish by focusing on this fact: The previous Liberal government blew through every fiscal anchor it established. I reviewed all the fiscal anchors it established. Do we remember the 2015 Liberal promise of a fiscal anchor, the one that they campaigned on in that election, that we would run budget deficits just on a temporary basis, capped at no more than $10 billion a year and just for a couple of years, and would return to budget balance? When they came to office, the Liberals threw that plan out the window, just like they chucked out the plan to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio they made in the last election. In the Liberals' first budget, they replaced that temporary set of deficits with a new fiscal anchor of a shrinking federal debt-to-GDP ratio over the medium term. Then they abandoned that fiscal anchor.

In the fall economic statement of 2020, Minister Freeland introduced new fiscal anchors tied to labour market indicators such as employment and unemployment. These guardrails were later dropped. Then the government came forward with a new fiscal anchor, which in some ways was the old fiscal anchor. The Liberals came forward with the fiscal anchor of refocusing on reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio. They introduced that fiscal anchor in budget 2022. That ratio did not move consistently downward, and so they later abandoned that pledge. The Liberals came up with a new pledge in the fall economic statement of 2023, where they decided that their new anchor would be to keep annual deficits below 1% of GDP.

Then we got a new Prime Minister and a new Liberal leader who replaced that fiscal anchor with two new fiscal anchors, abandoning the fiscal anchor he had promised in the platform and in the last budget. Those two new fiscal anchors were a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio and to balance operating expenses with revenue by 2028-29.

Here we are, less than a year later, and the government is going to blow through that umpteenth fiscal anchor that it established because the PBO projects that deficits to GDP are going to be increasing rather than decreasing, from 1.8% this year to 2% in 2027-28. I would note that this fiscal anchor is double the previous fiscal anchor that Minister Freeland had established.

The government and the Prime Minister are putting us on a reckless path of spending and ever-increasing deficits. That is particularly worrying when we look at what is going on with countries that are facing high debt loads, such as France, and when we look at what is going on with the pace of growth of the U.S. deficit and debt. We are not an island, and we are not a reserve currency. If there is going to be a crisis in sovereign debt borrowing, Canada is particularly vulnerable, as we were in the mid-1990s, and we will be buffeted by whatever crisis takes place outside of this country because of this ever-increasing debt and this ever-increasing interest on the debt.

The PBO is highlighting what many other reports have highlighted: that the government's economic plan is not working, that the national debt is growing at double the pace of deficits, that economic growth is slowing, that inflation is starting to take hold again and that affordability remains a crisis. For all those reasons, I encourage the House to vote for the motion.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the member opposite. He made reference to Canada, France and the U.S.A. I think it is important that, when we think of the G7 countries, which include the United States, France, Germany and England, Canada places exceptionally well. We are one of only two countries, Canada and Germany, that have a AAA credit rating. The Conservatives want to see cutbacks. Would those cutbacks be to military expenditures, where we are meeting the 2% targets? That is a $5-billion expense. Are the Conservatives saying that we should not be spending that money? Are the Conservatives saying that we should not have given the tax break for 22 million Canadians? Are they saying that we should reinstate the carbon tax, in order to justify what the member opposite is saying? Where is the overall plan to develop the Canadian economy, coming from the Conservative Party?

Madam Speaker, I disagree with the IMF's assertion that Canada's debt to GDP is in good shape. I think that fails to take into account the fact that Canada's subnational governments have some of the highest, if not the highest, indebtedness in the OECD. If I recall correctly, the Province of Ontario has more debt than the State of California, whose economy is bigger than Canada's. Subnational debt in the United States is much lower than in Canada, and that is not incorporated into the G7 rankings that the IMF has analyzed, nor is the fact that of the G7 countries, Canada is the smallest currency and is not a reserve currency, unlike the other members of the European Union, in the Eurozone, the United States or Japan.

I think that assertion fails to take into account what the member opposite has been talking about. In brief, to finish, the solution is to address supply-side reforms, rather than the government's approach of always subsidizing demand-side initiatives. That is the fundamental problem with the government's economic approach.

Madam Speaker, I also think this government's priorities are misplaced. For example, the entire budget for official languages support programs in Quebec, which was $120 million last year, is dedicated to strengthening English in Quebec, even though French is the language under threat.

The government also says it has no money for the Translation Bureau, so it plans to make cuts and eliminate 340 positions through attrition at the Translation Bureau, which is essential to ensuring access to both official languages here in Parliament.
What does my colleague think of that?

Madam Speaker, I think it is vital to defend the rights of francophones across Canada. I think that starts with ensuring that our economy grows significantly to make it possible to subsidize programs for francophones and the French fact in Canada.

The problem with the government's economic plan is that whenever a challenge arises, its response is more government spending rather than the kind of fundamental economic reforms that would create the conditions for stronger GDP growth and a more productive economy
That is the fundamental problem with the government's plan.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his very expensive speech, as it turns out. I just googled the debt. We are spending between $2,500 and $5,000 per second in this country on the debt. The 10-minute speech was a $3-million speech. It may only have been $1.5 million on the lower part. I would like my colleague to explain to the Liberals once again why debt is bad.

Madam Speaker, the growth in the debt is concerning, because we have seen this story play out before. It starts to chew up an ever-increasing amount of federal revenues, putting at risk the very social programs, like health care and education, that Canadians rely upon.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, it is good to be here this morning to combat the misinformation from the Conservatives. I do not know how many falsehoods the former member for Carleton can jam into one opposition day motion, but the Conservatives seem to have outdone themselves this time. No matter how many falsehoods they put together, they cannot constitute a truth, and that is what we see in this opposition day motion.

I welcome the opportunity to speak to the motion. It gives me the opportunity to speak to our government's plan for building a stronger Canadian economy while maintaining fiscal responsibility. It is an important debate at a time when events beyond our borders are having real impacts on economies and households around the world.

The global economy is changing rapidly, and we all know that. Long-standing trading relationships are shifting. Uncertainty remains very high, and countries around the world are competing for investment, jobs and opportunities. In that environment, Canada must be both ambitious and disciplined.

We begin from a position of fiscal strength, and we cannot understate this. It is really important that Canada, as a country, starts from one of the strongest positions, certainly in the G7. Many of our agencies internationally that look at and compare economies around the world say that Canada has one of the strongest fiscal positions in the world, including the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. Our responsibility, I would say, is to protect that advantage while putting it to work to build a more productive, resilient and self-reliant economy. That means making deliberate choices about where government spends, where it saves, and where we invest today so that we can deliver prosperity for tomorrow.

Budget 2025 marked an important shift in how we manage federal finances. Rather than allowing the cost of government to continue growing, we are shifting resources toward investments that can expand Canada's economic capacity. In short, we have shifted from government operations to boosting productivity. We are spending less on running government so we can invest more in building Canada.

Our fiscal anchors remain very clear: balancing day-to-day operating spending with revenues by year 2028-29 and maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio, and we are making progress. Despite what the Conservatives say, despite how much they talk down the Canadian economy, we are making significant progress in this country.

The government is now on track to balance the operating budget in 2027-28, which is one year ahead of schedule. Let us not forget that in the spring economic update, we reported $11 billion less of a deficit than was previously projected. At the same time, we are following through on the efficiency measures set out in budget 2025. That includes the comprehensive expenditure review, which, alongside other measures identified in the budget, will deliver $60 billion in savings and revenues over the next five years.

We are also reducing the size of government. We are rightsizing the public service to a more sustainable level through attrition, workforce adjustment and early retirement incentives. As that work advances, we are turning our attention to additional areas where government can operate more efficiently, including targeted horizontal reviews and efforts to rein in spending on external management and consulting services.

We recognize that rising debt servicing costs reinforce the very importance of maintaining sound public finances. That is precisely why we are taking action to constrain the growth of day-to-day operating spending, to find savings across government and to maintain clear fiscal anchors. However, we will not strengthen Canada's finances by weakening Canada's economy. We know the opposite is actually the truth, but that method is what the Conservatives propose over and over again.

The Conservatives propose to cut back and not invest strategically in the economy, which would really weaken the Canadian economy. This would not improve the public finances of the country at all. In fact, we know that if we make strategic investments, building a stronger economy will continue to strengthen Canada's public finances over time. That is the sustainable path forward. It is disciplined spending combined with strategic investments that expand our productive capacity and support stronger economic growth.

This is exactly what we are seeing in the economy today. We have seen the GDP up in the last quarter, Q2. It was up by 3.3%, exceeding expectations. It was the fastest growth in the G7. We saw GDP per capita up to 3.9%. Wages have been outpacing inflation, and we see new business investment on the rise at 8.9%, almost 9%. This is significant, especially when we look at the headwinds the country and the global economy are facing due to wars, conflicts and the oil price shocks associated with those, not to mention, obviously, the trading relationship with our southern neighbours, which has been strained and is affecting the Canadian economy.

This is where our approach differs from one presented by the opposition. Fiscal discipline is necessary, but cutting for the sake of cutting is not an economic strategy. Conservatives are known for that. They would cut indiscriminately in ways that do not make sense, that do not select the areas where government operating expenses can be improved or where government operations themselves can be optimized. Our approach to spend less on operations of government means we can invest more in building Canada's economy. The purpose of that discipline is not simply to spend less, but it is also to create the capacity or the fiscal room to invest more in the things that make Canada stronger and more productive. Those are capital investments in productive, revenue-generating assets that will return dividends to the taxpayer in the future. Yes, it will take time to grow the economy and see those investments realize themselves in the Canadian economy, but we are seeing that progress already being made.

This means making government work better, removing barriers to investment and creating the conditions for more capital to flow into the Canadian economy. One way we are doing that is through the new productivity mega deduction, which is one of the most significant changes to Canada's business tax system in half a century. I have talked to business owners all across my riding and in my region, and let me tell the House, they love this measure. They think this measure is really sound support from the government at a time where uncertainty is really the thing they are most grappling with. This measure creates long-term certainty. It allows businesses of all sizes to immediately deduct the full cost of a much broader range of investments, giving them a powerful incentive to build, expand and create good jobs in Canadian communities. This includes investments in everything from fibre optic networks, software, research and development, to mines, pipelines, railways, bridges and roads.

We are also making immediate expensing permanent. This is significant, because we know that when those policy signals from the government change, they can really disrupt investment flows and disrupt industries, because they are planning ahead for many years to come. Their capital investment plans are things that are very sensitive to those swings and changes. Giving them long-term certainty is the number one thing we hear from the industries and the business community across Canada. I have done two pre-budget consultations over two summers now, and one of the themes that comes out of those conversations every single time is how businesses need long-term certainty, how capital needs long-term certainty in order to flow. This is how they make better management and investment decisions, and they need those clear and crisp policy signals that give them long-term certainty. This is exactly what we are doing with this measure.

We have made immediate expensing permanent. This measure will increase the share of assets eligible for immediate expensing from roughly 15% to more than 65% of capital assets, while lowering the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from roughly 13% to 6.4%. We are cutting it in half. This makes Canada the most tax-competitive advanced economy in the world. It is significantly lower than the United States. It is 10% lower than the United States, and it is one-third of the OECD average. This is significant in terms of incentivizing new business investment into Canada.

Creating the conditions for investment is only one part of the equation. We also need to get projects built and built faster. That is exactly why the government stood up the Major Projects Office, to advance projects of national interest designed to connect our economy, diversify Canadian industries and trade, and create high-paying careers.

Since September 2025, 18 projects and 10 transformative strategies have been referred to the Major Projects Office, representing more than $126 billion of investment in Canada's economy. These are investments with the potential to transform Canada's economy, investments in critical minerals that the world needs, energy infrastructure that can help Canadian resources reach new markets, transportation infrastructure that can help move Canadian products faster and more efficiently across Canada into those global markets, and major projects that can create good jobs, strengthen our economic security and unlock new opportunities across the country.

I am particularly proud of the Darlington new nuclear project, just next door to my riding. It is significant, as it is the first deployment of small modular reactors as a major project. It got $2 billion of investment from the Canada Growth Fund, a fund that our government set up and capitalized with $15 billion a few years back. That Darlington new nuclear site is creating 18,000 construction jobs and 3,700 operational jobs in my region, in Durham region. That is significant employment and far outweighs the job losses that we have experienced since the trade war started with the United States. It is 10 times greater, in fact, than the job losses. Those are significant employment opportunities in my region. I am very proud of that work, of the Canada Growth Fund's investment, the private capital that was associated with that investment and the many job opportunities, the good, high-paying careers at OPG in Durham region.
This is what spending less to invest more looks like in practice: a more efficient government, a more competitive investment environment and more major projects getting built across Canada.

It is not just in my riding. There are all kinds of projects right across the country, the northwest transmission line in B.C., Churchill Falls, which was announced and is a massive clean energy project, Contrecoeur in Quebec and many more. There are quite a few critical mineral projects that are really exciting to see come online.
The measures we have put in place are the signs of a responsible government. It is not simply about how much we spend. It is about the investments we are making that deliver results for Canadians.

Canada has everything it needs to succeed: the resources, the talent, the ambition. We now need to put them to work. That means spending less, again, on running government and creating more room for investment. It means attracting capital, getting major projects built and creating good jobs in communities across the country. Above all else, it means making choices today that will strengthen Canada's economy for generations to come.

Canadians expect their government to be careful with their money. They also expect us to have a plan for the future. Those objectives are not in conflict. They actually complement one another. We can control government spending while investing in growth. We can protect Canada's fiscal strength while building the infrastructure our economy needs. We can attract investment and create opportunities while making Canada more resilient and more self-reliant. Those are the choices our government is making every day. That work will continue.

Next week, our government will introduce budget 2026, building on the progress already under way to strengthen our economy and create many new opportunities for Canadians. We have an opportunity at this juncture to build a stronger Canada and our government is determined to seize that opportunity to make Canada the strongest economy in the G7. I think we have been very clear and very consistent with that message and are staying true to it, with our compass pointed at true north, which is to build a stronger country, create more self-reliance and to ensure that we do so in a fiscally responsible manner that creates good-paying jobs for Canadians.

Canadians, above all else, want a highly productive economy. They want to see their standard of living increase over time. They want to feel like they are getting ahead. They want good incomes that outpace inflation. They want the extra income so that they can afford to feed their family, go on vacation and have a high quality of life.

That is what Canadians are known for, and that is what Canada is known for, so that is exactly what our government is focused on every single day, creating that prosperous economy where Canadians can feel like they are getting ahead.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member representing the government is omitting a key fact. The government, for the last 11 years, has been borrowing money and promising Canadians that the next day will be a better day. The government is printing money and piling on the debt. Our debt service is somewhere around $60 billion, and will probably be $80 billion in two or three years.

That is very concerning. Anyone with the right economic mind can understand how concerning that is to Canadians' lives. Canadians are still lining up at food banks. The Liberals are printing all this money, borrowing all this money. It is billions of dollars. The debt service is piling up and Canadians are not getting ahead.
How does that make sense to the member?

Madam Speaker, it does not surprise me that the premise of the member opposite's question is false. What I mean by that is that our government has been responding to crisis after crisis that has hit our economy. I do not think it is news to anyone in the House that the global economy is highly integrated and that Canada is subject to the pressures that the world is facing today.

We have had to borrow money to invest in the Canadian economy, but there is growth in the Canadian economy. I understand the Conservatives would not invest in that growth. They would cut all of the things that Canadians rely on. They would not invest in children. They would not invest in a groceries and essentials benefit. They would not feed kids at school. They would not invest in dental care. They would not invest in child care.

The Conservatives have made it very clear that they would not make investments. They would not have a productivity mega deduction to spur business investment in this country. They would not do those things because it is as if they think the economy will grow by itself without the government making strategic investments, and we—
The hon. member for La Pointe-de-l'Île.

Madam Speaker, not only are the Liberals running up massive deficits, but they are also forgoing sources of revenue. One example is that they are refusing to tax the web giants, despite the fact that they are causing immense harm to our local media.

Worse still, this outcome was entirely predictable. They did it to appease Mr. Trump as part of the negotiations, but they got nothing in return. They merely whetted the U.S. administration's appetite.

Madam Speaker, we have done everything we can to be a reasonable trade partner and reliable trade partner with our southern neighbour. At this point, we are pursuing diversified trade relationships all around the world.

We have seen the Prime Minister, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Minister of International Trade and others work to help Canada and our businesses access foreign markets all around the world. We have signed over 21 new trade and security agreements in just over a year. We saw the highest level of non-U.S. trade in our history in July of this year. There are very significant increases to Canada's trading relationships that are part of diversifying and of ensuring that we have a resilient economy.

There are results in the Canadian economy. The member opposite said we are borrowing money, but we are also seeing growth. I cited in my speech we have 3.3% GDP growth, the highest in the G7. There was 3.9% GDP per capita growth in quarter two. Business investment is up almost 9%. We have seen a 22.6% increase in business investment in new machinery and equipment since we put in place our—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Sarnia—Lambton—Bkejwanong.
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for all of his work.

In 2008, when we had the world economic recession, it was former prime minister Stephen Harper and former minister Jim Flaherty who put together a plan to infuse money into infrastructure and build to keep the Canadian economy strong, and it worked. We now see the Prime Minister taking that experience and having us build nation-building projects and infrastructure and diversify our trade. All of these things are working.
Can my colleague expound a bit on the evidence we are seeing that things are moving in a better direction?

Madam Speaker, I represent the riding that Jim Flaherty served for about a decade before he passed. He was a good finance minister, and I agree with the strategy, which is that, in hard economic times, often one of the things that governments do is to strategically invest in infrastructure. Canada is now ranked as the number one place in the world for new investment in infrastructure.

We are the most attractive in the world for infrastructure investment. That is significant, and we have seen lots of new private sector investment interest in Canada from around the world. The Prime Minister's investment summit got almost half a trillion dollars in new business investment commitments from our financial institutions here in Canada, our big banks and our pension plans.
We are going to build this country up, and infrastructure is one of the ways that we can invest in a more productive Canadian economy for all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, back in 2020, government tax revenue was $284 billion. In 2025, it is $417 billion. The GST went from $32 billion to $52 billion. The amount of money the government has racked up in debt means that a lot of money is going to be spent on debt servicing charges. The GST that is currently being collected is not even enough to cover the debt servicing charges, let alone things like health care transfers to the province, military spending and things like that, which Canadians are expecting.

I very simply ask the member, with the government set to blow the debt servicing charges all the way up to $83 billion in the coming years, and with all the extra tax revenue the government has been generating, where did the money go? Why is the government running such a massive deficit if it has increased tax revenue by over $130 billion in five years?

Madam Speaker, we know that debt servicing charges are rising, but that is not because of the Government of Canada. It is because of long-term bond rates that determine the interest rates the Canadian government will have to pay. We recognize that those debt servicing charges are going up, but what is the solution in that environment when Canada is facing a trade war and facing all these economic shocks?

The Conservatives would dial it all back so that we would have no growth in the economy. That is not the solution. The solution is to invest strategically in an economy that becomes more productive and is able to generate revenue, which is exactly why we have launched the capital budgeting framework. We are focused on revenue-generating assets and investing strategically in the Canadian economy so we have growth and productivity gains, so Canadians have a better standard of living in the future, and eventually, as those revenues come in, so we can pay down the debt and deficit, which is what we all want to see.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, my colleague made reference to the issue of dialing back. As an example, I think of Canada's commitment, through the leadership of our Prime Minister, to bring our Canadian Forces spending up to 2% of GDP, which I think we achieved within seven months of being in government. Now we are looking at eventually increasing it to 5% of GDP. These are important sovereignty-related issues. These are expenditures that are really important for us as a nation.

We hear the Conservatives talk as if they want investment in the Canadian Forces, but at the end of the day, it is questionable whether they even support that sort of an expenditure. What are my colleague's thoughts on that?

Madam Speaker, the question gives me the opportunity to point out that, under Conservative leadership, we were under 1% of our commitment to NATO. Under our government, we reached the 2% target way ahead of schedule, and way ahead of previous governments' commitments, which is a good thing. My constituents in my riding want Canada to be safe and secure for the future. We know that, in today's environment, in today's world, which is more dangerous and divided, we need to make those investments in defence.

It is unfortunate to some degree that the world is in that state, but those are investments that Canadians expect us to make. It is a shame that the Conservatives would not step up to make those investments at this time. They would claim some ideological stance on fiscal responsibility that makes no sense in today's environment in order to cut back even further from defence investment.

Our government has stood up, under our Prime Minister's leadership, to invest over $80 billion in defence in the last budget, budget 2025. Those are important strategic investments in our national security.

Madam Speaker, I send my regards to my colleague from Whitby, whom I have not seen in a while, and to you as well. You know how much I enjoy speaking when you are in the chair, especially since you are often the only person who listens to me, along with my Bloc Québécois colleagues. I doubly appreciate it. I did not want to start a debate on that, though, so I will start my speech over again and give back the 30 seconds I lost saying those things. We need to take this seriously. It is an opposition day.

As I said recently in the House, there are 343 members of Parliament—though there are a few vacant seats—and I do not think there is anyone in the House who is not concerned about the cost of living. I think that is important. When we visit our ridings, we see that people are concerned about the rising cost of groceries and transportation. There is also the anxiety and fear of what may lie ahead.

The Bank of Canada is talking about raising interest rates. That means higher mortgage rates. There is talk of increasing bond rates, which will also have an impact on fixed rates. People are not just worried about the cost of living and the price of gas at the pump today. People who are budget conscious and are stretched increasingly thin are worried about the impact in the medium term. This is a big problem, because a situation that we thought was temporary, with the Strait of Hormuz and the war in Ukraine, seems to be becoming permanent.

I have said this to a number of colleagues here, and I have also discussed it with the Minister of Finance and National Revenue: The least wealthy 20% of Quebeckers and Canadians must be foremost in our minds. We know that 80% of people have seen a significant increase in their purchasing power in recent years. We tend to forget that. People generally feel that they deserve pay raises, but do not deserve higher costs. The fact remains that some people have experienced a real increase in their purchasing power. Meanwhile, 20% of people have not seen their purchasing power grow. For those people, the slightest increase in the cost of meat, gas and utility bills hits hard. That is why I think we should vote in favour of this motion.

Why do I think that? It is because the Prime Minister who took over the reins of government told us that Canadians could judge him by the prices at the grocery store. I am not the one saying that. Quite frankly, I would never have said something like that during an election campaign. I would never have made such a statement, but the Prime Minister did. Perhaps he has some kind of superpower the rest of us do not have over food prices, which are set on the Chicago Board of Trade. I do not know what superpowers the Prime Minister may have, but he said it.

Now, the preamble to the motion does take a simplified view of the situation. We acknowledge that. It is a Conservative motion. If we are ever going to vote for a Conservative motion, we will have to accept some oversimplification, which I will discuss later on. However, I think that politely asking the Prime Minister to spend a little time here in Parliament and in committee, to pay a little attention to the parliamentary process and to come and speak about the cost of living, might not be such a bad thing.

As I said, ever since the Prime Minister took office, we do not really know what is going on at the Department of Finance anymore. We do not know who is truly making the decisions or where the initiative is coming from. In committee, the Minister of Finance does not answer our questions. He shows up with infographics, pages covered in little coloured bubbles, and says, for example, that ordinary people can do the math on the excise tax cuts using a paper and pen. The Prime Minister has expertise in economics. He knows the impact of taxes. He knows how these things are calculated. He has a background in economics. Perhaps that could compensate for those economic areas where the Minister of Finance is lacking. That might help increase the quality of debate at the Standing Committee on Finance.

We would be remiss in not having the Prime Minister appear before the committee. It is a sound idea. I think the Prime Minister would like that. He is a great communicator. He is someone who has learned over time to communicate, sometimes directly with the public. However, he needs to learn to communicate with parliamentarians, especially since there are legitimate concerns. For instance, the motion refers to debt and government spending.

When the Prime Minister arrived, when he first decided to take that position, the first step was to convince people that this was a new government, but it depends on how one defines a new government. A few seats changed hands, and there are a few new ministers. The truth is that the Trudeau government had been in office for nearly a decade, a decade during which we can all agree that fiscal restraint was not a priority. The Prime Minister therefore decided that there was not much he could do about that. He was in a tough situation. His hands were tied. On top of that, he arrived in the midst of a crisis.

The Prime Minister decided he would cover up the problem by inventing an investment concept that the Parliamentary Budget Officer does not understand and that CPA Canada was unable to explain to us in committee. Despite what the government says, this is not at all in line with what is being done in the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom has a unitary government, whereas here we have health transfers. When Quebec uses a transfer from Ottawa to build a hospital, who does the infrastructure belong to? Does it fall under Quebec's infrastructure plan or is it an investment expenditure by Ottawa? Is it counted twice?
Brushing problems aside or redefining them to sweep them under the rug does not get rid of the dust that is under there. I think that the Prime Minister needs to explain that decision.
Why is the government classifying tax credits as investments, as tax expenditures? That is not done anywhere else in the world.

To my mind, investments normally refer to assets that appear on a balance sheet: concrete, buildings, hospitals. Ottawa owns 2% of all capital, of all public infrastructure in Canada. That 2% comes from the investment advisory council set up by then finance minister Bill Morneau. It was tabled in committee. That means there are no federal investments. The few federal investments that do exist are already accounted for in private sector accounting. Some of our colleagues come from the business world. Airports, which the government is seeking to privatize, along with ports and many Crown corporations, are already accounted for elsewhere. That means they cannot simply be folded into the government's figures through creative accounting.
When a government's response to a problem is to obscure it, redefine it and deny its existence rather than resolve it, I think that raises a number of questions.

As I said, CPA Canada representatives appeared before the committee. This is the organization that people look to for expertise on tax rules and definitions of what constitutes an investment in Canada. When I asked the CPA Canada representatives if they considered this to be an investment, things got pretty awkward. Sometimes, the people who appear before the committee do not want to upset the government, but they did not have an answer. The Minister of Finance does not have an answer. All they can say is that a written response will be provided to the committee.

Now, the motion oversimplifies a few things. Is it true that federal government spending caused inflation? I think the House should know that this is not an entirely accurate interpretation of reality.
Our GDP is below its potential. In other words, we could produce more without creating inflation or inflationary pressure.
Our unemployment rate is above what is known as the “natural” rate. In other words, we could have economic growth and reduce unemployment without creating inflation.

We know very well that, in a situation like this, government spending does not systematically cause inflation. That is taught in school. Decades and decades of empirical research prove it. However, that does not mean that borrowed money does not carry interest. That does not mean that the government should spend money willy-nilly. That does not mean that it should not have fiscal anchors. That does not mean that it has to spend years saying it is keeping an eye on the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Now, all of a sudden, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are blowing through the targets.
When targets are not met, they cannot be redefined. They cannot.

Obviously, the Conservative motion oversimplifies a few things, but the concerns about the stewardship of public funds are not unreasonable. What the Conservatives are essentially asking is why we do not put questions directly to the Prime Minister, who seems to be making all the decisions himself.

It is a bit hard to object to that, especially since the government has decided to forgo certain revenues. The Parliamentary Budget Officer says that we will have to wait and see what the budget says, because certain things could still change. Decisions are going to be made. We will find out next week. Based on the current trajectory, however, the Parliamentary Budget Officer says that the deficit expectations will not be met, that the deficit is going to be bigger and that the resulting additional deficit will add up to roughly the same amount as the tax holiday recently granted by the government. The parliamentary debate on that issue just ended, but the government is giving itself two or three weeks to draft a budget, which we know will very likely pass, barring a major upset. Considering all the toing and froing between the two sides of the House, anything could happen in a week, but nothing is expected to happen.

Anyway, there was the excise tax, and there were also the tax cuts for the rich over the past few years. The government tells us that it cut income tax rates for the middle class. However, while it lowered them for the first and second tax brackets, the wealthiest people, earning $200,000 to $300,000 a year, pay taxes at the marginal tax rate.
I see some puzzled faces.

As members know, we have a marginal tax rate. A wealthy person gets the basic exemption and pays a lower rate in the next tax bracket. In the next tax bracket up, they pay a higher rate. The wealthiest fall into every tax bracket. When the government says it is lowering the second bracket, the people who benefit the most are those who make a great deal of money. There are other mechanisms for redistributing wealth. The government is forgoing revenue without achieving the intended redistributive effect on households. Since we have a budget management problem, it is important to redistribute the money to people who have less. Spending is high, but it is not achieving the goal. We could be doing more with the same amount of money, so it is worth asking the Prime Minister some questions, and even asking the Minister of Finance some questions too, if he is willing to answer. Now that is a challenge. The Minister of Finance is very talented when it comes to sidestepping questions, but I think we deserve some answers on this.

We also deserve answers on oil subsidies. The last time I checked, oil is not subject to tariffs. It is the sector that has received the best treatment from Donald Trump. It seems that Donald Trump is just as passionate about oil as the Prime Minister is. Why has this industry been getting 90% of the government's attention for some time now? I was listening to the member for Whitby speak earlier. Before becoming a parliamentary secretary, the member for Whitby was one of the Liberal caucus' most ardent advocates for combatting global warming. He moved motions about it. He held press conferences with the people who are now suing the government for its inaction on climate change. Someone is paying for these subsidies. The Liberals are counting them as investments. There are people paying for these subsidies. They have an alternative use. If these are indeed investments, there are other types of investments that would be more beneficial for future generations. We deserve some answers about that.

The government tells us that it is going to make 15% cuts to all departments, downsize the public service and speed up attrition. At the same time, it is creating Crown corporations. First, there was an agency for defence contracts. That was under Bill C‑31. The government is now introducing Bill C‑40, saying that it will undo everything that Bill C‑31 did. We do not even know what the right system is anymore. Bill C‑40 is going to undo what Bill C‑31 did and create a Crown corporation whose CEO will earn twice as much as the Minister of Finance. We are wondering why the government is doing this. Are there issues of transparency or issues of conflict of interest? Did the Ethics Commissioner ask about it? We do not know. Why not ask him these questions? The Prime Minister is a smart guy. He is known for his intellect. He is capable of answering our questions.

I would like to get an answer to that, especially since he keeps cutting public service positions while telling us that AI is going to solve the problem at the Canada Revenue Agency, never mind that AI is making 80% of the errors. Then he goes and creates agencies like this one. Are the staff at these agencies counted as part of the public service? These agencies will of course have staff. Do they count? When he says he has been very successful in reducing the number of public servants, will those be real numbers or not? I asked that question in committee, but we did not get an answer, so I think that still warrants hearing from the Prime Minister.

Then there are the provinces' finances. There are public services. We were talking about the cost of living. People want to be able to afford their groceries. They want to be able to go to work. They want to be able to afford daily essentials, but people also get sick and they want to receive health care too. They want decent hospitals. They want infrastructure. Last year, the Minister of Finance met 50% of the provincial premiers' requests for infrastructure funding, and he attached all kinds of conditions to it. Receiving health care is important. People continue to get sick even though the federal government does not run the hospital, and those folks need to be taken care of. The conditions need to be scaled back as well. Transfers come with a bunch of conditions attached.

The Liberals are saying that there are interprovincial barriers and that they should be doing something other than dealing with regulations, red tape, bureaucracy and so on. They are now saying that they are going to make transfers and that there are going to be two million conditional federal-provincial agreements, each of which will take a whole floor of public servants to manage. Is that not the opposite of the approach preferred by the Prime Minister, who has the heart of a Conservative, and by the Conservatives, who, in many ways, have the hearts of new Liberals? Should we not ask questions about that? We should, because the provinces, Quebec and the federal government are interconnected. That is part of the cost of living.

As for seniors, they are now divided into two classes: those aged 65 to 74, and those aged 75 and over who are entitled to more than the others. The long-standing understanding has been that, when people plan for retirement, everyone begins receiving OAS at age 65. By the way, OAS benefits are taxable and subject to the progressive income tax system, as I was explaining to my colleague opposite a few minutes ago. There is therefore an element of fairness and targeting at play. How is it that the government has money for the excise tax but it suddenly does not have the same amount of money to give to Quebec seniors? These are questions that must be answered.

The same can be said of fiscal anchors. When a government is first elected, it promises fiscal discipline, but when its fiscal anchor no longer suits its purposes, it simply changes the anchor. Why? I looked up the definition of “anchor” in the dictionary. It is something that is supposed to be solid, otherwise the ship would run aground. A fiscal anchor is not meant to be changed with every budget.

That is what the Parliamentary Budget Officer lambasted the government for. She says that we need to pay attention to the debt situation overall, not just to the deficit as defined by the Prime Minister. According to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, over the next five years, cumulative deficits are projected to total $333.3 billion, while the debt will increase by $732.9 billion. That is more than double. We need to ask questions about that.

We need to challenge the investment expenditures. Are they really investments? Incidentally, Ottawa does not have an infrastructure plan, unlike the provinces, which follow proper accounting rules. Ottawa tells us that these are investments, but there are no assets backing the liabilities. There is no annual depreciation of those assets. It is all a fiction.

Quebec actually records the money it deposits into the generations fund as an expense. In other words, Quebec sets aside cash in a fund for the benefit of future generations and accounts for it as an expense. Ottawa, on the other hand, records spending as an investment when there is in fact no investment. That raises questions.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer tells us that, in five years' time, by 2031, the debt-to-GDP ratio is going to rise from 40.8% to 42.6%. That is just the federal debt. Canada's public debt includes provincial and municipal debts as well. When the Liberals compare themselves to the G7, they compare Canada's federal debt to the debt levels of unitary states and announce that things are just fine.

On that note, I want to say that the government has had an obsession with the G7 for the past year and a half. The G7 is all it thinks about. G7 countries have high-speed trains, so it wants them too. G7 countries have this, G7 countries have that. It seems to be stuck on the G7, or maybe its G7 key is stuck—I will work on that and ask for a correction to the blues later.

Who is this government comparing itself to? Perhaps it is comparing itself to France. How are things going in France when it comes to the cost of living? How are things in France? Perhaps it is comparing itself to the United States, which is part of the G7. The debt situation in the United States is great. Perhaps it is comparing itself to the United Kingdom. Are things going well in the U.K.? Is that an example to follow? Let us keep looking. It is comparing itself to Japan, where the savings behaviour and public debt ownership are primarily Japanese, and there have been significant problems with public debt and demographics for years. It is comparing itself to Japan.
The Liberals point to the G7 to argue that things are going well in Canada and in Germany.

The questions being asked about the trajectory of public debt in Canada and the questions that the Conservatives want to ask are legitimate. Those questions deserve answers. If the Prime Minister disagrees, he can say so.

In the last minute of speaking time I have left, I would like to return to what our priority should be. A budget is coming, and our priority should be the people who are at risk of losing their jobs today. The government has announced a $9-billion fund for Ontario's steel industry, yet not a single penny has been set aside for Quebec. Where is the fairness in that? There are steel mills in Quebec, but they are not getting a single penny. We need to protect those jobs, too.

The 20% of households that will be hit hardest may find themselves unable to buy school supplies for their children when food prices rise by even half a percentage point. We need to look after these people. We need to increase the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. We need to look after them.
The Liberals know that their suspension of the excise tax is set to expire early next year. They need to prepare for it. They must keep in mind the people I have just spoken about.

If the Prime Minister keeps these people in mind, rather than business leaders, then I am confident he will agree to appear before the committee and work constructively with us and the rest of the opposition.

Madam Speaker, there was so much in that speech that I agreed with and quite a bit in that speech that I did not agree with. I think the main thing I do not agree with is that the Prime Minister has the heart of a Conservative. A Conservative would never run up such ridiculous amounts of debt. There has been more debt added to our national debt load during the terms of former prime minister Trudeau and the current Prime Minister than there was under all of the other prime ministers combined.

In fact, we see now that in a lot of the COVID spending, all the bonds that were sold during that time were short-term bonds, and $600 billion or 29% of our national debt is going to be turned over this year. When the member was mentioning hospitals and the infrastructure needs in Canada, I could not agree more with him. We are now spending more on debt repayment than we do on health care transfers.
Could the hon. member explain a little further how the debt that is crippling us now is actually halting the investment in infrastructure?

Madam Speaker, I did not want to get into a psychoanalysis of who has what kind of heart. What I am saying is that, for a number of years now, the Government of Canada has been maintaining certain fiscal anchors. It said it would increase spending, and by a large amount, considering the billions of dollars involved, but it believed that the debt-to-GDP ratio would decrease or stabilize over time. That means that it is important for the government to control the debt-to-GDP ratio.

Now, in her report, the Parliamentary Budget Officer is telling us that the government is abandoning that fiscal anchor and that the debt-to-GDP ratio is going to increase. Since the government is not following its own rules, it is now saying that it is going to change the rules and the definitions.

Basically, the motion says that we have questions for the Prime Minister. Perhaps he is the right person to answer those questions. Sometimes we cannot ask him those question in the House, for reasons that I am not allowed to mention, so perhaps we need a more relaxed setting, a little more time and a different format to ask the Prime Minister questions. I think that the Standing Committee on Finance would be a very appropriate forum.
That is why we support the motion.
Madam Speaker, our government has introduced a number of affordability measures. At the same time, we have a plan to build projects of national interest to create jobs.
Given the ongoing global crisis, does the Bloc Québécois not think that this is justified?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my colleague very much. We have worked together in the past and are likely to continue to do so. However, why does the Prime Minister not come and discuss this with us in committee?
