Our national food security strategy will allow us to help independent grocers buy and transport products at competitive prices without relying on the big grocery chains. We need to make it easier for independent grocers to access supply chains through various programs, increase competition in the sector and improve grocery prices for consumers.

Thanks to the national strategy, we will also be providing nearly $130 million to the Competition Bureau and the Competition Tribunal to investigate, prevent and counter anti-competitive business practices.
Rules are in place, but we must have the means to enforce them.
Finally, we need to reduce red tape. In fact, a bill has already been introduced to this end, because red tape can have an impact on production costs.

Strengthening the Canadian economy and supporting Canadians also requires strategic investment in our infrastructure. These investments must be made in partnership not only with the provinces, but also with municipalities. At the end of the day, there is only one taxpayer, and it is that taxpayer who ultimately foots the bill. When we invest alongside local governments in infrastructure projects that are essential to our communities, we help place those municipalities on a sounder financial footing. If the federal government does not contribute to major infrastructure projects, local governments may have no choice but to adjust their tax rates, and this will be reflected in our constituents' property tax bills.
That is why I think it is important for the federal government to be involved when there are plans to upgrade water and sewer systems to increase housing capacity in our communities, for example.

Last summer, I was involved in making three announcements where the federal government, the provincial government and the municipalities made joint investments in water and sewer infrastructure projects, not only because these systems were aging but also to increase housing capacity in the areas where the work is being done. If we want to grow our communities and increase our housing stock, we must ensure that we have the proper water and sewer infrastructure in place to support that growth. I am thinking about the announcement that I made last June in Campbellton, alongside the late Mayor Soucy, regarding the upgrades to infrastructure on Notre Dame Street in the Atholville area. I also made an announcement in Grand Falls about the relocation and replacement of older sanitary sewer infrastructure on Taylor Street, Park Street and O'Regan Street. In addition to supporting residential development in this area, this project will also address critical environmental challenges because the Saint John River is nearby and we could see that a manhole was on the verge of collapse. This could have led to a serious environmental incident in Grand Falls.
Through these investments, we are not only supporting the construction of more housing but also addressing an environmental imperative.

My last example is the announcement of more than $1 million that we made in Edmundston to extend water and sewer lines to service a residential project on Laboissonnière Avenue, des Mélèzes Street, and Mgr Lacroix Avenue.
These are tangible ways that we can help our communities and all citizens who benefit from these projects.

As for the cost of living, we know that the price of electricity is also a major concern for Canadians. We know that the heating method used can have a significant impact on electricity bills. That is why we recently announced the launch of the national heat pump rebate program to help up to 820,000 households across the country switch to more efficient electric heat pumps. Our goal is to increase the number of homes that are more energy efficient in order to reduce electricity consumption and save people money every month. Heat pump systems have several advantages over traditional heating systems. They are more energy efficient, lowering energy costs for consumers. They also combine heating and cooling within the same system for year-round comfort, in the summer with air conditioning and in the winter with heating. What is more, it helps us meet our greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets. Under this program, households with below-median incomes will get up to $10,000, and other households will get up to $2,000. This is another concrete measure put in place to help people cope with the cost of living and also to meet our environmental objectives.

As for the cost of living, I think it is also important to mention our affordable child care program, which we launched in 2021. The results speak for themselves. The statistics show that the labour force participation rate of young parents, particularly young mothers, has increased since this program was launched. Child care spaces have been created and made available to families in multiple communities across Canada, and we continue to work with provinces and territories to strengthen the early learning and child care system across Canada for the long term.

Huge progress has been made over the past five years, but we know that the needs are great and that there is still a need for more affordable child care in our communities. There are still waiting lists. There is more work to be done, but when we look at the progress made over the past five years in expanding access to affordable child care in Canada, we see that great strides have been made. In fact, last June, an announcement of up to $5.4 billion over two years was announced. This is in addition to the more than $58 billion in funding that has already been allocated to this program since 2021 under the current extension agreements with the provinces and territories. This is another example of a concrete investment that has an impact on the cost of living, on Canadian families and on their ability to fully participate in the labour market.

I will conclude by saying that addressing the cost of living and strengthening the Canadian economy so that it works for everyone requires concrete measures and action, not just empty rhetoric. The official opposition's rhetoric is always followed by votes against every measure we put in place.
On this side of the aisle, we take the issues seriously, take action, and implement concrete measures.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, public debt charges are the fastest-growing major expense and have already surpassed Canada health transfer payments. That means Canadians are paying more to service debt than they receive for health care.
Can my hon. colleague think of a few ways the Liberal government could improve the amount of debt? Could it cut back on its spending so that Canadians can live more affordably?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are managing our fiscal situation meticulously. We have undertaken a review of government spending across the various departments. We are ensuring that public finances are managed effectively. The goal is to have sufficient fiscal flexibility to be able to meet the needs of Canadians. When we implement various measures to strengthen and stimulate the Canadian economy, the idea is to have a thriving economy that allows us to fund the various social services that help Canadians cope with the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, I know that my colleague defends French and culture, and we all agree that debt servicing costs are huge. In this context, we find it hard to understand why the government is forgoing considerable revenue by eliminating, for example, the digital services tax on American tech giants, which are a threat to our culture and our media. Furthermore, the government refused to allow the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission to collect levies from these same tech giants, which would have brought in considerable revenue for culture. Instead, it dipped into people's taxes to try to compensate for the cancellation of the levies.
What does my colleague say to that?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my colleague alluded to the official languages in the preamble to his question. It gives me an opportunity to remind the House of the Liberal government's historic investment in the official languages. The action plan for official languages 2023-2028 invests $4.1 billion in supporting the official languages and the vitality of francophone minority communities. Even taking inflation into account, this is the largest investment in the official languages in the history of Canada.

It lets us support French-language education in our communities, take measures to support health, access to justice and employment services, and document our realities better through Statistics Canada data. In all, over a dozen federal organizations are involved in implementing the action plan for official languages, which is generating tangible benefits across Canada. I know what I am talking about, because I represent Madawaska—Restigouche, one of the ridings with the highest concentrations of francophones outside Quebec. These investments in the official languages are vital to my region.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his excellent speech.
One of the issues in my riding has been children coming to school without having breakfast or something to eat. I know the government has been doing some work on this.
I am wondering if the member would be able to explain more about how we have been helping families through food at school.
Mr. Speaker, I share my colleague's concern. No child should ever have to spend a day in the classroom with an empty stomach. It is not conducive to learning.

As a government, we have taken this issue seriously. We established Canada's national school food program, and given the program's success and importance, we made it permanent. For example, in my province of New Brunswick, this translates into an agreement valued at $11.3 million over three years. This investment is making the free breakfast program available in all schools across the province of New Brunswick. In addition, the government is supporting the launch of a pay-what-you-can lunch program administered by our provincial partners. This is a good example of a concrete measure that allows us to support children and families, while helping to create a healthy learning environment that meets their needs.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kody Blois (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure, as always, to rise in the House on behalf of my constituents in Kings—Hants, but also in my role as Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, to take part in the debate on the Conservative opposition day motion moved today concerning Canada's fiscal situation.

I would like to raise a few important points for the benefit of Canadians who may be watching at home today and following the debates in the House of Commons in order to better understand the overall situation. In my view and in the government's view, the wording of the motion moved today by the Conservatives is problematic because it fails to take some crucial context into account, including Canada's fiscal position in general.

I am going to start by going to the first point in the text of the motion. The Conservatives assert that “the cost of government is driving up the cost of living.” I would reject the premise of that. The text of the motion fails to take into consideration the fact that the government has a comprehensive expenditure review, and the government will be reducing government expenditures by $80 billion over the next five years. Part of that includes downsizing the number of staff of the Government of Canada, the federal government, and targets have already been met in that domain.

The motion fails to recognize that global events are having an impact on the cost of living for all countries, not just Canada. There is a blockade at the Strait of Hormuz, which is impacting global energy prices, and that is being felt globally. That is, of course, being felt by Canadians because it is a domestic challenge we are facing, but it is being felt by countries around the world. There is also a war in eastern Europe, in Ukraine, and while we have been a steadfast ally in supporting Ukraine, the implications on food security and energy security are felt globally.

We are in a global trading environment, but our government has focused on controlling what we can here at home. The Conservative text of the motion today fails to understand the work that the government is doing to reduce operational costs. The text of the motion does not take into consideration the government's promise to balance the operating spending of the government by fiscal year 2028-29. That is important.

I am a proud Nova Scotian. I get to see the work of rebuilding the Royal Canadian Navy in Halifax, in my home province, where we are making generational investments that started under a previous government but have continued. We have also reinvested in the River-class destroyer. Those are long-term investments that I hope all members of this House understand are important for protecting our sovereignty and providing for the women and men of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Our goal as a government is to make sure that the expenditures the government takes on are part of the long-term industrial capacity and long-term economic growth of the country, and that we have a true balance in the types of operational spending the government is going to be taking on. The Conservatives ran on a platform in the last election that included approximately $130 billion of new spending. My hon. colleagues across the way can appreciate that it feels somewhat facetious to raise this type of measure when the platform promises of the Conservatives, had they been in government, would have led them to spend $130 billion above and beyond expenditures at the time. That is an important piece.

Let us talk about Canada's fiscal position. Governments are different from household finances, but let us think about the average Canadian. My wife and I, when we were able to buy a home, did not have the money to outright buy a home. We had to get a mortgage from a bank. We had to take on debt to build a future, raise a family and live in our community. Governments are no different. Governments have to look at the borrowing costs of making longer-term investments versus the sustainability of taking on the debt obligation to drive longer-term outcomes.

Nowhere in the Conservative motion today does it highlight that Canada has the best fiscal position and net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. Canadians need to understand that Canada's overall debt, as a relative size, is proportionate to the economy. We are four times the factor in the better than Germany. On the net debt-to-GDP ratio, our fiscal position is nine times better than the United States's. We also have the second-lowest deficit in the G7.

This is at a time when the government is cutting in certain areas and making tough choices, while at the same time making massive investments in energy, critical minerals, defence and the things that we believe are important long-term for the Canadian economy and our sovereignty. Nowhere in the opposition day motion does it highlight that to Canadians. It is the prerogative of His Majesty's loyal opposition to choose how these texts are developed, but nowhere does it recognize that that is the case.

The one area where I would agree with the Conservative position is that we have to remain vigilant. Bond rate increases are happening around the world. If we look at what is happening in France right now, its government bond yields are continuing to go up, which means the cost for the government to borrow is going higher and higher. That is now starting to be priced into the market. Our Prime Minister and this government understand that we need to maintain Canada's fiscal position. That is exactly what we are doing in the face of global market uncertainty, particularly around financing.
Today's motion is also about affordability. The wording of the motion moved by the Conservatives links government spending with affordability and the cost of living in general.

It is unfortunate that the Conservatives fail to mention the affordability measures that our government has introduced. For example, the national child care program is a concrete measure that is intended to help educate our young people, but it is also intended to make life more affordable for parents. We are working with the provinces and territories.

As my hon. colleague from Cumberland—Colchester mentioned earlier, there are school programs in place across the country. Through Canada's national school food program, we are ensuring that 400,000 students across the country have the opportunity to eat breakfast or lunch made with food from local farms.
There is also the Canada child benefit. In my riding, that benefit offers families nearly $17 million to help them provide for their children. The amount is calculated based on household income.
Those are concrete measures that the government gas put forward.

I also mentioned the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. That is why the government proposed eliminating the federal excise tax on gasoline and diesel. This is important. This measure is not there to guarantee that everything goes smoothly, but the government is using this concrete measure to give farmers, businesses and the general public a helping hand.

I really look forward to the debate. I did not have the opportunity to be on my feet this morning. I look forward to hearing from my colleagues about how the Conservative position seems to not reconcile the fact that Canada is in a strong fiscal position. I have no problem with His Majesty's loyal opposition highlighting that the government needs to remain diligent and needs to be thoughtful about its approach in the days ahead, but the text of the motion was presented to the House today without presenting any of the key statistics that actually outline Canada's fiscal position. It is difficult, certainly, for a government, and, I would say, many members of Parliament, to be able to vote without those key statistics that provide Canadians a better overall picture of where we are at.

The ability to talk about the fact that the debt servicing costs of governments across the world are rising because of bond rates and that governments need to be fiscally responsible and thoughtful, balancing operations and balancing budgets, while at the same time making long-term investments, is all fair game, but that level of nuance is something that I have rarely seen from the Conservative Party in my seven years, even though I have great friends across the way and there are some thoughtful colleagues, for sure. I would like to see the party in general try to find the types of texts that we could vote on and that, I think, are a little bit more balanced in terms of how they move forward.

Mr. Speaker, the member said that the motion was short on text, but the motion referenced the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report, which is full of data and statistics. I bring to his attention page 3, which reads:

Quote.QuotePara: Public debt charges are the fastest-growing expense. They are projected to more than double from $24.5 billion in 2021‑22 to $59.3 billion in 2026‑27.

Content.ParaText: I will let him reflect on that and maybe check through the report for some of the other data there. He spoke about households and talked about buying a house and getting a mortgage. I was in the mortgage business for 22 years. The government's household analogy would be more like buying a house and then going back to the bank every year to refinance the house and borrow continually against the house. Sooner or later one hits a wall. Sooner or later the debt becomes unsustainable.
Is he concerned about the Parliamentary Budget Officer's warnings about sustainability?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, with regard to the household analogy, what that member fails to recognize is that if he is concerned about the overall debt as a proportion of the size of our house, he should take a look across the street and in the neighbourhood and realize that, actually, we are in one of the best positions. That does not mean that we still do not have work to do, but nowhere in his public commentary that I have heard in the House today does he recognize that Canada actually has the strongest fiscal position within the G7.

If he would like to highlight that we should take that barometer out wider and look at the G20 or other comparable countries, I think that is a fair question to raise, but when he talks about debt servicing charges going from $24 billion to over $50 billion, what he is failing to recognize is that the size of the economy also grew at the same time. When we deal in nominal numbers, it can feel like a very big number to the average Canadian. Again, I am not trying to shed the responsibility. The government has to be careful and thoughtful on this question.
In the context of his framing, he does not highlight the fact that the overall economy has grown to such a size that Canada's fiscal position remains sustainable.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative opposition day motion is not one I could vote for, but I do sense a reason for asking the Prime Minister to come up for a committee.

It is very hard to have the level of response and accountability from the current Prime Minister that we got from Justin Trudeau. Prime Minister Trudeau tried to create a tradition of Wednesday questions, where he would answer every question that came up through a Wednesday question period. I think he was trying to create a tradition that maybe the next the Prime Minister would continue.

Does the hon. member for Kings—Hants think there is a way that is less confrontational and partisan than what we have before us today to encourage the Prime Minister to be more available and accountable to other members of Parliament?

Mr. Speaker, I actually did not have the chance in my remarks to address that particular point. I mean, it has not happened often that a sitting Prime Minister is going to sit in front of a parliamentary committee. My hon. learned colleague knows that that is quite rare in circumstance.

We have a very talented team of government ministers, including the Minister of Finance. Obviously the Prime Minister is the one who is ultimately responsible as the first amongst equals within the cabinet. At the same time, we have a competent bench that can respond to these questions. The hon. member has time every single day the House of Commons sits to ask these questions of the government.

I would differ as to whether or not it is the Prime Minister that has to be before a committee. Hopefully, today, that hon. member will get a chance to ask some of these questions to the Minister of Finance when she has her turn in this place during question period. That is accountability every single day that we look forward to.
Mr. Speaker, in the same vein, Bill C-5 and Bill C-39 are concentrating power in the PMO, which can declare that an oil project is in the national interest and which makes all the decisions.
It seems like the Minister of Finance is merely a mouthpiece for the Prime Minister. That is why people would like to speak with him directly in committee.
What does my colleague think of that?

Mr. Speaker, again, the ministers responsible for Bill C-5 or Bill C-39 are the Minister of Transport and the Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs and One Canadian Economy. They are fully capable of responding to the Bloc Québécois and other members of Parliament.

We believe we have a system of accountability both here in the House of Commons and outside it, with the media and with our constituents when we go door to door. We have a system of accountability here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Barrie South—Innisfil.

Today, the opposition moves that the House call on the Prime Minister to appear as a witness at the finance committee. For 11 years, the cost of government has driven up the cost of living. The result of these accumulated deficits is that interest on the national debt is the fastest-growing cost of the government. The Liberals now spend more on debt than they do on the Canada health transfer. This works out to $6,000 in federal taxes per Canadian family of four. The Prime Minister promised that he would reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio and the deficit-to-GDP ratio, but the Liberal government has broken every fiscal promise, has jettisoned every fiscal anchor and has smashed through every fiscal guardrail that it has ever set for itself. In the wake of a truly horrific Parliamentary Budget Officer's report, it is time for the Prime Minister to explain himself at the finance committee.

It is worth remembering how we got here. In 2015, on page 12 of their campaign document entitled “Real Change: A New Plan for a Strong Middle Class”, the Liberals promised modest short-term deficits of less than $10 billion in each of the next two fiscal years. They immediately broke that promise when they tabled a $30-billion deficit in 2016 and another $30-billion deficit the next year. They acted like they had never promised maximum modest short-term deficits and a return to balance by 2019. That is a return because that is where they started from. They said not to worry because they had a fiscal anchor. They promised, “a low and consistently declining debt-to-GDP ratio”.

They made that promise in 2015 and again in the 2016 budget, when Bill Morneau actually said, “our interest rates have never been lower, so we can borrow on excellent terms”. Never mind that he was breaking a campaign promise from only a few months earlier, never mind that the deficits would only get worse, never mind that without a plan to ever return to balance, they might eventually have to refinance their debt at higher rates and never mind that despite Justin Trudeau's claim, budgets do not ever just balance themselves.

They cut loose this first fiscal anchor in the fall 2018 economic statement when their debt-to-GDP ratio jumped up. Then in 2019, they again promised to reduce debt as a function of our economy “each and every year”, and they failed to keep that promise, too, because even before the pandemic began in March 2020, the Liberals were already on track to break that promise. They had already baked in a structural deficit and added $100 billion to the national debt before COVID without any COVID spending. After the pandemic, they went back to claiming that a declining debt-to-GDP ratio was their fiscal anchor, “a line we shall not cross, and that will ensure that our finances remain sustainable so long as it remains unbreached.” So said Chrystia Freeland in 2022.

Of course, they breached it again. They breached it in the very next budget in 2023 and again in 2024. By late 2024, the finance minister resigned rather than table a fall economic statement that blew through her own promise, breaking projections that she had made just six months earlier regarding new spending. Then the new Prime Minister arrived. Their 2025 platform again promised declining debt to GDP “over the budget horizon”, but right after he won the election and ran on that promise, he ignored it and came back with a new plan. He resorted to accounting trickery, a promise to balance the operating budget and to do so by 2028-29.

He promised a declining deficit to GDP, but their spring economic statement earlier this year already projects that the debt-to-GDP ratio will continue to rise and will not decline until 2029, at which time it will still be higher than it was in that 2024 fall economic statement that precipitated the resignations of both Freeland and Trudeau. We have seen that for 11 years, the government has broken every fiscal promise, smashed through every fiscal guardrail and repeatedly cut loose every fiscal anchor, which brings us to this month's Parliamentary Budget Officer's report, the “Economic and Fiscal Outlook”.

According to the PBO, “The federal debt-to-GDP ratio...is projected to rise each year...[through] 2030-31.” So much for the line they shall not cross. So much for their finances remaining sustainable so long as that line goes unbreached. So much for another fiscal anchor cut loose and sunk to the bottom of the ocean.

The PBO projects that “the Government will not meet its second [fiscal] anchor of...a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio”. Anchors away. The report goes on to say that “the two fiscal anchors have imposed limited fiscal discipline on government spending and borrowing.”
It continues:

Quote.QuotePara: Public debt charges are the fastest-growing expense. They are projected to more than double from $24.5 billion in 2021-22 to $59.3 billion in 2026-27 and are projected to reach $83.0 billion by 2030-31....
On a per capita basis, public debt charges [climbed] from $640 in 2021-22 to $1,419 in 2026-27 and are projected to reach $1,952 in 2030-31....

Content.ParaText: This is a terrible report. The short-term outlook, though, for the balance of this year actually reflects higher than projected revenues, but the higher revenues are because of world oil prices, not increasing economic output. In fact, the higher revenue comes “Despite weaker real economic activity”. The government receives higher revenues, and consumers face higher prices. A brief sugar high of unexpectedly higher revenue will not pay down the national debt, and it is not going to anchor the government's finances.

The rapidly rising cost of debt service on the national debt is entirely due to accumulating deficits. It is not from higher than projected interest rates, but the possibility of higher interest rates in the years to come has been identified by the PBO as an emerging risk to Canada's fiscal health. The report states, “Public debt charges are now...twice as sensitive to higher interest rates as in pre-pandemic outlooks, mainly because the Government carries a larger stock of interest-bearing debt.”

We must remember, this is the government that was willing to pile on debt long before COVID and continues to do so long after, and these are the same Liberals who said back in 2016 that low interest rates meant it was safe to run deficits. Now we are twice as vulnerable to factors beyond our control because interest is now the fastest-growing government expense. We now spend more on interest than we do on national defence. We now spend more on interest than we do on the health transfer. It is now over 13% of the federal budget and rapidly rising.

The per capita interest cost is rising faster than per capita income. An average family is already paying nearly $6,000 in taxes just for interest on the national debt, and the number is going to grow quickly in the next four years. Canadians cannot afford to pay more taxes in order to pay more interest, and this government continues to rack up debt. Canadians are not getting ahead. Their incomes are not keeping pace with inflation. They are already highly taxed, and the portion of their taxes that is going straight to bondholders is increasing.

As for the portion of Canadian taxes that goes to interest, the government's options narrow. The room to lower taxes, increase services, increase defence capability or pay down debt is more and more limited. That is why Conservatives want the finance minister to come to the finance committee and testify on saving Canadians money by cutting spending, debt interest and taxes. It is time for the Prime Minister to take responsibility for his broken promises and his government's failed approach to budgeting.

This government inherited a balanced budget. The Liberals inherited a rapidly declining per capita interest expense. It is right there in the report. They inherited what The New York Times called the world's most prosperous middle class. They had every advantage that a new government could possibly ask for back in 2015, and they blew it.

This PBO report should be a wake-up call to the government. It is time for the Prime Minister to admit that up until now, the Liberals' fiscal anchors and campaign promises were not kept. Some say it is never too late to do the right thing. I would hope that the Prime Minister may actually welcome the opportunity to attend the finance committee. He can apologize to Canadians for his broken promises, and he can still reverse course and save Canadians money.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will go to the facts. Out of the G7, only Germany and Canada have the AAA credit rating. The difference between us and the Conservatives is that we understand and appreciate the value of investing in Canada, in Canadians, to build a stronger and healthier economy.

Just moments ago, I was talking with members from CentrePort in Winnipeg. CentrePort is going to be one of the driving forces of Manitoba's economy. By doing that, it will make a difference, with both private and public investment growing job opportunities. That is not unique to the northwest area of Winnipeg. It is happening in every region of Canada.
Why does the Conservative Party oppose government and private sector investment?

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure where the member was really heading to there. I know he is impervious to shame. This member ran on a platform way back in 2015. The Liberals do not care that they do not keep their promises. The government that he speaks for breaches every fiscal anchor it lays down for itself, and this member does not care.
Mr. Speaker, one of the factors making the deficit so big is the billions of dollars in subsidies that have been handed out to oil companies.
Does my colleague think that this type of subsidy should continue?

Mr. Speaker, Bloc members always raise this. I think they are quite confused about what a subsidy is. The government, for all of its misgivings and all of the terrible policy that it has, is not squandering Canadian tax dollars on subsidizing oil and gas, other than its failed and failing approach to project development. It took a pipeline like Trans Mountain that would have been built by private investors, chased the private investment out of the country, and built it at the public expense at about a 500% cost overrun. I do oppose that style of policy-making.
The problem with this government is that its entire approach to industrial policy is to cherry-pick projects and use the power of public money behind construction.

Mr. Speaker, to pick up on what the member just said, TMX would not have happened had the government not been directly engaged in building that pipeline. I can understand why Conservatives are confused, because the Conservative Party, while in government, did not even build an inch of pipeline to to the west coast. It took a Liberal administration to do that, just like it has taken a Liberal administration to have LNG and this particular Prime Minister for LNG phase two to be among the numerous major projects in progress today in every region of our country.
Will the member now recognize the value of a proactive government working in collaboration with provinces to build projects?

Mr. Speaker, it is always entertaining to listen to the Liberals talk about something they broke and then demand extraordinary recognition for their attempts to put things back together. They chased Kinder Morgan out of Canada. They chased it out by moving the goalposts and refusing to champion the approvals that existed and then afterwards want enormous credit for nationalizing that project although they had forced the proponent out.

Mr. Speaker, in Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith, there is a famous scene where Obi-Wan Kenobi is on the high ground and Anakin Skywalker, who eventually becomes Darth Vader, is getting burned. In that scene, Obi-Wan says to Anakin, “You were the chosen one.” He says, “You were supposed to bring balance to the Force. You were not supposed to join the Sith. You were supposed to defeat them.” Well, in April 2025, the Prime Minister billed himself as the chosen one. He was supposed to bring balance to our fiscal force. He was going to spend less, and things were going to improve. Things have done anything but improve in this country. In fact, I would suggest that they have gotten a lot worse under the Prime Minister in terms of fiscal mismanagement.

We have had two PBOs, the previous one and this one, who have sounded the alarm on the state of the country's fiscal finances, and the most recent report should cause anyone to pause. For anyone who has kids, anyone who has grandchildren or great-grandchildren, it should cause great concern about the direction this country is heading in terms of fiscal mismanagement. Frankly, what concerns me, not just as a parliamentarian but as a father, is that my kids will be picking up the scattered pieces of what is left economically in this country after the Prime Minister and the Liberal government are done with it.

The alarm was sounded by the latest Parliamentary Budget Officer. Members will recall that the Liberals were not happy with some of the things the previous Parliamentary Budget Officer was reporting to Canadians. He referred to the state of our finances as “stupefying”. The current Parliamentary Budget Officer has picked up where the previous one left off and has raised the alarms in a great way in this country. The latest fiscal update from the Parliamentary Budget Officer goes like this. The interest on the debt this year is going to be $59.3 billion, which is more than we send to the provinces for health care transfers.

She went on to say that by 2030-31, the interest on the debt is going to be $83 billion. This means that an average family of four in this country is going to be paying $6,000 on the debt this year, and that is going to rise to $8,000. This is money that could be put in people's pockets. It could be put toward the health of their children through sports programs or better nutrition. We are seeing food banks in this country reporting that millions and millions of people a month are going to the food bank. Many of them are working-class Canadians who cannot afford the necessities of life anymore.

It is not just the deficit that is a problem. Cumulatively, over the next five years, the Parliamentary Budget Officer has said, the level of debt is expected to increase by $732.9 billion. That is $732.9 billion added to the already existing debt. The only ones who make money off this are the bondholders and the bankers. With the interest that is paid on that debt, and in some of the examples I gave earlier, this is just what those numbers are going to look like.

This motion calls on the Prime Minister to not stand in the House for 35-second questions when he is here. It calls on the Prime Minister to stand before a parliamentary committee and answer questions about the state of the finances in this country, which has been created by government spending and by programs that have gone to well-connected insiders, and to answer questions about Alto, questions about foreign aid and questions about why Canadians are in such bad shape when he said and made a promise to them in April 2025 that he was going to make things better.

These are very simple questions that need to be asked, not in 35-second sound bites in this place, but before a parliamentary committee so we can have a fulsome discussion about the state of finances in this country for Canadians to be made aware, truthfully and honestly, of the state of their finances and what it means to the future of this country and the future of their kids and grandkids, who, like I said earlier, are going to be picking up the scattered pieces of what is left of this country after these Liberals are done with it financially.

There is a budget coming up November 5, and it is curious to me why it is being presented on a Thursday afternoon. I have been here 11 years, and I have never seen a budget presented on a Thursday afternoon. Typically, budgets take place on Tuesday afternoon. There is then a full opportunity for opposition members to call into question some of the issues related to the budget, but this is happening on November 5 of this year, a Thursday afternoon. This means that Friday, which is generally a reduced session, will be the only period we have to ask questions about the budget, and then we are back in our ridings for the week of Remembrance Day.

I think the purpose of this is that Canadians and parliamentarians may actually forget about what is in the budget. I also think the government is fearful about what it is going to report in this budget, and that is why it is being introduced on a Thursday afternoon. This is equal to government news coming out on a Friday afternoon when it does not want anybody to pay attention to it. That is concerning in and of itself.

When we talk about accountability and transparency, we talk about the Prime Minister coming to committee to answer these questions. We know he is not willing to answer the questions here. Otherwise, the government would not be introducing a budget on a Thursday afternoon when members of Parliament will be back in their ridings the next week for Remembrance Day. At a minimum, because he said that he was going to make things better for Canadians, the Prime Minister needs to come to committee to answer those questions.

As I said earlier, what these numbers mean is that the average family of four is going to be paying roughly $6,000 a year in interest on that debt. This is just absurd at a time when Canadians are struggling and dealing with food insecurity and housing affordability. They are dealing with issues of anxiety and stress. There is not a day that goes by, and I am sure there are other members of Parliament on all sides who are dealing with this too, when we are not walking somebody in off the ledge who is dealing with these issues of affordability.

In 2015, Canada had the wealthiest middle class in the world, and now we have 2.3 million people a month, and in many cases, these are working-class people, who are visiting food banks in this country. Food banks are reporting that their shelves are bare now because of the demand that has been happening. We have seniors in grocery stores putting items back on the shelf because they cannot afford them.

This is not a normal state for a G7 country. The Prime Minister said that he was going to fix it, and he has done anything but. In fact, I would suggest that he has made this situation much worse with the lack of control in spending, the debt and the deficits. It is disturbing. It is disturbing for my kids. It is disturbing for all of our kids and grandkids. They are the ones who are going to pay the price for this.

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to congratulate the mayor-elect, Alvin Tedjo, as our new mayor of Mississauga. He is a person of conviction and one whom I look forward to working with. The people of Mississauga made the issues very clear: affordability, safety and jobs. I look forward to working with our new mayor and our collective councillors to ensure that we deliver for the people of Mississauga.

These issues affect our safety and our entire community, and they must be addressed through consensus and through collaboration between everybody who has stood up and raised their hand to run and to serve in our community, so I want to thank everybody in our Mississauga community for coming together and for ensuring that Mississauga continues to be Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, they say, “You meet the nicest people [in] a Honda.” As the MP for York—South Simcoe, the proud home of Honda Canada, I can say that the people who build Hondas are every bit as nice too.

Next week, Honda celebrates 40 years of continuous car-making excellence in Canada since its plant first opened in Alliston, Ontario, on November 3, 1986. Today, it produces the Honda Civic, the Canadian car of the year. More than 4,000 Canadians work there, and it supports 30,000 more jobs across the sector. From the associates on the line to the suppliers and dealers who put Canadians behind the wheel, every one of them has helped build this legacy. Canadian manufacturing succeeds when we stand behind it.
To everyone at Honda, I wish a happy 40th and all the best, as it keeps the power of dreams driving themselves forward.

Mr. Speaker, earlier this spring, Doctors of BC recognized the recipients of its annual awards, celebrating physicians whose leadership, service and dedication continue to strengthen health care across British Columbia.

Among this year's honorees was Dr. Gulzar Cheema, who received the Silver Medal of Service. For over 40 years, Dr. Cheema has made exceptional contributions to medicine and public service as a physician, educator and former MLA in both Manitoba and British Columbia. In 2001, Dr. Cheema was appointed British Columbia's first minister of state for mental health, a landmark role that brought cabinet-level leadership and advocacy to mental health and wellness more than 25 years ago.

Doctors of BC also recognized outstanding physicians including Dr. Charlotte Yong-Hing, Dr. Edith Blondel-Hill, Dr. Steven Goodchild and Dr. Eric Yoshida, whose work continues to make a meaningful difference in communities across the province.
I congratulate all this year's recipients on this well-deserved recognition.

Mr. Speaker, on June 2, 1866, nine Canadians were killed at the Battle of Ridgeway. It was Canada's first battle fought on Canadian soil using Canadian troops with Canadian officers. Ultimately, 32 young Canadians died. Most were barely out of adolescence. Many people argue that this battle against Fenian raiders who crossed from the United States intensified discussions leading to Confederation. We may not have been standing here in the chamber today were it not for the sacrifice of these men who died on Lime Ridge in my riding of Niagara South along the shores of Lake Erie.

After 160 years, it is time to finally recognize the sacrifice of these men, who defended Canada on Canadian soil, in Parliament's Books of Remembrance, just a few short steps from the chamber. I call on the government to add the names of those who perished on Lime Ridge 160 years ago, recognize that sacrifice and show their names to future generations through respect by a grateful nation.
Mr. Speaker, today I want to highlight the work of the Brigade de propreté, a cleanup crew in Trois-Rivières.

Every day, this cleanup crew helps make our city cleaner and more welcoming. This wonderful initiative is the result of a partnership between Point de rue, an organization that works with people experiencing homelessness, and the Société de développement commercial du centre-ville de Trois‑Rivières, or SDC, which, incidentally, is celebrating its 35th anniversary this year.
This initiative goes far beyond maintaining our public spaces. It also supports people who want to get their lives back on track, by helping them return to the workforce and regain their confidence.
I want to congratulate Karine Trahan, from Point de rue, and Ève‑Marie Marchand, from the SDC, for their commitment to establishing this cleanup crew.
I want to congratulate the entire cleanup crew and thank them for contributing every day to keeping Trois‑Rivières clean and making our community proud.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, October 16, in Miramichi, we honoured the retirement of Court of King's Bench Justice Fred Ferguson, KC. Although born in Dalhousie, he has long been regarded as one of our own.

After law school, he worked as a Crown prosecutor for three decades alongside colleagues Jack Walsh and Bill Morrissey. He prosecuted some of the most serious and widely noted criminal cases in the country. Appointed to the provincial court in 2003 and elevated to the King's Bench in 2008, he is widely respected across Canada for his unmatched knowledge of the criminal law. He earned a reputation for being approachable by young lawyers and by all those who appeared before him. Colourful and courageous, and sometimes called “the oracle”, he is a devoted husband to Debbie and a proud father to Adam and Jess.
I ask the House to extend its best wishes to Justice Fred Ferguson on a distinguished career and a well-deserved retirement.

Mr. Speaker, Ottawa voted last night, and today I rise on behalf of my Ottawa MP colleagues to congratulate Mayor Mark Sutcliffe and all the city councillors who were elected yesterday. Special congratulations go to the three new councillors joining the table: Erin Coffin, Joanne Chianello and Chelsea Walton.

Ottawa made history last night because, for the first time, women will outnumber men around the table. That is a milestone worth celebrating, and one that reflects the strong women who lead and build communities in our city.
We look forward to working with Mayor Sutcliffe and the council to tackle the challenges ahead and to continue to build a strong and vibrant national capital. I congratulate all. Let us get to work.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the House and Canadians about Bob Gibson, who is a retired air force pilot. He and his wife, Charmaine, are on Parliament Hill today. Their son followed in his dad's footsteps and is also a pilot in the air force.

Something members might not know is that members of the Canadian Armed Forces are more likely to be diagnosed with ALS. Unfortunately, Bob has an ALS diagnosis and is worried that his son, who followed in his footsteps of serving the country, may also face the same diagnosis.

The ALS community is calling for a $50-million investment from the Government of Canada, and I support its request. The funding would open clinical trials, help researchers understand the disease and explore the link between military service and ALS. We know that time counts. Members of the House will remember our late hon. colleague Mauril Bélanger, who had nine months from diagnosis to his passing.
We can do more than offer hope and best wishes to people living with ALS and to those who serve our country. We can help fund research and hope.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to Jean‑Eudes Senneville, who passed away on October 4 at the age of 86.

A disciplined businessman and visionary, Mr. Senneville was a true pioneer of the wild blueberry industry in my riding of Lac‑Saint‑Jean. He was a community builder who helped shape the blueberry economy for more than half a century, but his legacy extends far beyond his company.

In 1979, he opened his first freezing plant, which became the cornerstone of Quebec Wild Blueberries. Nearly 50 years later, four state-of-the-art processing plants are helping our wild blueberries reach markets far away from our region.
Although his forthright manner occasionally ruffled a few feathers, he forged lasting partnerships and left an indelible mark on the blueberry industry.
Mr. Senneville's influence on Lac‑Saint‑Jean and Quebec will continue to be felt for years to come. To his family and loved ones, we offer our most sincere condolences.

Mr. Speaker, as Women's History Month comes to a close, I rise to honour Lynda Kosowan, a true trailblazer of our community, who recently retired after 40 remarkable years of leading the Scarborough Women's Centre. Under her leadership, the centre has supported more than 175,000 women and their children. Through professional counselling, mentoring and workshops, the centre has helped women move away from abuse, poverty and isolation toward independence. Thanks to Lynda's leadership, no woman who walked through the centre's doors had to face her challenges alone.
On behalf of Scarborough Southwest, I want to thank Lynda for her extraordinary service and wish her a joyful and well-earned retirement.

Mr. Speaker, Les Cuisiniers différents is a noteworthy organization doing remarkable work in Longueuil—Saint‑Hubert under the leadership of executive director Chantal Pagé. Thanks in part to Canada's national school food program, Les Cuisiniers différents provides meals to students while advancing its mission to promote the inclusion of people with intellectual disabilities.

The Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities had the privilege of hearing Ms. Pagé share her experience and expertise regarding these programs and their tangible impact on young people. I am always very proud to see an organization from Longueuil—Saint‑Hubert contribute to the discussions shaping public policy.
I want to congratulate everyone involved with Les Cuisiniers différents on their commitment and their invaluable contribution to our community, and I am grateful to Ms. Pagé.

Mr. Speaker, 22 days ago, the industry minister threatened legal action against Stelco's American owner. Today, Cleveland-Cliffs claims it has complied with all 34 undertakings, while the minister alleges breaches of six binding commitments. Meanwhile, hundreds of workers face layoffs, and the government continues to issue warnings instead of taking legal action. It is enough letters and enough deadlines. It is time to act.

Our Conservative steel plan calls for enforcing Stelco's job guarantees, cracking down on unfairly traded Chinese steel, eliminating the industrial carbon tax, fast-tracking LNG projects using Canadian steel, and negotiating a deal with the United States. From Stelco to Algoma, steelworkers are paying the price as our industry faces mounting pressure. Canadian steelworkers can compete with the best people in the world. They should not have to compete with their own government.
It is time for the Liberal government to stop extending deadlines, start enforcing commitments and start protecting Canadian steel jobs.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to pay tribute to a constituent of mine. Roger Barrette has dedicated 47 years of his working life to the health and social services system, including 40 years at the Thérèse-De Blainville CLSC, now known as Santé Québec Laurentides.

Mr. Barrette has witnessed the major changes in our health care system from the early days of CLSCs to the present. Throughout all these years, he has demonstrated an unwavering commitment to our community. Even today, he continues to come up with innovative ideas for the benefit of our community. I recently had the pleasure of meeting with him and presenting him with a certificate of recognition to honour his exceptional career.
Our public services are sustained by women and men like Roger Barrette, who dedicate their careers to serving the public and contribute every day to the well-being of our constituents.
On behalf of the people of Thérèse-De Blainville, I thank Mr. Barrette for his 47 years of service, and I offer him my heartfelt congratulations.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of all struggling families not just in my hometown of Calgary, but across the entire country.

Every month, the Liberals manage to set new records. Unfortunately, these records are for food bank visits. Food Banks Canada recorded 2.35 million food bank visits in a single month, the highest number ever recorded in our history. This crisis is being made even worse by high fuel prices, which make it more expensive for farmers to grow crops and harder for truckers to deliver food to Canadians.

That is why Conservatives will continue to fight to make life more affordable for all Canadians, so that no family has to choose between putting food on the table and paying for the fuel they need in order to get to work.

Mr. Speaker, common sense is coming back to British Columbia. For the first time in nearly 100 years, my fellow British Columbians have ended a decade of NDP rule and elected a new Conservative government, one that shares our goal and vision to make life more affordable in B.C., to bring back safe streets and fiscal sanity and to unleash the true potential of B.C.'s resource economy.

The resurrection of this movement and this party did not happen overnight. Over the past five years, I have been honoured to work alongside a number of passionate and principled individuals to bring this vision into reality. They include Angelo Isidorou, Aisha Estey, Sacha Peter and Harman Bhangu. I would also like to congratulate Premier-elect Lorne Doerkson for his crushing victory and for meeting this unprecedented moment with steadfastness, resilience and grace.
The future is once again bright in B.C., and I know that Conservatives here in our nation's capital are ready to play our part.

Mr. Speaker, last week, Canadians marked National Forest Week, and sector leaders from across the country gathered in Ottawa at the Forest Products Association of Canada's annual conference to strengthen this vital sector.

There is no question that U.S. trade actions and the decline of newsprint have made for some challenging years, but we are a nation of forests. Forestry quite literally built this country, and forestry will continue to build this country. Next week, we will release our forestry strategy. This strategy will build on the work of the forest sector transformation task force and the action plan released this spring.

I want to recognize the workers, innovators, researchers, indigenous partners and industry leaders whose dedication helps keep our forest community strong, last week, this week and every week. When forestry is strong, Canada is strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we already have a free trade agreement with Europe and a military alliance with NATO and 30 European countries, but the Prime Minister is threatening to cede our sovereignty to costly European policies on taxes, immigration and regulations. This is not going to reduce the cost of living, and it is going to encroach on provincial premiers' jurisdictions without their consent and without their input, including the Premier of Quebec on his own turf.
How can the Prime Minister be so out of touch and so arrogant?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that the European Union represents 450 million consumers and 18% of global GDP. I am very proud that there is a rapprochement happening between the European Union and Canada. Our diplomatic efforts are bearing fruit.

It should also be noted that the benefits that Canada negotiates in the interest of Canadians are in the interest of Quebec. These are opportunities for our businesses and our citizens. I would like to commend the Quebec delegation in Brussels for its contributions to Canada's diplomatic efforts.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is no rapprochement happening. No agreements have been signed, either. Ten European countries have not signed the agreement we already have. There have been no results. The Prime Minister is all talk and no action.

The same goes for spending. Inflation caused government revenues to skyrocket, but the Prime Minister squandered the money. The Parliamentary Budget Officer reports that he is planning to add $733 billion to our debt over the next five years, which amounts to an additional $40,000 in debt for every Canadian family.
How can the Prime Minister be so out of touch and so costly for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is far too much to unpack in that question. First, he said we are “all talk and no action” and that there have been few results, but I would point out that our non-U.S. exports have increased by $33 billion in recent years. That is an 11% increase at a time when we are seeing a realignment of the Canadian economy to be more resilient and more self-reliant.

Now, whenever he talks about inflationary programs, I always ask the Leader of the Opposition the same question, but he is never able to come up with an answer: What exactly is an inflationary program? For example, is it the 213,000 children in Quebec who benefit from the Canada child benefit and the $819 million that is sent to Quebec families to meet their needs? Is that an inflationary program?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, inflation is going to bring a $20-billion revenue windfall to the government. That is great news for the Prime Minister but terrible news for the people lined up at food banks and the young people who cannot afford a place to live. It is still not enough to offset the irresponsibility of the big-spending Prime Minister, who is going to add $733 billion to our national debt over five years according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer. That is $40,000 for every family in Canada.
Will he acknowledge that he is out of touch and that Canadians are out of money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the leader, as Canadians know, has no credibility when it comes to the economy. He has never worked one day in it.

On this side of the House, we have a plan. We have a plan to build Canada strong. At the Canada investment summit, there was $500 billion in investments. Non-U.S. exports are set to double over the next decade. Foreign direct investment is at levels not seen in decades.
On this side of the House, we have a plan to invest in our economy and to build our economy strong. The leader continues with the rhetoric.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister had any results at all, he would stand up and answer questions about his record deficit and the fact that the fastest-growing item in the budget is not health care, not the military and not borders, but interest on the national debt, enriching his banker buddies at the expense of hard-working Canadians.

The average family of four will spend $6,000 this year on taxes to fund interest on debt. Will he acknowledge that he is out of touch, that Canadians are out of money and that the debt is out of control?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, do members know what a good leader does? A good leader does not raise his hands up, blame everybody else and offer nothing constructive as a solution. On this side of the House, let us look at some economic facts: the best net debt-to-GDP in the G7, the fastest-growing economy in the G7 and the best credit rating in the G7.

On this side of the House, we have a Prime Minister with economic and business credentials. The leader has never worked one day in the economy and is in his third decade in the House producing nothing.
I would advise members not to be provocative, because it creates a reaction and leads to a bit of chaos in the House.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, a good leader stands up and answers questions in the House of Commons, and a good leader gets results.

Now we learn that the government is admitting it will not get the Prime Minister's promised results on housing. In a response to an Order Paper question, the Liberals have now admitted that the Prime Minister has broken his promise to double homebuilding and that construction will actually fall to near-record lows over the next three years, blaming immigration, as the Liberals do, for the housing shortage.
How could the Prime Minister be so out of touch with Canadians who need homes?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gregor Robertson (Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, first and foremost, I would reprimand the member opposite for constantly attacking immigrants.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The hon. member may continue. Let us listen to him.
Mr. Speaker, I think almost every member of the House comes from immigrant stock. Canada is a country of immigrants, and to blame immigrants for a housing crisis is absolutely unfair and unjust.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
It is a little loud. I do not want to reprimand anybody.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member says he wants to reprimand anybody who blames excessive immigration numbers for the housing shortage. Well, let me read directly from a document he tabled in the House of Commons. It is a document on the housing shortage. It says, “One of the drivers of the housing shortage has been the strong growth in housing demand driven by immigration.”
Will the minister stand up now and reprimand himself?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gregor Robertson (Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is a difference between immigrants and immigration, first and foremost. When the member opposite—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
We need to reset the clock to the beginning.
The hon. member from the top, please.
Mr. Speaker, there is a big difference. The member opposite demonizes immigrants, which is specifically what he said. The member opposite said, “immigrants”.

Many countries in the world, including Canada, have challenges around immigration. Lots of people want to come to Canada. We need to keep up with the housing we build, and as the Prime Minister has said, we need to make sure the housing we build fits the immigration levels. We want immigrants in Canada. This is a country of immigrants. We believe in immigration. It has to be controlled, and our housing builds have to match accordingly. That is what we are focused on.

Mr. Speaker, in the wake of the Parti Québécois' election victory, the Prime Minister telephoned the Premier of Quebec to offer his congratulations and express his desire to work together on key priorities, including the economy, housing, support for workers and homelessness. It was a gesture of goodwill, but that collaborative spirit appears to have been short-lived.
How can the Prime Minister justify muzzling the Premier of Quebec on his own turf, during the Canada–Europe summit taking place this week in Montreal?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will leave it to the leader of the Bloc Québécois to choose his own analogies, but I believe that is a bit of a stretch.

Does the member know what I am hearing from the Quebeckers I meet? I am talking about the Quebeckers who elected 44 Liberal members from Quebec, including the recent election in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, where the Liberal candidate received more than 50% of the vote.

They are saying that they want us to continue diversifying our markets and strengthening the resilience of the Quebec and Canadian economies. They are encouraged to see that exports to markets outside the United States have increased by 11% over the past year. They are pleased that, over the past year, Canada has signed 20 trade and security agreements with countries around the world.
It is the Government of Canada doing that work, in partnership with the provinces and territories, and we will continue that work in the interest of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that that lines up with what we were hearing in Quebec this morning.

The Premier of Quebec asked to give a speech at a summit examining issues like culture, workforce mobility, the fight against global warming, and agriculture. The Premier of Quebec is entitled to take the floor in the largest francophone city in North America. Ottawa's response was that no, Quebec's voice does not need to be heard at international fora.
Does the Prime Minister claim to speak for the Government of Quebec as well?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what we hear in Quebec City, what we heard today and yesterday, is that Quebeckers want us to pursue our efforts to diversify our markets, especially with the European Union. Why? It is because the EU represents 450 million consumers and 18% of global GDP.

Also, Canada negotiates in the interest of Canada, in the interest of all the provinces and in the interest of Quebec. I commend the Quebec delegation to Brussels for its contributions to our diplomatic efforts to strengthen our ties with the European Union. We are going to stay the course.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's leading exporter to Europe is Quebec. However, if we are not at the table, we are on the menu, as the Prime Minister himself said, and we now know that the federal government does not want Quebec at the table. He will talk about issues that fall exclusively under Quebec's jurisdiction, and Quebec will have no say. He will talk about pipelines, fossil fuels and maybe new markets, the forestry industry, labour, the environment and culture. Quebec's future is at stake, but we are clearly on the menu.
Will the Prime Minister agree to remedy the insult he delivered to all Quebeckers in front of the whole of Europe?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the Premier of Quebec was invited to welcome the dignitaries and attend the dinner, as were several other provincial premiers who will be there, as well as a number of representatives of major industries, major businesses and major institutions in Quebec who will also be there. The invitation is still open.
I think it would be good for the Government of Quebec to be there.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal tanker ban is a gigantic multi-billion-dollar gift to Donald Trump's America. Right now, we are getting a $26-a-barrel lower price in the U.S. than we could get on the world market, because we cannot get our oil overseas. What if there were a company with a railroad already in place, promising to move 250,000 barrels a day and ship it from Prince Rupert to get world prices through the Pacific? Well, it turns out there is one. What is standing in the way? It is the Prime Minister and his tanker ban.
Will the Liberal government vote for Conservative Bill C-264 to get our oil to the world?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada, B.C., Alberta and affected first nations are working together to build the Pacific link, which will massively increase exports. We are building in partnership with indigenous people all across this country.

Rather than pick fights with indigenous people, why do the Conservatives not join us on the north coast transmission line and help us build that with indigenous people? Why do they not help us build the Darlington SMR with indigenous people? Why do they not stop fighting indigenous people and start building Canada strong?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is all well and good to build a pipeline to the Pacific 10 years from now with tens of billions of dollars of taxpayer money, but that does not stop us from also allowing a project that could begin today and that could start shipping oil in two years on a rail track that already exists, without any taxpayer subsidy required. There is only one thing standing in the way, and that is the Prime Minister and his tanker ban.
Will the Prime Minister get out of the way, vote for Conservative Bill C-264, get rid of the tanker ban and get our oil to the world?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will repeat it. The Conservative leader can join us with indigenous people and help us build the sunrise pipeline expansion. He can join us and help us build the Taylor to Gordondale expansion. He can join us and build the Pacific link. He can join us and build the north coast transmission line. Instead of fighting indigenous people, he should work with indigenous people to build Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal government over the last decade blew through every single fiscal anchor it had established. Last year, we got a new Prime Minister and new Liberal leader, who established new fiscal anchors in the last budget, with deficits double that of its predecessor. Well, here we are, less than a year later, and the PBO projects that the Prime Minister is going to blow through these new fiscal anchors.
Will the Prime Minister confirm the PBO's projection that the upcoming budget will blow through the fiscal anchor?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our government has been clear: We are spending less to invest more in the Canadian economy.

We found over $60 billion in government savings, reported a lower deficit in the spring economic update, and are on track to balance the operating budget a year ahead of schedule. We have done all that while cutting taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment, and supporting Canadians with groceries and essentials, while seeing the highest level in foreign direct investment in nearly two decades. That is how we demonstrate fiscal discipline and build Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what stats the member is cherry-picking, but business capital formation has declined in five of the last six quarters, and GDP growth is under 1%, effectively zero. As to spending, the debt is growing at double the rate of the deficit, and interest payments on the national debt are skyrocketing to 14¢ per dollar of revenue by decade's end.
I ask the government to answer the question. Will the government blow through the fiscal guardrail in the upcoming budget, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada starts with the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have seen the net debt-to-GDP ratio is the best in the G7. We have a AAA credit rating, the best in the G7. In Q2 of this year, we had the highest GDP growth in the G7. I do not know how many stats the member opposite needs. We saved $60 billion in government operations. We have attracted over $500 billion of new commitments in investment in the Canadian economy.
I am not sure what the member opposite needs in terms of stats to understand that Canada is doing well and only getting stronger under the current government.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada health transfer child benefit, EI, the child benefit and equalization payments do not have much in common, but they do have one thing in common: Canada spends less money on each of those than it does on interest on the debt. After the Liberals doubled the national debt, the Prime Minister doubled the deficit in his first year alone. Eleven cents of every federal dollar is now for interest payments. That is not social programs, it is not health care and it is not police. It is just interest.
Will the Prime Minister get out of his seat and tell Canadians which matters more to them: their services or his creditors?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are blinded, I think, by their pessimism and negativity. They cannot even see the opportunities that our government is seizing in the Canadian economy: $500 billion in new investment commitments from domestic investors; doubling non-U.S. trade by the year 2030; and projects such as Darlington, Contrecoeur, Grays Bay, Roberts Bank and Churchill Falls. These are generational projects that will secure long-term prosperity for Canadians.
Budget 2026 next week, on November 5, will build on that progress. The Prime Minister says, “Fortune favours the bold.”

Mr. Speaker, in just the time that it took the member to answer that question, Canadian taxpayers were forced to pay $112,000. That $112,000 will not pay for one of the government's social programs. In five out of the last six quarters, investment has been down in this country, despite what the member says. That is Liberal hypocrisy in a nutshell. Their fiscal recklessness means less money today and even less tomorrow. The member cannot explain it.
Will the government support our motion today and have the Prime Minister come to committee and at least try?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let me put a few facts on the record for the member. We are building a strong economy that benefits all Canadians. We have the second-fastest growth in the G7 and the best balance sheet in the G7, and we are the most competitive country for business investment. We have higher per capita job creation than the United States.

This is a government that is focused on what matters to Canadians, like bringing the cost of housing down, ensuring that they have affordable child care and ensuring that there are investments in the skills, training and education that they need to build the brightest future possible. That is our record.

Mr. Speaker, the federal deficit will reach $63 billion this year. National interest payments will cost the equivalent of $6,000 for a Canadian family of four. However, the government continues to run up deficits while families are struggling to make ends meet. One of my constituents wrote to me and said that she is collecting empties to be able to fill up her gas tank to pick up her daughter. That is what life is like under the Liberals.
I asked the Prime Minister to appear before the Standing Committee on Finance. Will he accept my invitation?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):
