Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, no one can remain indifferent to the account he shared concerning his constituent. Keeping in mind those families who are struggling to make ends meet, for example, let us look at the Conservative reality. At every turn, they vote against measures that have a real impact on people's lives.

I am thinking of the member opposite and, more specifically, his riding of Richmond—Arthabaska—des-Sources, where 20,587 children are receiving an average of $4,176 a year through the Canada child benefit, and 34,563 of his constituents are benefiting from the Canadian dental care plan.
I know he is very active in his riding. Does he tell the people he meets that he has consistently voted against all these measures that are helping residents?
Mr. Speaker, Bill C‑39 continues to raise concerns. Yesterday, the United Steelworkers sounded the alarm regarding workers' rights:

Quote.QuotePara: The power the government is trying to give [the] minister here is a power that does not exist in other G7 countries. Even in the United States...there is no such power to force an end to a strike and send employees back to work. This is something that...should send a signal. There are a lot of red flags being raised....

Content.ParaText: No other G7 country goes as far as Bill C‑39. Why do the Liberals want to continue trampling on workers' rights?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Bill C‑39 is intended to build Canada strong by advancing major projects and major construction initiatives, as requested by workers, among others. People are also looking to make significant investments. At the recent investment summit, we know that commitments of $500 billion in investments were announced. We want a very healthy labour-management climate. We want to provide a framework for these discussions and support them so that many more collective agreements can be reached at the bargaining table.
Mr. Speaker, there is a big difference between the wishes expressed here and what is written in the bill.
People are still talking about Bill C‑39. Here is what the CSN said this morning:

Quote.QuotePara: The powers given to the minister to suspend a strike...are...a serious infringement on freedom of association. Even framed by the national interest, it remains arbitrary, vague and...unacceptable.

Content.ParaText: Yesterday, law professor Maxime St‑Hilaire criticized Bill C‑39 for making emergency measures permanent without any guardrails. He said that he has observed several instances of totalitarian behaviour on the part of the current government.
Will the Liberals finally realize that they are out of control?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think that is an exaggeration. We obviously do not share that view.

What we want to do is support the parties. Ninety-five per cent of parties successfully negotiate collective agreements. We want to better support the remaining 5% with special mediators and support from the Department of Labour, so that collective agreements can be reached in the federal sector.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday at the fisheries and oceans committee, the Liberals blocked a motion to have the Prime Minister's wife, Diana Fox Carney, appear to explain her appointment as Canada's new ocean envoy. The request was straightforward: explain her mandate, her priorities and how she plans to oversee more than $1.2 billion in taxpayer funding tied to the role created by her husband, the Prime Minister.

If there is nothing to hide, why are the Liberals preventing Mrs. Carney from appearing before the committee responsible for fisheries and oceans, and being accountable to Canadians for this appointment and the taxpayer funds associated with it?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ernie Klassen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Madame Carney is an expert in climate policy, and we thank her for stepping forward as Canada's ocean envoy.
The Conservatives are trying to score cheap political points, but we are focused on the work. Our Liberal government will protect Canada's oceans and build our coastal economy.

Mr. Speaker, Diana Fox Carney has been given an official government role that her husband, the Prime Minister, created, and she has been given more than 1.2 billion tax dollars to work with. The government is not a family-run business. It is not The Sopranos, but it is looking more and more like well-connected Liberal insiders are taking care of themselves while the people they govern are suffering.
If that is not the case, why not allow Mrs. Carney to come to the committee responsible for fisheries and oceans to explain her role and be accountable to Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is a particularly spurious attack coming from the opposition.

Canada is a world leader in oceans protection and oceans conservation. We have multiple departments, multiple ministers and multiple initiatives, including on our west coast, where we are working very hard on the southern resident killer whale population.
We will continue to be world leaders in oceans protection. We thank the Prime Minister's wife for volunteering to spearhead our efforts.

Mr. Speaker, the industry minister said Cleveland-Cliffs has broken its commitments. Now just today the company again said it is fully compliant with all 34 of its undertakings, including employment. Meanwhile, Stelco workers remain laid off. Competing press releases do not help workers.

Yesterday, the industry minister stood in this House and said that she would provide the demand letter to this House. Today, the member for York—Durham formally made that request. I am assuming, since she is so confident that the company is in breach, she will have no problem providing that letter. Will she do it, and when?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what is most important is this morning I met with Marty Warren, who is the head of the steelworkers. The steelworkers in Canada are 100% behind the government when dealing with this issue.

Of course I am willing to work with the opposition, because I believe that not only do we have a strong case but this should not be a partisan issue. We should be working together to make sure that we protect jobs. Meanwhile, what I expect from the Conservatives is that they take a strong stance on American tariffs, while also making sure that they support us while trying to protect these jobs.
Mr. Speaker, it is just a letter. I did not hear a date there, and hopefully this is not more “all talk and no action.”

Meanwhile, I am hearing from steel service centres and downstream manufacturers all across the country that are having difficulty securing supply. Now, idling of Stelco's coated lines is certainly adding pressure, and a complex tariff rate quota regime is making some of these companies scramble. These are businesses that buy Canadian and employ Canadian workers. We need to make sure that their voices are heard.

Will the industry minister and the Prime Minister commit today to ensuring steel service centres and downstream manufacturers are part of their steel task force, so we can make sure they are getting what they need?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, yes.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have completely abandoned the Canadian steel industry. The American tariffs are costing businesses a fortune. Just ask Groupe Camnor, Beauce Atlas or Garaga. The tariffs are costing them each an extra $1.5 million a month. That amounts to an additional $54 million a year for these three incredible businesses in Beauce.
The Prime Minister promised us a deal with the Americans, but he has completely failed. Can he set his pride aside and sign a good agreement with the United States?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to reassure my colleague that this is not about pride. I think he should have thought about his question before asking it. Everyone across the country needs to be united in standing up to the White House, which is basically trying to make us more dependent on the United States and weaken our economy.
I would like my colleague to know that I would be pleased to work with him to protect jobs in the steel sector. We are already doing that, but we can always use more help from the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, we have studied many issues of importance to veterans and their families. These discussions will continue informing our understanding of the modern veteran. They will shape how we respond to the unique realities veterans face following military service, and they remind us that we must support veterans and their families beyond just Remembrance Day on November 11.
Could the Minister of Veterans Affairs share how she and our government are advancing recognition and commemoration of our service members?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jill McKnight (Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, remembrance lives on when one generation inspires the next. As the Royal Canadian Legion's poppy campaign begins, Canadians will pause to honour the Canadian Armed Forces members who have served and sacrificed. This year, our remembrance can also take inspiration from Chaelyn Han, winner of the National Youth Remembrance Poster Contest. Her artwork reminds us that remembrance is not only about looking back, but also carrying forward the stories and sacrifices that shaped our country.
Let us wear our poppies with pride and carry commemoration—
The hon. member for Calgary Nose Hill.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in response to a question about why the Prime Minister is suggesting he will increase immigration levels, even though government officials are warning that housing supply has been impacted, the housing minister gave a completely inane answer that is unbefitting of the gravity of the situation.

When newcomers are invited to Canada, they should be able to afford a place to live, and Canadians should be afforded that opportunity, too. If the Prime Minister plans to increase immigration levels, where are all these people going to live?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canadians understand that immigration and immigrants have built this country and have contributed to building Canada. Quite literally, when I say “building Canada”, 23% of all contractors and builders are immigrants, and in some regions it is a lot higher.

Immigration is critical to addressing skill gaps in the construction sector when Canadians are not available to fill those jobs. In the coming months, we will continue to take a responsible approach to immigration to maximize benefits for all Canadians.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the government's own officials are saying that housing is outpacing demand.

It has been reported that the Minister of Housing held a $10-million real estate portfolio. That must be nice. I want him to know something. Millions of long-time Canadians and newcomers alike cannot afford housing, and that is because he, the Prime Minister and the immigration minister, a real trio of quality there, are setting levels so high that people cannot afford or find a place to live.
Levels must be decreased. Will they agree?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gregor Robertson (Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the immigration minister said, the levels are under control right now. We are working very closely between immigration levels and housing starts.

We see the success we are having on the housing front. We have seen 141,000 homes created by the MLI select program. We have seen over 80,000 homes in the apartment construction loan program. With Build Canada Homes, there are over 19,000 non-market affordable homes. We are seeing a scale of construction right now across Canada that is unprecedented, and we are making sure it fits with our immigration levels.

Mr. Speaker, here is the reality. When housing supply cannot keep pace with demand, the result is higher rents, higher wait lists and young people giving up on their dream of ever owning a home. That is not fair to young Canadian couples who cannot afford a home to start a family, and it is not fair to the newcomer who was promised an opportunity and ended up in an overcrowded basement suite or a shelter.
This is something the government does not get. Why does the government not understand this basic principle?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gregor Robertson (Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, that is rich coming from the other side who vote against affordable housing measures at every turn. That is hypocrisy.

We are focused on scaling up construction of housing across our country. I have just recited the latest numbers we have. We have positive news on rent. Rents have come down for 23 months in a row, making life more affordable for Canadians and for newcomers.
We have to make sure we continue that trend and that we build strong. We could use more support from Conservatives on that front.

Mr. Speaker, what is rich is the housing minister blaming immigration for the housing shortage that his government created. The Prime Minister's own officials warned him that his out-of-control immigration levels were causing a housing shortage, yet he told The New York Times that he wants to increase immigration levels.
His decisions are destroying support for immigration in this country. Conservatives would restore Canada's consensus for immigration. Why will the government and the Prime Minister not do the same?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the member in the opposition, who cannot seem to listen, here are the facts. The temporary resident population has dropped by 80% for international students and 59% for temporary workers, with a 69% decline in asylum claims. The StatsCan figures show the population has declined for the first time in our history. Rentals.ca reports that rents are down by an average of 9.2%. TD Economics reports an immigration slowdown, reduced housing prices—
The hon. member for Elmwood—Transcona.

Mr. Speaker, Canada faces a 29-year low in workforce participation. The job-finding rate has dropped again, now down to 30.6% under the Liberal government. Canadians are losing jobs and they are losing hope.

While Canada has a job crisis, the government has chosen to give public subsidies to a company that fired Canadian workers to hire foreign workers. Why did the fisheries minister approve a public subsidy to Ichiboshi L.P.C. after the company had already been caught firing Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Conservatives, while they talk down Canada and talk down our workers, that this country is building. Let me give some examples. Maybe the member has forgotten about LNG Canada phase two, with $33 billion in private investment and 4,000 new construction jobs. The Nouveau Monde Graphite project means 1,000 new jobs. At the Darlington nuclear station, there are thousands of jobs.
Canada is building. I hope the Conservatives join us.
Mr. Speaker, that response had absolutely nothing to do with the question that was asked.

Canada faces a 29-year low in workforce participation. This question is about fisheries. There was an Order Paper question the government tabled on February 19, question 885, that admitted that the government provided public subsidies through that department to a company that had fired Canadian workers to hire illegal workers.
Why can the fisheries minister not stand up and answer that question? Why are you subsidizing a company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers?
Again, it is through the Chair, please.
The hon. Secretary of State for Labour.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member talks about workforce participation. What this government is doing is building. We are building projects right across the country, with Canadian steel, Canadian lumber and Canadian unionized workers.

Let us remind the Conservatives of some of the projects that are going on in this country. There is BHP's Jansen potash project, six new icebreakers in Quebec City and LNG Canada phase two, with 4,000 construction jobs. There is the Pacific link pipeline.
We are building this country. Workers are excited. Unions are excited. Let us go build this country.

Mr. Speaker, the question is about fisheries. The fisheries department gave a subsidy to a company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers. The government tabled the Order Paper question response in the House, question 885, on February 19. Again, why did the government, through the fisheries department, provide public subsidy to the Ichiboshi L.P.C. company after it fired Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ernie Klassen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the minister recently announced the renewed Atlantic fisheries fund with her provincial counterparts. This new fund will provide $300 million over five years to our fishing sector to spur innovation, enhance infrastructure, build on science and develop new markets. We are providing harvesters with the tools they need to grow the sector and create market diversity during these uncertain times.

Mr. Speaker, how are things going for young people today? According to most of the indicators that matter to our young people, things are not going well at all. Buying a home is virtually impossible. Physical and mental health are declining. Now our young people are looking for jobs.
A committee has learned that companies are hiring illegal workers but are receiving government subsidies, even though the government is aware of the situation.

Is there anyone on the other side who will stand up and explain to taxpayers why their money is being given to companies that are taking opportunities away from our young people in order to pay illegal workers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ernie Klassen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the minister recently announced the renewed Atlantic fisheries fund with her provincial counterparts. This new fund will provide $300 million over five years to our fishing sector to spur innovation, enhance infrastructure, build on science and develop new markets. Our government is here to build, and that includes strong fisheries and coastal communities.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals rise every week to tell us how many people in our ridings need government subsidies to survive. They are so proud to give us the numbers, not realizing that this is the result of 10 years of Liberal policies that have stretched people to their limit. I imagine that for them, the ultimate achievement will be when all Canadians need Liberal subsidies.
We believe that the real task is to build a country that gives our young people opportunities so that they can work, buy a home and start a family.
When will the Liberals stop living off announcements and start building opportunities so that our young people can learn to stand on their own two feet?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our colleague talks about building opportunities for young people. That is exactly what our government is doing across the country. Whether through investments in major projects in Quebec and the rest of Canada, student aid, summer jobs, or assistance for industries facing unjustified tariffs, our government is always looking for the best way to help and support young people and all workers in Canada.
We will never stop doing that.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has everything the world needs: skilled workers, innovative businesses, strong infrastructure, abundant natural resources, as well as a reliable, stable country and government. That helps explain the success of the recent investment summit in Toronto, which unleashed $500 billion in commitments for our businesses and workers. Another reason for that success is the productivity mega deduction, which will allow businesses of all sizes to deduct a wide range of assets so they have more money to invest in their workers and their companies.
Can my colleague from the Quebec City region, the Minister of Government Transformation, tell the House how Canadians—
The hon. Minister of Government Transformation.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Québec Centre. He is right. We made a choice: to invest in Canadian businesses and create good-paying jobs. That is exactly what we are doing with the productivity mega deduction, which will generate $22 billion in annual economic benefits and support up to 80,000 new jobs each year. In fact, what we are doing is making Canada the OECD country with the most competitive tax rate by a wide margin. This will empower our small, medium-sized and large businesses to achieve their ambitions, to grow, succeed and innovate. That is how we build Canada strong and ensure that we remain masters in our own house, now and forever.

Mr. Speaker, B.C.'s new Conservative premier wants to build out ports and rail to get Canadian energy to global markets. Strathcona Resources proposes to ship 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day through Prince Rupert. It is a Canadian company, Canadian oil, Canadian jobs and a direct deepwater route to Asia, but the Liberals' job-killing Canadian oil exports ban blocks it.
Will the Liberals finally get out of the way, repeal Bill C-48, cut dependence on the U.S. and let Canadians sell Canadian oil to the world?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we are working with Alberta, we are working with British Columbia and we are working with first nations to sell Canadian oil to the world. We are doing it. We are selling electricity. We are selling oil. We are selling hydro. We are selling nuclear. We are selling copper. This is all in partnership with indigenous people.
They want to fight with indigenous people. Why do they not stop fighting and start building with us?

Mr. Speaker, no other major energy producer in the world derails and stops its own exports like the Liberals do to Canada. During the last antidevelopment decade, smaller companies got killed. Multinationals moved investment out but got golden handshakes from the Liberals. Canadian-owned Strathcona invested more in Canada and does not want tax dollars.

If the Liberals mean a single word about making Canada an energy superpower, will they support the Conservative plan to repeal their shipping ban to export Canadian oil so Canada can be self-reliant, affordable and united?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, here is who is investing in Canada. Shell just put $30 billion into the upstream in Alberta. Equinor is putting $10 billion into Newfoundland. Petronas is putting billions of dollars into this country. There are people from all over the world coming to invest in this country because of Liberal policies. Maybe the Conservatives should get on board.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals like to talk a big game when it comes to dealing with the United States, yet they refuse to lift the ideological and unscientific tanker ban that land-locks Canadian resources and depresses the Canadian dollar, giving our oil away on the cheap to the Trump administration while Canadians struggle with the cost of living crisis here at home. However, there is now a plan, a private sector proposal, to export Canadian oil by rail through Prince Rupert.
Will the Liberal government finally get out of the way, repeal the tanker ban and allow this country, Canada, to achieve true energy independence from the United States?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are all very proud of the work that my colleague is doing with these major projects across the country. We are talking about Coastal GasLink. We are talking about LNG one and two. We are talking about the north coast transmission line. We are talking about some of the biggest port infrastructure investments in Canadian history.
Guess what. The member is new. He lives with regret because he is not the premier of British Columbia today. We built not one, but are about to build two major pipelines to the west coast of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as Canada works to diversify its trade and reduce reliance on any single trading partner, how can we build our long-lasting relationship with the European Union to strengthen our economic ties, expand opportunities for Canadian businesses and workers and unlock the full potential of this important partnership?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anita Anand (Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada and the EU are turning our shared interests into action. This week we are welcoming EU leaders here to Canada to build on SAFE, to build on the CETA and to build on the strategic defence partnership. It is our second-largest trading partner, and that is $178 billion in trade last year alone. We are building our national resilience, we are building our domestic economy and most importantly we are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer's latest report revealed that the deficits over the next five years will total more than $330 billion. In addition, the Alto project represents another $150 billion. The Liberal government is digging itself deeper and deeper into a bottomless pit of debt.
Can the Liberals confirm whether or not the $150 billion for the Alto project is included in the $330-billion deficit?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Quebeckers have no reason to take note of the Conservative Party of Canada's opposition to a transformative project that will create 51,000 jobs, add points to our GDP, and change the game when it comes to mobility in our country, especially between Quebec's biggest cities, namely Quebec City, Trois-Rivières, Laval, Montreal and Gatineau.
I urge and implore my colleague to get on board with high-speed rail. Let us get Canada moving.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives want to scrap B.C.'s north coast oil tanker ban, putting our coastal communities and indigenous livelihoods at risk. The Prime Minister has already promised to uphold the ban, yet Canadians are being asked to shoulder the financial risks of another costly pipeline. As the Prime Minister meets with first nations leaders and premiers, this is a moment to build trust, not break promises.
Will the Prime Minister stand up today and unequivocally commit to protecting the north coast tanker ban, respecting indigenous rights and keeping his government's promise?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rebecca Alty (Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to be very clear. The building Canada strong act would not change the duty to consult. The bill proposes a centralized Crown consultation hub so that indigenous peoples can spend less time navigating government red tape and more time having meaningful conversations.
Our government is focused on building Canada strong, and we cannot do that without indigenous peoples.

Mr. Speaker, BC Ferries has parted ways with its CEO, but that will not build shipyards. Conservatives and Liberals blame BC Ferries for sending jobs overseas, but Ottawa shares responsibility. Conservatives eliminated the 25% tariff on foreign-built large ferries. Then the Liberals extended it to all ferries. That revenue could have built Canadian shipyards. BC Building Trades and the Build Them Here coalition demand action.
Will the Liberal government commit in this budget to expand Canada's capacity to build, repair and recycle ships, including in Port Alberni, creating good-paying union jobs?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the member knows, we have spoken many times about the possibility of further developing those industries at Port Alberni. We are obviously very interested in that.

As for BC Ferries, as the member well knows, that is a provincial Crown corporation that reports to the Minister of Transportation of British Columbia, and I think his questions for BC Ferries are best asked of that minister.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Opposition Motion—Appearance of the Prime Minister before the Standing Committee on Finance

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is important to recognize that the Conservatives like to give a false impression. Canada does have financial capabilities, and we still get the AAA credit rating from credit agencies. I see the member is closely following what I am saying. Hopefully, he is actually listening.

At the end of the day, we have the financial resources to be able to invest in Canadians. The Conservative Party of Canada has made the decision to not invest in Canadians and to not see the value of growing Canada stronger and healthier for all to be able to participate. It has focused strictly on one issue, not recognizing that we do have a AAA credit rating.

Mr. Speaker, there will be deficits this year of $59.3 billion, meaning that every single family in the country will be paying $6,000 toward the federal deficit. The government is adding $733 billion to the national debt. The least the Prime Minister can do, with all of his experience, all of his expertise and all of the things he claimed to be to Canadians, is to come to a committee of parliamentarians who are here representing the people of Canada, to be accountable and transparent, and to answer the question that parliamentarians, on behalf of Canadians, want to put before him. That is, why are we in this position when he said we would not be?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, based on the last question from the member for Winnipeg North, it just shows that the Liberals have no credibility on this file anymore. They, under Justin Trudeau, spent and spent without care. Now, even despite having fiscal anchors that they pinky swore they would follow, the PBO has said that they are set to blow through them.
In the member's opinion, if he were a credit rating agency, how would he rate the performance of the government, from its rhetoric a year ago to the state of the finances today?

Mr. Speaker, I would give it a new rating measure, and that rating measure would be that it is my kids and my grandkids who are going to pick up the scattered pieces of what is left of this country after the Liberals do even more damage economically and fiscally than what they are doing right now.

That is what the PBO said, that the debt and deficit are going to increase. They have raised the alarms. Not only one PBO but two independent officers have now said that this is an alarming trend that is happening. There are no fiscal anchors. The things that worry me are my kids, my grandkids and the future of the country after the Liberals are done with it.

Mr. Speaker, it is not bad enough that the new Prime Minister has split the budget between operating and capital and is distributing the debt that he is creating among those. He is also passing debt on through Crown corporations. To hide all of that, as my colleague brought up, the Liberals are introducing the budget on a Thursday afternoon before a break week.
If things are as great as the Liberal government decries that they actually are, why are the Liberals behaving this way?

Mr. Speaker, it is a relevant question, and there is a very simple answer to that. It is that there is probably nobody in this place who knows better how to game the fiscal system than the former central banker in this country. The member is quite right. The Prime Minister is actually putting this on multiple credit cards, and the debt is just mounting.

What we are asking is for the Prime Minister to come to a committee and explain himself, not in the 35 seconds that he has in question period. We saw today that there were literally no questions that were answered. That is why we now call it the non-answer period.

He can come to committee. He can be accountable, be transparent and allow parliamentarians the oversight, on behalf of Canadians, that they need to get the answers to the questions that we are asking, not avoid the questions.
Before we resume debate, there are still quite a few members having side conversations, potentially raising the volume in the House. I would invite them to take their conversations into the lobby.

As well, for those outside of the chamber in the courtyard around us who are having conversations, there is still quite a bit of noise coming out of question period. I would invite those people to leave the courtyard and perhaps take their conversations elsewhere so they do not disrupt the House.
With that, we will resume debate with the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, at the get-go, I want to follow up on what the member for Barrie South—Innisfil just finished saying about the leader of the Liberal Party having been the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I would remind my friend across the way that it was Stephen Harper who recognized the skill set he has by appointing him Governor of the Bank of Canada. In fairness, he is not the only prime minister to have recognized that. So did the Prime Minister of England in ensuring he would then become the Governor of the Bank of England. That is something that is worthy of noting.

Not only did Prime Minister Stephen Harper and the Prime Minister of England recognize the leader of the Liberal Party's credentials, but Canadians as a whole did just that. In the last federal election, Canadians were very concerned about a wide spectrum of issues. They looked at what the leader of the Conservative Party had to offer and contrasted that to what the leader of the Liberal Party had to offer. Never before has the Liberal Party of Canada received as many votes as a direct result—
I have to interrupt the parliamentary secretary. I have a point of order from the member for Saanich—Gulf Islands Islands.
Mr. Speaker, despite your best efforts to remind people to lower the noise in the chamber, I very rarely hear the voice of the hon. parliamentary secretary. I would hate to miss it this time.

I thank the member for the reminder. The Sergeant-at-Arms is going around the courtyard asking those guests and others who may be circulating in the courtyard to keep the volume down because it is disturbing the work of the House.
I invite the parliamentary secretary to continue.

Mr. Speaker, what I was trying to highlight is the fact that Canadians have a very good understanding of what our Prime Minister brings to the table in terms of economic credentials. I think it is important that we take a look at the larger picture.

I had the opportunity to ask questions today in debate to the leader of the Conservative Party and the deputy leader. For those who are following the debate, the question I asked the deputy leader was in regard to very important programs. I talked about two programs in particular. I talked about the national dental program that provides support to seniors who are on fixed incomes, as an example, literally tens of thousands of seniors in every region of our country. I highlighted that program, along with the national school food program, which has 400,000 children benefiting from that particular program. I asked her to provide her thoughts on it.

Now, I will put the personal shot she took to the side, but she made it very clear that those programs are failures. I was disappointed in the manner in which, in a very clear and concise way, she said that those programs were failures. She should tell that to the senior who is on a fixed income in her own riding or a child who is receiving the benefits in a classroom.

That is the type of insensitivity that we see coming from today's Conservative Party. They talk about affordability, but when it comes to actual actions, the government has delivered a wide spectrum of actions, and I will go over them. What we see is the Conservative Party, time and again, devaluing these programs. I have heard members of the Conservative caucus calling the school food program garbage. Talk about being insensitive to the issues of the day, like affordability. They talk about it; they like to get those clips, but in reality, their actions speak louder than words. We saw that demonstrated today when I posed a question to the deputy leader of the Conservative Party.

For those who were around or who followed the speech of the leader of the Conservative Party, they should take a look at what he said. I am sure he will cut and paste, and try to make it look good for the far right. However, if we listen to the entirety of the speech, we cannot help but walk away thinking that Canada has a serious problem and, in fact, that we are broken. Talk about depressing.

There is no doubt that there is always room for us to look at ways in which we can improve. We do not question that. However, I say to the leader of the Conservative Party that Canada is not broken. Canada is doing exceptionally well when compared to our peers. We have people, companies, other governments and pensions looking at investing in Canada in a very real and tangible way. They are not going to do that if they believe that Canada is broken.

Let us take a look at last month. For the first time ever we had a Prime Minister host the world in Toronto, where we were asking people to come and take a look at what the government had been doing over the previous 12-plus months, and to look at ways in which they might be able to invest in Canada, in those major projects. We had over $500 billion, that is half a trillion dollars plus, that recognized that Canada is worth looking at. That is what they are actually doing.

It is a historic amount of money. They would not be doing that if they honestly believed what the leader of the Conservative Party was saying today in his remarks on the opposition motion. I believe that the Conservative Party is way off base. To Conservatives, it is all about the deficit.

We have the second-lowest deficit-to-GDP ratio in the G7. If we want to talk about the AAA credit rating, think in terms of the G7 countries. Everyone would like to be a part of the G7, I would suggest, but take a look at those G7 countries. We are talking about the United States, England, France and Germany. There are only two nations, Germany and Canada, that have a AAA credit rating.

When I had the opportunity to state that fact to the opposition critic of finance, his response was like, “Well, they don't know what they're talking about”. He then went into the reasons he believes that of the credit agencies, which also provide credit reports to provincial entities. He indicated that, “Well, they don't know what they're talking about.” I have a lot more confidence in those credit agencies than I do the official opposition, because day in and day out, the Conservatives want to talk down Canada.

What is at the core of the motion the Conservatives have before us today? It is hard to believe, but they are saying that, as we have the budget coming down, they are concerned about the deficit. They want to have the Prime Minister go before a standing committee. Maybe the opposition can tell me if, when they were in government, Stephen Harper ever went to a standing committee dealing with the budget. I will save them some time: It never happened. At the end of the day, if we want to do a comparison, the leader of the Conservative Party today, when he was in government, was in the only Conservative government that was ever found in contempt of Parliament. It was the only government in Canadian history.

When we start looking at fiscal capacity, what is it with the Conservative Party in terms of not recognizing the potential that Canadians have? There is potential in our resources, commodities, ingenuity and technology, which is there and real in every jurisdiction in Canada. The Conservatives' response is that they are not prepared to see that sort of investment take place, because they constantly criticize the projects we bring forward. All they say, and focus their attention on, are two things. One is character assassination, whether it is the Prime Minister or other ministers. The other is the deficit situation, but we have been very careful in demonstrating that everything is, in fact, under control. It is by making these investments that we are going to create additional revenue in the future. All one needs to do is to take a look at the projects that are on the table.
There are a couple of quotes I would like to share, and then I will go on to some of these projects I made reference to.

In regards to the Minister of Finance, I thought he made it very clear the other day in dealing with the financial issue. He said, “The International Monetary Fund just said that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and the second-fastest growth in the G7, almost twice that of Germany and Japan.”

I see that as good news. The Minister of Finance would reinforce some of the statements I have made, if not all the statements, such as that AAA credit rating. When I talk about having our finances in order and the financial capacity to look at building a stronger, healthier Canada that works for all Canadians, I would suggest it would be irresponsible of the government not to take advantage of that. It pleases me greatly to be able to say that we very much have a proactive Prime Minister who really understands how an economy works and has the relationships not only in Canadian borders but outside of Canada in order for us to advance that.

I do not say that lightly. Let us look at the things we have done as a government that led up to the Investment Summit that Canada hosted just last month that I commented on earlier with regard to half a trillion dollars. If we want to support small, medium-sized and large businesses, we need to find customers. In the last federal election, when people were genuinely concerned about Trump's tariffs and trade, the Prime Minister made a commitment to Canadians in that campaign that we would look at ways to expand trade opportunities that went beyond the Canada-U.S. border, and that is exactly what this government has been doing in good part. We have signed 20-plus trade and security agreements. It is probably 22 or 23 at this point, with many more in the works.

Whether it is the Minister of International Trade, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Foreign Affairs or the Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade among the provinces, there are numerous ministers, led by the Prime Minister and supported by every member of the Liberal caucus, out there in the world encouraging and promoting trade opportunities. That is why we are seeing the types of trade numbers today in terms of opportunities gained, at least in good part, working as a team with small businesses, provinces and indigenous people. This is what is making the difference. We have the opportunity to grow the economy, but it means we have to also be prepared to invest in it.

Earlier today, representatives of CentrePort in Winnipeg were in the government lobby, and I had a chance to have a very brief chat. I thanked them for what they are doing in building a stronger economy in Manitoba. It is both private and public investment that is feeding that growth because they know they can count on the federal government, the provincial government and private businesses investing in CentrePort. That is exactly what is happening today, which is creating jobs and opportunities into the future. That is a very small example, which is important to my province, of investment that takes place. We can take that snapshot and apply it to every region of our nation.

That brings me to the whole thought we have been talking about, which is how we can build, build big and build now. Since the last federal election, we have been working collaboratively with provincial governments and indigenous leaders at ways we can build and expand the Canadian economy, and at the same time protect our environment. There are many projects.

In the past, I have talked about the premiers and Prime Minister working, virtually from day one after the last federal election, to build one Canadian economy, and the federal government has done its part in passing the legislation that was necessary to enable that to happen at the federal level. We continue to work with the provinces so that more provinces will take down some of their barriers, because Canadians made it very clear that they want one Canadian economy.

They also made it very clear that they want to expand the economy, and expanding the economy means major projects. Let me try to summarize the major projects. We can go from coast to coast to coast, from Arctic sovereignty to what is taking place in B.C. We can talk about LNG phase two and of billions of dollars of investments. We can talk about MOUs in Alberta with a Conservative government. We can talk about copper mines and about the canola issue in the province of Saskatchewan. I already talked about CentrePort, in Manitoba, but we can also talk about the Port of Churchill. We can go into Ontario and talk about nuclear power. We can talk about, in the province of Quebec, something the Conservatives often bring up, the port of Montreal or about the expansion of hydro in Atlantic Canada, among other major projects.

From coast to coast to coast, we have a federal government that is working with provinces to make big projects happen and work, and we will all benefit from that. This is one of the ways we can secure more financial resources coming into the country, and if it takes time to be able to secure that, we will put in that time, because we want to make Canada the strongest and healthiest nation in the G7, and that is what we are fighting to achieve.

Mr. Speaker, I do not even know what to begin to say about the member's speech, but let us just look at some basic numbers here. The Government of Canada's own data shows that, in 2020, it had $284 billion in tax revenue. In 2025, it was $417 billion in tax revenue. The government's favourite line is to say that it is spending less so that it can invest more. However, $130 billion more in tax revenue is coming into the government than it did in 2020, yet Canadians are wondering what on earth they got for the $130 billion, plus the extra debt that is tacked on top of that.

Mr. Speaker, the entirety of my speech, with the exception of the reference to Stephen Harper, was about the time since the last federal election. Canadians elected a new Prime Minister and a new government. If we were to take a look at the expenditures, I would tell the member to look specifically at the Canadian Forces, because in the Canadian Forces, for the first time in generations, we have actually hit 2% of the GDP.

This is something that has been called for, for years. Stephen Harper dreamed of it, and even the previous administration with Justin Trudeau hoped to achieve it. The Prime Minister actually achieved it within six months of being elected. I believe that it is a good expense to support members of CAF and our sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, we have a Prime Minister who has plenty of time to have plenty of meetings in many places around the world. He is even meeting with the European Union soon, and he will try to sign trade agreements on things that are the responsibility of Quebec. They will be implemented in Quebec, yet the Premier of Quebec, who represents the Quebec government, is only invited to a cocktail party.

If the Prime Minister has time for cocktails and if he has time for meetings, then why can he not find the time to come to the parliamentary committee and show some deference to the parliamentary system? I know he has ministers. I know he has people around him. Some people think he has a good team. That is an opinion, and it needs to be confirmed. Nonetheless, why is it that, in this time of crisis, in this time of great transformation, the Prime Minister is able to find 15% to cut from the public service, but is unable to find a mere 15% to cut from his daily schedule in order to free up time to appear before a parliamentary committee for just one hour and show the deference he is expected to show toward the parliamentary system?

Mr. Speaker, I think that members, at times, undervalue the important role that ministers of government play. We have ministers who go to standing committees. We have parliamentary secretaries who are at standing committees. There is an opportunity in opposition.

I sit just two seats behind the Prime Minister. I constantly see members from the opposition go up to the Prime Minister prior to question period when he is here, whether it is Bloc members or other opposition members.
An hon. member: When he is here.
Hon. Kevin Lamoureux: Mr. Speaker, I suspect everyone is absent from the House at times, but the point is that there is ample opportunity.
I think members opposite should recognize that we do have a cabinet and we do have parliamentary secretaries, so there is ample opportunity to ensure there is accountability.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. One of my colleagues just referred to the Prime Minister's absence from the chamber. We are not allowed to mention the Prime Minister's absence from the chamber, even if it is true.

I want to clarify that, when a point of order is raised, it is best not to violate the rule about which the point of order was raised. Members cannot do indirectly what they are not allowed to do directly.

I am going to switch to English for a moment just to make sure that members understand that we cannot do indirectly what we are not supposed to do directly. Members should not mention the Prime Minister's presence or lack thereof. I thought the parliamentary secretary went around that artfully. I know he is a very seasoned member of this House and a provincial legislature that has the same rule. Members should be mindful about not making a reference to the presence or lack thereof of a member of the House.

All members are called upon to do work outside of the House, both directly in parliamentary committees and in conducting the business of the House beyond just this chamber. It is just a good reminder for all of us to be mindful of that.
I thank the member for Lac-Saint-Jean for raising this point of order. That is a very important rule.
Questions and comments, the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jennifer McKelvie (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member spoke about the proactive approach of our government, so I was just hoping that he could really elaborate on what it is that excites him the most about the investments that are being made. It is important that we are investing in ourselves right now so we can build Canada strong. I would really like to know what he has found to be the most important investments, not only for the country but also for his home province.

Mr. Speaker, for me, I have always perceived myself to be a nationalist, first and foremost. I love the fact that the government's approach has been to ensure that every region of our nation is getting major projects. We are working with indigenous people and provinces to make sure that every region is going to benefit from major projects and investments.

For me, in terms of my home province of Manitoba, of course, I am somewhat partial to that. I love the attention that is being given to our aerospace industry through investments in the Canadian Forces. I love the idea that Port of Churchill, for the first time, is being talked about as a viable port into the future. I like the idea that we are working so collaboratively with Wab Kinew as a premier, as well as the other premiers, in building a stronger and healthier nation for all.

Mr. Speaker, I did, of course, notice the investment summit to which my hon. friend, the parliamentary secretary referred, and it is with a sense of déjà vu. The hon. member was not at the Glasgow climate negotiation in 2022, where the Prime Minister was basically the star of the show because he was the special climate envoy for climate finance to the UN Secretary-General. He announced the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, which he pegged at $128 trillion of available investment. Now, this may have a familiar ring to some of us here. Nothing is quite as ephemeral as bankers' non-binding promises, so that $128 trillion announced as GFANS, as they actually made it an acronym instead of a website, is all that is left of it. The only thing that was net zero was the actual investment that emerged from the $128 trillion.

Now, the question I have for my hon. colleague is a precise question: Why will the government not amend the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board Act? We have real dollars, $800 billion of Canadian pension plan dollars, that right now, by law, can only be used and invested where it gets the best return on investment.

To my hon. friend for Winnipeg North, I, in retirement, would like to look down the road at my investment in a local school or a local hospital and not where it went, that $200 million, because the investment board decided it would make more money in Grok developing AI and deepfakes.
Mr. Speaker, I think I will save the CPP issue for another day. I am going to provide a comment on the Toronto summit.

The Canada investment summit attracted the potential for a half trillion dollars of investment. To give the member opposite a sense of the excitement that was created around this summit, we had the premier of Manitoba there, Wab Kinew. He said that, if somebody wanted to invest in the Port of Churchill, Manitoba would exempt them from paying provincial sales tax.

I think there is a wide expectation because this is not just the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister might have been the one who brought everyone to the table, but we have provincial jurisdictions, indigenous people and investors from around the world. I believe there will be billions of dollars of investment as a direct result of that particular summit. It is only a question of time, and I am glad to see that we had so much take-up, in particular from provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians know that the Liberals just changed the math around a bit to make it work with their 2% commitment, such as making the Canadian Coast Guard fall under national defence so they could take credit for the money being spent on the Coast Guard. They did not actually, truly or properly reach that 2% by providing our military with the things that it needs.

What I want to double down on here is that the Prime Minister became Justin Trudeau's adviser in 2020. Again, tax revenue for the government was $284 billion. When the current Prime Minister was advising the former prime minister, it went all the way up to $417 billion. I know that number is going to continue climbing. At the same time, the government is blowing past a balanced budget. It is on a path to keep it going up to around $80 billion a year. At one point, it was projected to be sustained at $63 billion a year. The PBO said that.
Canadians are still wondering what they got for this, other than more people at the food bank.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to recognize that the member wants to talk about Justin Trudeau, and I would talk equally about Stephen Harper. Both of those former prime ministers saw the merit of seeking the advice of our current leader of the Liberal Party, today's Prime Minister. I see nothing wrong with seeking advice. I see that as a positive. I can assure the member opposite that there are many people who sought the advice of today's leader of the Liberal Party, the Prime Minister of Canada. I suspect that it has a lot to do with his economic credentials.

At the end of the day, if we were to be judged on the last 18 months, whether on issues of affordability, the Canadian Forces, investments in Canada or major projects, I believe Canadians would see through the Conservative games.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the House before I begin that I will be splitting my time today with my esteemed colleague from Vaughan—Woodbridge. I am happy to share time with him.

Today, we are going to talk about the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report. I agree with parts of it. The House will hear my critiques of parts of it as well, because all of this is open to debate. I hope my colleagues across the way will listen to some of this debate on how we forge our direction in Canada economically going forward.
I will quote from the report:

Quote.QuotePara: PBO anticipates that federal borrowing will grow significantly faster than deficits, which are measured on an accrual basis. Over the next five years, cumulative deficits are projected to total $333.3 billion, whereas federal borrowing is projected to rise by $732.9 billion....

Content.ParaText: Let us look at the delta there, the change, if we can. There is over $400 billion more in borrowing than deficits. This is a partial result of what the financial wizards on the other side of the House are bringing to Canadian federal government budgeting. It is a whole bunch of cash out the door that Canadians have to pay interest on without it looking like debt. This is the issue about investments versus spending. They have changed the way we look at debt and deficits in Canada and have categorized them differently.

Nevertheless, the number Canadians need to worry about is the amount of interest they are paying on that debt. That number has gone from $24 billion a year in 2020, around when I first came to the House in 2019, up to $59 billion this year and $83 billion in four years' time. Let us think about that escalation of debt. That escalation of debt is two things: It is more money we are paying interest on, but it is also a higher rate of interest. The Parliamentary Budget Officer illustrates clearly that the stress we have on the debt and the amount in bonds outstanding are going to cause Canada to start paying a higher interest rate. It is right in the report.

We can talk about our AAA rating, but the fact is, because we are borrowing so much, we will have to start paying a higher rate of interest. It is not just more interest on more debt and more debt, but a higher rate of interest as well. This is what we call a waterfall. This is going to continue to impact Canadians. It is $83 billion at the federal level alone.

If we take a look at all the debt in Canada in U.S. dollars, we have about $4.6 trillion in debt across the nation. This puts us as one of the most indebted nations in the world. This is a problem. It is a combination of consumer debt, corporate debt and government debt.

The government always tries to say that our debt-to-GDP ratio is only 40% plus, but let me say that that is an illusion, because government debt in this country is not just federal government debt; it is federal government debt plus provincial government debt. The amount of debt that provincial governments are in collectively across the country is about $1 trillion. If we add up the debt, not the amount outstanding, of $1.6 trillion at the federal level and $1 trillion at the provincial level, plus the massive amount of debt that consumers and corporations have outstanding, we have a massive wall of debt in Canada that is almost the worst in the world.

There comes a point in time when this becomes a problem and we have to start addressing it. That time is right on our horizon, because interest rates are starting to rise. Not only are they going to rise for the federal government, making it pay more money, but they also going to rise for consumers, who are going to have to start paying more for their mortgages and more for their consumer debt. They are also going to start rising for corporations, which will have to cut back because they are paying more in interest and have less money to invest, as the Prime Minister likes to say.

Let us look at the $83 billion in debt interest, which is ridiculous. When Canadians ask why we cannot fix health care, I am going to bring them back to the Jean Chrétien years. I remember the Mulroney years when we talked about an operating balance. Brian Mulroney was a very good prime minister, in my opinion, and he got us to a point where we had an operating balance. We still had a huge amount of debt we were paying, but we had an operating balance.

This is where the current government pretends it wants to go, although it is very selective about what it uses in the numbers in the operating balance. The Parliamentary Budget Officer's job is to assess the government against its performance, but a lot of the numbers are now hidden. I am glad she points out the accrual basis and the extra $400 billion in borrowing under the government's new way of accounting for these programs.

It is a mirage. We have to get ahead of this. This $80 billion a year in debt interest payments is far too much for Canada. That is $2,000, give or take, per person in Canada, not per family. For a family of four, $8,000 goes out the door before they even see it. Most families in Canada are probably not paying $8,000 in taxes, but that is going out the door whether they like it or not. Everybody is behind, not counting their personal debt as well.

What effect does this have on the economy? It causes inflation. If we look at what the Parliamentary Budget Officer says in this report, she talks about the reduction in real GDP growth, to 0.9% in this economy. The nominal is 5.4%. What is the difference? It is called the GDP gross domestic product deflator, which is 4.6%. If anybody tells us the interest is only 3% or 2.5% in Canada, then why is the GDP deflator, which is a proxy for inflation, at 4.6%? If we measured these things, as they are real and affect people's lives, we would understand the pain that Canadians are feeling right now, as opposed to hiding behind a bunch of numbers.

Let me correct the Parliamentary Budget Officer, because she buys into this mirage of what net debt is. When the government describes its net debt, what it is doing is taking hundreds of billions of dollars of pensioners' assets and saying that it is the government's asset. It is not the government's asset; it is the pensioners' asset.

The government should tell Canadians directly that when things get rough, because things are going to get rough with our financial situation, it is going to reach in there, grab some of their pension earnings and put them on its balance sheet, because the bankers across the world we owe interest to are expecting us to do that. If that is part of the arrangement, the government needs to make it clear to Canadians that their pensions, and Quebeckers' pensions, which are not managed by the same management team, are on the table for the government to use. That is how it calculates its debt-to-GDP ratio. It is dishonest, unless the government has some arrangement with the Canada pension plan behind the scenes to make that happen.

What makes this even more troubling is that Canadians were promised fiscal discipline by the very well-educated Prime Minister. We have to acknowledge that he is a well-trained economist. However, the results we are getting from this well-trained economist are anything but good. If he is hiding the numbers in different balance sheets and raising the debt that Canadians have to pay, he is not performing as expected.

Canadians were promised fiscal anchors. There is not one fiscal anchor, in the seven years I have been here, that the government has stuck to. It keeps making things up as it goes along. Even the Parliamentary Budget Officer in her report has said that it is not going to meet its fiscal anchors.

When are we going to say enough is enough? It has no fiscal discipline whatsoever. An economist like the Prime Minister must understand our debt position in the world. He must understand that he is visiting inflation upon Canada. He must understand the cliff we are getting to as far as our outstanding debt in this country goes, including in the provinces.

Commitments are made to balance the budget. Commitments are made to get back to fiscal discipline in this country. None of them have been met. If anybody has been watching over the last several months, even though the government set itself a $60-billion-plus deficit, it has continued to make announcement after announcement as if money is no object. If money is no object to our Prime Minister and he thinks he can continue to keep spending, making announcements and blowing $40 billion here and $50 billion there without any consequences, then we have to go back to the drawing board and figure out what exactly is going to happen.

I will tell members what happened when Jean Chrétien had to deal with the debt. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien had to cut payments to the provinces. The result of those cuts to the provinces is that they had to adjust their health care spending, and health care was cut across Canada. That was the result of a choice that that government had to make because it was fiscally off base. The debt had gotten too high in Canada. We are approaching that position again.
When I ran for this position, a key consideration was to get this country back to balance. We need to get back to balance. Will the government commit to getting us there sooner rather than later?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is important to recognize that the government has made a commitment with respect to the operating balance, which I think is a positive thing. The member might find some light in that.
He made reference to the PBO quite a bit in his comments. I wonder if he is aware that even under Stephen Harper's administration, warnings came from the Parliamentary Budget Officer.

At the end of the day, I believe we have fiscal capacity. Does the member believe that if we have fiscal capacity, we should seriously look at investing in Canadians to try to build a larger economy, which would help out in the long run?

Mr. Speaker, we have talked about the operating balance. I have pointed out a bunch of numbers that were part of the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report. Fiscal capacity is there until it is not. Suddenly, it all turns around overnight, and it turned around when Jean Chrétien was Prime Minister. I pointed out the example. It happens very suddenly when the IMF, the International Monetary Fund, comes in and says that we can no longer pay our bills.

What is on the horizon here? I will point out to the member that interest rates are rising around the world, primarily because of excess government debt everywhere, in Canada in particular. The increase in government debt is going to cause more risk. Therefore, bond rates will go up and more people will have to pay money. This avalanche will happen before it is planned. It will happen very suddenly, and we need to get it in front of us. We need to make sure we are aware of it. We need to make sure we know how to deal with it. Fiscal capacity will disappear very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister was the governor of the Bank of England, he had a fancy for printing money. We know that the Trudeau government's response to COVID was to print money. Some $600 billion of extra currency was printed in Canada. Now we are starting to see the effects of that through inflation.

When we see the government trying to use creative accounting practices to cook the books in its favour, I am wondering if the member could explain a bit more the problems that it creates for Canadians, who are really struggling with the cost of living crisis, because opposite to what the government claims, affordability is the worst it has been in a generation.

Mr. Speaker, the issue is that there is one pool of money in the world but a whole bunch of people dipping into it. As I pointed out, in Canada we have federal government debt, we have provincial government debt, we have consumer debt and we have corporate debt. All of these are in the same debt pool, so when there is a risk, it all goes up. When it all goes up, inflation happens. Inflation is going to happen as far as the expenses go on interest, but when the government excessively spends and runs huge deficits, it causes massive inflation in the economy, asset inflation in particular.

One of the reasons we have what is called a K-shaped economy in Canada right now is that people who have assets have seen those assets inflate. People without those assets have gone without, so those people are waiting in line for a home that is going to take far longer to build. They cannot enter the housing market for a much longer period of time, into their mid-thirties and forties now, when it used to be in their mid-twenties and early thirties. This is a problem. This is the cause of inflation. This is a result of governments spending too much and thinking that somebody down the road will pay the bill. That is not going to happen.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to go back to the issue of the ability to invest. If we are investing in projects that will generate wonderful revenues into the future for government, is that not a wise thing? I think of LNG two. Yes, there is a cost to the federal government, but in the long run, there will also be phenomenal financial resources coming, with a return to the federal government.

Would the member not agree that investing can mean many different forms of returns for Ottawa? That could be anything, including income tax and beyond. I would like his comments on the value of investing.

Mr. Speaker, that opens up a good avenue for me to talk about. LNG Canada should not require any government investment. Quite frankly, LNG one did not require any government investment. LNG two should not require any government investment.

What the Government of Canada is doing right now, under the Liberal Prime Minister, is effectively replacing private sector investment with government investment. It is inflated. It is not getting anything done particularly well, as far as what they call investment goes, if there is no test to it. Frankly, it is displacing the investment that should be happening in our economy rather than adding to it. It has to stop. We have to get the private sector back on track.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise today on behalf of the wonderful people in the great riding of Vaughan—Woodbridge.

Canadians have been told for years that Ottawa needs to spend more to make their lives better, yet every time Conservatives in the House raise the affordability crisis, we are met with the same response from the Liberal government: another list of programs, another spending announcement and billions more dollars in borrowed money. Why is the measure of success for the Liberal government always how much money it spends, not tonnes produced, businesses opened or even jobs created?

We constantly hear from the Prime Minister and the Liberals that they are not spending but are investing. We have been hearing this for almost 11 years at this point, and I think it is time we ask a very fair question. For most Canadians, for Canadians watching at home, is their life any better today? Despite all the announcements, all the billions of dollars in allocated funds, has their life marginally improved at all?

Canadians are struggling to afford groceries. I hear from young people all the time in my riding and across this country who say they have almost given up on the dream of home ownership. They find it increasingly expensive. There is a report out of the Bank of Canada on the brain drain that is happening here. Young people are moving to different jurisdictions such as the United States in order to find employment due to cost of living constraints.
Just last week, Food Banks Canada reported 2.35 million food bank visits in a single month, an increase of 117% since 2019. The CEO of Food Banks Canada says this is:

Quote.QuotePara: the story of what happens when millions of people are running out of options. In the past, most people in Canada could absorb a small financial setback... Those days are over. Canada's bleak new reality is that millions of people are making impossible trade-offs every day as they choose between food or rent.

Content.ParaText: A statement such as that should alarm every single member of the chamber.

Taking all this into account, it is hard to even fathom that the Prime Minister had the audacity to stand up in this place and say, “Affordability is the best it has been in...a decade.” These are not me putting words in his mouth; those were his words. However, I would not blame him. After all, he is only the Prime Minister of Canada, and as a matter of fact, colleagues, he just got here.

Well, he has been Prime Minister for almost two years at this point, and at some point he has to take responsibility for the country he is governing. We are beginning to see a very familiar pattern with the Prime Minister: He tells Canadians one thing, but his record demonstrates something that is very different. His promise to get federal spending under control is one example. How often have we heard the Prime Minister state boldly that the Liberals are going to spend less and invest more? I know he just got here, but surely a year and a half is enough time to explain how he intends to keep that promise he made to Canadians.

Last week, the Parliamentary Budget Officer released her latest assessment of the government's finances, and the numbers raised some serious questions. Allow me to list just a few of the PBO's findings. This is sourced from a CTV news article:

Quote.QuotePara: The PBO released her latest economic forecast on Tuesday, which is projecting slower growth in the country’s real GDP forecast... The outlook also spells trouble for the federal government’s debt, and the cost of servicing that debt, projecting a growing debt-to-GDP ratio in the coming years.

Declining deficit-to-GDP ratio is one of the federal government’s [own] fiscal anchors. But, according to [the] PBO..., the charges to service the debt is “the fastest-growing piece of government spending right now.”

Content.ParaText: When the Prime Minister tells Canadians his government is going to spend less, I think they are entitled to ask exactly what he means by this. There is simply no factual evidence to support that he is spending less, as he claimed time and time again that he would. In fact, he is spending so much more. It is not just the size of the deficit that should concern Canadians. It is all those years of borrowing and what exactly that is now costing us.

Five years ago, Ottawa spent $24.5 billion servicing the national debt. This year, that bill is projected to rise to $59.3 billion. In four years from now, that is going to climb to a whopping $83 billion. That is 13.6¢ for every dollar of federal revenue. It is a number so big that the human brain can barely even conceptualize what that is or just how massive it is.

At a time when Canadians are struggling to access health care, the government is now projected to spend more on debt-servicing interest than it transfers to provinces and territories through the Canada health transfer. I ask the House and Canadians watching at home, what does that money actually provide? I will say what it does not do. It certainly does not shorten the wait times Canadians are facing to see their doctor. For a family of four, this year's federal interest bill will cost each family $6,000. Canadians are being asked to live within their means by a government that has yet to explain exactly how it is going to live within its means.

Next Thursday, the finance minister is going to come to the House, stand here and deliver yet another federal budget. I think we should all take note, and Canadians watching at home should certainly be well aware, of the timing of the introduction of that budget, which is the Thursday before the break week, to limit accountability and scrutiny of the budget, which will raise some serious questions about what we will find in that budget when we get to dig into it.

I would love to be proven wrong on all this, but judging by all the metrics, including what the PBO said recently, all roads lead to Canadians' having a very good reason to be concerned about what is in the fiscal budget this year. The Liberal government's answer to nearly every problem seems to be to spend more money. Where does that money come from? It certainly does not grow on trees. It certainly does not come from Santa Claus.
