It comes directly from Canadians, either through taxes they pay today or through the borrowing that taxpayers will have to service for years down the road. The government continues to mortgage the future of my kids and the kids of every single Canadian watching at home today.

There is something else in the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report that Canadians should hear before the budget is released. Excluding new announcements, total revenues are $9.2 billion higher, on average, over the next five years. Much of that comes from higher prices, particularly for oil and other commodities, which have boosted the federal tax revenue. In fact, the PBO has actually lowered their forecast for economic growth this year. While Canadians are dealing with higher prices and a slowing economy, Ottawa and the Liberal government are collecting more revenue than previously expected.

What happened to all that additional revenue? The government has announced new spending and tax measures, costing some $52.6 billion over the same five years. I am sure the government will tell us how important each and every single one of those measures is. If the Prime Minister's promise is to spend less and get the deficit under control, should we not at least expect some improvement in the country's finances when the additional revenues come in?

Instead, the PBO is projecting that the deficit will reach $70.2 billion next year. That is before we have even seen what the government plans to announce in next Thursday's budget. We also keep hearing that the government is going to balance the operating budget. It is the government itself that decides what constitutes operating or capital expenses, and it does so quite arbitrarily, might I add. This leaves open the possibility that the Liberals move an expense from one category into another, simply to say that they have reduced or eliminated the operating budget.

According to the PBO, spending on capital expenditures is far outpacing the deficit. This is why Canadians should be very concerned about this classification issue. Federal borrowing is expected to rise by $732 billion, while the cumulative deficit will be $333 billion over a five-year period.

For Canadians, I come back to the question I have been asking throughout my this speech: Where is the Prime Minister's plan to spend less? Canada is still running enormous deficits, debt interest is growing significantly and the Parliamentary Budget Officer now projects that the government will miss its own commitment to maintain a declining debt-to-GDP ratio. Which spending is being reduced? When will Canadians see the deficit brought under control? How does the Prime Minister intend to stop interest from consuming more money than they send to Ottawa?
This is why the Prime Minister's image as a banker seems to be collapsing and he needs to come to the finance committee to answer these very serious questions.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think today's official opposition underestimates the value of accountability through the different ministers and parliamentary secretaries. Stephen Harper was here for question period but never showed up at the finance committee to address budget issues. There is no change there. Every day we sit, the Conservative Party gets to ask literally dozens of questions, whatever questions they want. There are always ministers here to field those questions.

The Minister of Finance presents the budget and will be held to account for the government budget. Does the member believe that the Minister of Finance has an obligation to be the one held accountable for the finance budget?
Mr. Speaker, absolutely we would love to see the finance minister at the finance committee as well. I know he will be coming to the finance committee when the budget is introduced.

However, given the state of the fiscal position we are in, the PBO's own assessment that was released recently and the fact that the Prime Minister of this country is a trained economist who ran on his image as a banker, as somebody who understands the fiscal conditions of this country, these conditions are deteriorating rapidly. If he is the man, he is the man to answer the questions, so he should come to the finance committee, address the committee and let Canadians know exactly what is going on with this fiscal position and the government's record.

Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader said that Stephen Harper never appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance. However, Stephen Harper did not have a 27% attendance rate at House of Commons debates.

The fact remains that the Prime Minister travels all over the world. He is involved in foreign policy. He is always closely followed by Brookfield, whether in Saudi Arabia, India or at an announcement about condos in British Columbia. We even wonder whether this company might not be his economic and political right-hand man.

However, he does not come to talk to us. He could come talk to us in committee about his vision of investment, or rather his obsession with investment. He is willing to invest $150 billion in the Alto project, although there is no business case, and to destroy the 2% of farmland we have left in Quebec.
I would like to hear the member's comments on my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question.

I would like to start by saying that the Prime Minister is probably the least accountable and least transparent prime minister I have witnessed in my lifetime. My colleague mentioned question period appearances, which are severely lacking in the chamber, but I would also say that we notice, as the Prime Minister goes around, that most of his announcements are actually made in foreign media, not here in the press galley to Canadian media. Where is the transparency? Where is the accountability? I am sure members of the media and the Canadian public would like to hear much more about the Prime Minister and his plans announced right here on Canadian soil.

With respect to big projects such as Alto's, I will say that it seems the government does not have a ceiling on these projects. It cannot demonstrate profitability, and we do not know what they are ultimately going to cost.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague's speech was excellent. I would like to ask a very simple question: Could the member think of just a few ways the Liberal government could lower federal spending to get its budget under control?

Mr. Speaker, we have already outlined some $200 billion in spending that we could eliminate today. For instance, we could eliminate foreign aid. We could eliminate costly projects, such as the Alto project, that are just going to cost us a totally inappropriate amount of money without delivering results for Canadians. We can talk about all the consultants that the government has spent money on over time. Everywhere we look, we find misuse of funds. There are plenty of areas where we would see a place to cut spending so we could direct that money at better projects.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform you that I will be sharing my time with the member for Scarborough Southwest.

I am very pleased to rise today to speak to the motion put forward by the leader of the official opposition. It touches on an issue that affects all of us: the state of our public finances and what they enable us to do for Canadians.

I believe there is at least one thing members on both sides of the House can agree on: The world is changing fast. It is changing unpredictably; trade tensions are on the rise, supply chains are being reshaped, and decisions made far from here are being felt in our kitchens, our factories and our small and medium-sized businesses. I see this in my riding of Bourassa every day. Families are carefully budgeting, and business owners on our main streets are wondering what tomorrow will bring. They do not expect slogans from us; they expect us to take this seriously.

Faced with such uncertainty, what does a responsible government do? Our government is focusing on what it can control. It is strengthening the economy here at home. It is diversifying its trade relationships abroad. It is making strategic investments to build a stronger, more independent and, above all, more resilient economy. All of this rests on one essential condition, and one condition alone: a solid financial position. A sound financial position is not an end in itself. It is an asset for the country and a tool for the government. It is what allows us to protect Canadians when the storm hits. It is what gives us the means to respond to shocks. Above all, it is what allows us to invest in the future rather than simply endure it.

The good news is that Canada is entering this period from a position of strength. The government is not the only one saying so; the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, agrees. It should be noted that the IMF does not engage in politics; rather, it produces calculations, figures and rather interesting performance indicators. According to its most recent projections, Canada will have the second-lowest deficit in the G7 this year as a share of its economy. That deficit will continue to decline over the coming years. It is expected to fall from 2.5% of GDP in 2026 to 2.4% in 2027, before falling to 1.7% by 2031.

Across the globe, budgetary pressures are mounting, yet Canada remains among the strongest performers in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the entire G7. Canada is one of only two G7 countries, alongside Germany, to hold a AAA credit rating from the major credit rating agencies. The AAA rating cannot be bought; it must be earned. This rating is not merely a badge of honour. It is a vote of confidence from investors around the world. This confidence has measurable value: It helps keep our borrowing costs as low as possible, and that directly protects taxpayers.

There are other assets in addition to that. Canada is the best-connected economy in the world, with free trade agreements that open the door to 1.5 billion consumers. We offer by far the most competitive tax environment in the G7 for new business investment.

We are not letting those strengths go to waste; we are putting them to work. In fact, last month, Canada hosted the first-ever Canada investment summit. We brought together some of the world's biggest investors and gave them a simple message: Come and see what Canada has to offer. The result was nearly $500 billion in new funding and investment commitments in Canada. However, attracting investors is not enough. They need a reason to want to stay, to build and grow here in Canada. That is why we announced the new productivity mega deduction.
What does a mega deduction actually mean?

It means that businesses will be able to immediately and permanently write off their eligible investments in a broad-based range of assets. The percentage of assets covered will increase from about 15% to more than 65%.

This measure would help an SME that is hesitating over whether to buy a new machine. There is an industrial area in my riding of Bourassa. If an SME wants to buy a new machine or modernize its systems, this measure is a reason to say yes to that investment. If a large company is torn between Canada and another country, this measure is a reason to choose our country, Canada. Whether small, medium or large, all our businesses benefit. Whether in Quebec, Alberta or elsewhere in the country, everyone benefits. When businesses invest in their equipment and their workers, our overall productivity improves.

Canada has a financial advantage, and we are determined to protect it, because investing in the future does not mean spending recklessly. On the contrary, budget 2025 marked a real shift in how public finances are managed, and this plan is working.

As the Prime Minister recently announced, the government is on track to balance its operating spending as early as 2027-28, a year earlier than our government had projected. We are also committed to rigorously implementing the efficiency measures set out in budget 2025.

The Minister of Finance and National Revenue will table the 2026 budget on November 5. On November 5, we will not be tabling slogans. We will not be tabling a motion. We will be tabling a budget. The logic is very simple: fewer resources devoted to the day-to-day operations of government and more resources devoted to the things that build our economic capacity for decades to come, such as infrastructure, major projects and revenue-generating assets.

Every family understands the difference between the money we spend to meet our day-to-day needs and the money we invest to build our future. A prudent family keeps a close eye on the former. A wise family never neglects the latter. That discipline is not optional. Our fiscal position is strong today, but in no way does that mean we can take it for granted.

That is why the government has adopted two clear and essential rules. First, operating expenses must be balanced with revenues. Second, the deficit must remain on a downward path relative to the size of our economy. These are two simple, measurable rules, and our government is abiding by them.

This brings me to my conclusion. Canada's fiscal strengths are real. We have one of the strongest financial positions in the G7, with the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio and a AAA credit rating. Our responsibility is twofold. The first responsibility is to preserve these strengths. The second is to use them for growth.

That means investing in infrastructure and major projects, attracting more private capital, empowering our businesses to grow, diversifying our trade so that we are less dependent on a single partner, and diligently managing our public finances. That is exactly what we are doing. As I was saying, we live in a rapidly changing world. Neither the Speaker of the House, nor I, nor the Prime Minister, nor any member of the House can control what happens outside our borders. However, we can control the choices we make, and our choice is clear. We are choosing to build on our strengths, invest in the future and build a more resilient and more prosperous economy for our children. We do not control the world, but we can control our choices.

Mr. Speaker, the government often says health care is a priority, yet the PBO shows that the debt servicing spending this year already exceeds the health transfers. By 2030, the debt servicing cost will hit $83 billion, while health care transfers are projected to only be $67 billion.
Will the Liberal government commit that no future budget will allow the debt charges to exceed the Canadian health transfers?
Mr. Speaker, here is what Canadians watching us need to know about interest charges: They have increased, but they have increased around the world.

Given the rise in rates that the whole world has experienced, the real question is this: Who is weathering it best? That is the real question, not whether interest charges have exceeded health transfers.

As I just said, Canada has the lowest net debt‑to‑GDP ratio in the G7 and a AAA credit rating. That rating is what keeps our borrowing costs as low as possible. In addition, our deficit is on a downward path.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Bourassa, with whom I have the good fortune to serve on the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs.

He spoke about what a responsible government does. He said we needed to diversify our alliances abroad. He said that while we do not control what happens outside our borders, we can control our choices. Now to my question. Does he think that we share common values with the Erdogan regime when it comes to democracy, respect for human rights, the rule of law and freedom of expression?
Can my colleague tell me if we share the same values as, for example, Saudi Arabia, where there is outright gender apartheid?

Does my colleague think that Mohamed bin Zayed is involved in what is happening in Sudan? He was welcomed with a huge banquet last night, but at the same time, he was condemned this morning in a press release.
Is my colleague telling me that, if the current tariff crisis had occurred in the 1980s, his government would have signed deals with South Africa, which was under the apartheid regime?

So far, that is what I see. I see a government that is setting aside its principles and values under the pretext of a trade war. Members are talking about what a responsible government does. They are rewriting history. It is Orwellian.
I would like him to answer my question.
Mr. Speaker, once again, I would like to say what a pleasure it is to sit alongside my colleague on the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs.
The first answer is very clear and simple: The Government of Canada will uphold its values, no matter which country it does business with.

Economically speaking, we are in a situation where we need to diversify our trade. Of course, without compromising our Canadian values, we have economic interests in other countries such as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, and throughout Europe, with which a summit will soon be held.
We are going to pursue that with the values that Canada is known for. People want to invest in Canada for its values, its economic strength and the opportunities we give to our investors.
Mr. Speaker, in his speech, my colleague and friend from Bourassa mentioned Canada's fiscal position relative to other G7 countries.
Can he explain why those facts are so important for our economy and our country?

Mr. Speaker, to answer the question, I will just talk about the mega deduction, although there is also an opportunity to attract investors. For example, I had an opportunity to host a round table in Bourassa's industrial area. Industrialists and businesses want to invest, and the mega deduction will help them upgrade their fleets and machinery. That will create jobs. It is good both for employment in our ridings and for our industries.

To repeat what I said earlier, this is about our ability to attract investment, as we did at the first-ever summit. I think the future will be a lot more promising because we can attract a lot more investment, because of our potential and, as I said in the previous answer, because of our values.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions among the parties, and if you seek it, I think you will find unanimous consent for the following motion.
I move:

Quote.QuotePara: That, notwithstanding any standing order or usual practice of the House, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, following Private Members' Business, the House shall continue to sit until midnight for the sole purpose of debating Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, provided that, during the proceedings on the said bill, no quorum calls, dilatory motions or requests for unanimous consent shall be received by the Chair, except for a unanimous consent motion to see the clock.

Content.ParaText: All those opposed to the hon. parliamentary secretary’s moving the motion will please say nay. It is agreed.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. All those opposed to the motion will please say nay.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Opposition Motion—Appearance of the Prime Minister before the Standing Committee on Finance

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the constituents and residents of Simcoe North to talk about some important issues facing the economy and the importance of promises.

What is a promise if one has no intention of keeping their word? When a politician makes a promise, some people immediately think the politician has no intention of keeping their word. I think many politicians make promises they intend to keep. Should we not hold politicians accountable for the promises they make to Canadians, and for promises on subjects that go directly to the underlying credibility of the politician? What do I mean?

The Prime Minister was elected, I think in part, on a record or a résumé that many Canadians felt was credible, especially in the areas of budgetary economics or fiscal discipline. The Prime Minister introduced a new fiscal anchor, which is really a fancy term for a fiscal target. It has only been one year since that target has been in place, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer recently indicated that the Prime Minister will blow through his own self-imposed fiscal target. I mean, this is barely a year since that target has been in place, and the Prime Minister has chosen, and I say “chosen” because it is a deliberate choice, to blow through the anchor. The Parliamentary Budget Officer also indicates that revenues are up and that if the government had not increased its spending, it could have met its own fiscal anchor or fiscal target.

This is a deliberate choice by the Prime Minister to break a promise that he made to Canadians less than one year ago. Paul Martin, when he was finance minister, met every single deficit reduction target that was imposed. He met every single fiscal anchor that was imposed. There has not been a Liberal finance minister in 10 years who has met their own self-imposed fiscal targets. At the very first opportunity that the new Prime Minister and the new finance minister had to keep their fiscal promise to Canadians, they chose to break it.

How is it possible that the fiscal genius who is the Prime Minister, as some people will say, is breaking a fiscal promise? He is supposed to be the one who was fiscally restrained and cared about the finances of the nation, yet he is showing himself to be about as reliable, or perhaps I should say as unreliable, as Prime Minister Trudeau in this department. This is an example of the Prime Minister undermining his own credibility on the fiscal finances of the nation by choice, less than a year after he made the promise.

David Dodge, in 2023, wrote, “We have argued in the past that an interest cost/revenue ratio above 10% and a federal debt/GDP ratio that is not declining steadily from close to...where it currently stands signal risks of unsustainability.” He is talking about unsustainability of fiscal finances.
I had a chance to ask Mr. Dodge, former central bank governor, about this point, and he responded:

Quote.QuotePara: If you're spending 10¢ out of every tax dollar that you collect on servicing past debts, that obviously leaves you with less to spend on providing current goods and services.

The problem that we collectively face now and going forward is that we're going to have growth of the economy or growth of the base revenues of government that will be equal to or perhaps even less than the interest rates. The burden of past debt will increase year after year rather than being eroded.

Content.ParaText: That was in 2023. At that point in time, we were just about to approach spending 10¢ of every dollar of government revenue on interest on the debt. In just a few years, the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects, Canada will spend nearly 14¢ of every dollar it receives on interest on the debt. In fact, interest on the debt is the fastest-growing expense line item in the budget. It is growing faster than health care spending increases and faster than any other expenditure.

I am asking myself how it is possible that the Prime Minister, who was elected in part because of his financial credentials, who is a two-time central banker, who is a very well-known economist, who was chair of the Financial Stability Board, who was a Goldman Sachs banker, who, to many people's applauding, was successful as chair of Brookfield and who has fiscal credentials, is making a deliberate choice to break a promise he made to Canadians.

He did not just make the promise to Canada in general. He made a promise to our young people that they would be able to inherit a government and fiscal finances that were not going to be eroded. He said he would spend less to invest more, yet we find out that the government is going to spend nearly 14¢ of every dollar paying interest on the debt. Those obligations will be passed to future generations, and they will have no choice but to meet those obligations. This means less money for social programs, less money to spend on the things Canadians want and a heck of a lot less money to provide significant tax relief to Canadians.

In the face of all of this, the Prime Minister's fiscal plan is actually to borrow record amounts of money in the bond markets. Next year, we will have to borrow almost $600 billion. The year after that, it will be $563 billion, and that is before the new borrowing we are going to see in the budget next week. The government believed interest rates were going to go down last year and into this year, but they have gone up. What is going to happen to debt service costs then?

This is why the deficit target is even worse this year than it was last year. The deficit is at least $3 billion a year higher this year and every year going out. If there is continued trouble, or shocks in the bond markets, our debt service costs are going to increase substantially, and that 14¢ might become 15¢ or 16¢. Members might think I am making something up, but in the late 1970s, debt service costs were, I think, around 15¢. They then went up to 30¢. In fact, I think they peaked at 36¢. We are going in the wrong direction.

This was a primary promise the Prime Minister made to the House, to Canadians and to the next generation, and he is breaking that promise. He should feel the need to answer not just to the House but to all Canadians.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, where I fully agree with the member is on the Prime Minister's credentials. The Prime Minister has put Canada in a great financial position to look at ways we can invest in Canada and Canadians. In the long term, we will see additional revenues coming in to the federal government. This is part of investing. This is something that is direct. There are many indirect ways in which investing helps.

When we listen to the Conservatives, they seem to oppose investing in Canadians to build a stronger, healthier economy. A good example of that is how I was criticized because I made reference to LNG phase two. The Conservatives said the government did not need to invest in that, that it would have happened without the province and the federal government.
Does the member believe in government support and investment?
Mr. Speaker, I was unaware that the member was such a proponent of supply-side economics.

The truth is that the fiscal position of this country is being eroded. It is not getting better under the Prime Minister, even though he made that commitment to Canadians, when we are going to spend nearly 14¢ out of every tax dollar brought in on interest on the debt. Interest on the debt is the fastest-growing expense of the government. We used to spend only 10¢ on the dollar, and before Prime Minister Trudeau came in, we spent only about 7.5¢ of every dollar on interest on the debt.

This is going in the wrong direction, and I am quite shocked. I am surprised that the two-time central banker and much-lauded Goldman Sachs wunderkind has put Canada's fiscal health at risk by borrowing record amounts of money year after year and continuing to stay on this course.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, the member for Simcoe North, for his excellent speech. He is a member who brings a great deal of substance to parliamentary debate.

I would like to discuss the form of the motion, because the motion simply calls for the Prime Minister to be invited to appear as a witness before the Standing Committee on Finance. He does not even have to accept. I think that is necessary. The Minister of Finance appeared before the committee recently. He was unable to answer questions or understand how the tax system works. He showed up with an infographic featuring coloured bubbles that looked like something a seven-year-old would draw for Halloween.

Earlier, the member for Bourassa told us that, as the government, they do not move motions. They are above that. They bring down budgets. They are the ones doing the real work. We supported his private member's bill, incidentally. He seems to have forgotten that. I get the impression that all of this shows a kind of neglect or contempt for parliamentary work. The Liberals will probably vote against the motion.
What do they stand to gain by voting against the motion? We want to invite the Prime Minister to come answer questions. He can even decline the invitation.
Why would they vote against that?
Mr. Speaker, I have shared many good conversations about economics with my colleague. I find him to be incredibly smart, and his question is quite correct.
The Prime Minister does not need to show up to question period every day, and he does not, which is maybe why we are asking that he might show up to a committee to answer some questions about this.

While I have a lot of respect for the finance minister, and I hold him in very high regard as a parliamentarian, this fiscal promise to Canadians was not the finance minister's promise. This was the Prime Minister's promise. It is the Prime Minister's choice to blow through the fiscal anchor. It is the Prime Minister's choice to put our debt on a bad track. Frankly, the Prime Minister should want to answer questions.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague channelled Paul Martin in his speech, and so I would ask him how exactly the Liberal government of that era got back to fiscal responsibility when it came to downloading responsibilities and costs to the provinces. Conservatives have been talking about what is going to happen with our social programs. What happened with social programs when the Liberals of the past were in the same situation that the Liberals of today are going to be putting us in?

Mr. Speaker, it was devastating for social services delivery across the country when the Liberal government started downloading additional responsibilities, because it had to drastically cut its spending to make the bond markets happy. The bond markets are not happy right now, and we might see continued pressure on our fiscal finances as a result.

It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Saanich—Gulf Islands, Indigenous Affairs; the hon. member for Brandon—Souris, Finance; the hon. member for Riding Mountain, Health.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to be here today. I will be splitting my time, to acknowledge that at the front end.

We have been asked to speak today on an opposition day motion, but it is so much more than that. This is about where Canada is right now in the world. We have a government that continues to spend recklessly, which is driving up the cost of living for all Canadians. We have a Parliamentary Budget Officer who has been using certain terms for over a year: stupefying, not hitting financial targets, mesmerizing, and additional costs that are driving up costs for Canadians.

We now know that the Liberal government is set to spend more on interest than it is on health care transfers. We know that the share of interest for a family is about $6,000. That is money going to bondholders and bankers across this country. We also know that the Prime Minister, in an election that occurred a year and a half ago or so, promised that he would have a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio. We will talk more about the deficit-to-GDP ratio too, because that in itself is a way to avoid accountability.

Let us talk about the impact this is having on Canadians. We can see that inflation is starting to creep up. It is now up to 2.8%, and it continues to grow. In fact, all of the experts are now ringing warning bells and telling everyone. From markets to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, they are all predicting that the rate of inflation will increase and interest rates will also increase. Even Tiff Macklem is indicating that he will increase interest rates. That means that if someone is renewing a mortgage in the next three to six months, a $250,000 mortgage at standard rates for a five-year term, they could see an annual increase somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3,000 to $5,000. I would ask all members in this House which families have an extra $3,000 to $5,000 to spend.

Just to do some simple arithmetic, if it were not for the Liberal government, we would not have an interest cost for the federal government of $6,000. We would not have an increase in the cost of mortgages, which is now up to $3,000 to $5,000. That is thousands of dollars.

Here is a simple thought exercise. Let us think about what could be done with that money if it were not going to interest. It is money that could go to health care. It is money that could go directly to Canadians to be used for their children to play hockey. It could be used for Canadian kids to do the extracurricular activities they desire. It could be used for families to feed themselves at the end of the month, so they would not have to scrimp, save and put their grocery bill on their credit card.
Let us talk a bit about the fiscal anchor. The promise the Prime Minister made is not something the Conservatives or the leader of the official opposition made up. It was from the Prime Minister.

Most of the world, nearly all of it in fact, judges debt by something called the debt-to-GDP ratio. Our debt is a big, scary monster. In fact, it is $1.4 trillion. Instead of linking his promise to that, because he must have already known, this Goldman Sachs wonder kid, that he would not be able to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio, he chose a different number. It sounds a bit like debt to GDP but is entirely different. He chose deficit to GDP. Instead of the cumulative debt, it is the amount the government is spending over what it is earning each year, which is eminently more in the control of the government of the day.

He said that we were going to have a declining deficit-to-GDP number, but he cannot achieve that. The Parliamentary Budget Officer said that the government is going to miss it for the next two years. When it comes to promises from governments beyond two years, I do not put a lot of stock in them, because two years is a long way out for the Liberal government. For the foreseeable future, the government will not hit that mark.

Some on the progressive left will say the problem is that we need more taxes and revenue, but the government is raking in record revenue. Is it because our economy is growing and doing great? No, not at all. It is because the government's inflation is driving up the cost of everything, suffocating our ability to live. It also drives up government revenue. That, combined with high oil prices, means the government is taking in more money than ever, yet somehow this banker has been able to outspend our record revenue.

Let us talk about a few more stats. As I said, Canadians are going to the grocery store and are realizing that a dollar does not go very far. It is $50 to fill up one bag of groceries. The $100 that used to pay for groceries for a week now lasts but a day or two. It is because of two issues. One we have talked about: inflation and higher interest. The other side of the ledger is income.

Generally, when a government has an expansive fiscal policy, we get higher income. It makes sense. If we are lowering taxes and spending more, according to Keynesian economics we should get economic growth. However, the government has managed to spend more and not get economic growth. It almost defies reason that it was able to do this. Only the Liberal government could spend billions and still have our GDP per capita, which is analogous in many ways to our income per capita, stay flat over the last 11 years.

If we do a comparison, our gross debt is about 110% and the U.S.'s is, to be frank, about 125%, which sounds a bit better. The U.S. has the reserve currency, which puts it in a stronger position compared to our country, as the Canadian dollar is not the reserve currency. The other thing that the U.S. and some other countries have going for them is economic growth. At the same time, we have had practically zero economic growth, GDP per capita, over the last decade.

America's economic growth has averaged well in excess of 2% to 3%, in some years even touching 4%. We can imagine our personal finances. If someone has a large mortgage, even if they have some credit card debt, and has a high income that is consistently increasing, that problem is fixable. The challenge for the Canadian economy, because of the Liberal government's poor economic and fiscal management, is that we have high debt and low, flat incomes. Our GDP per capita would put us at the very bottom of any U.S. state's. These are significant economic challenges that have real economic consequences.

When we talk about bond yields, interest rates, inflation and other metrics, the reality for the people of Northumberland—Clarke is that they are suffering. Over the summer, I spent numerous days going to various food banks across my riding. Every single one of them has had a massive increase since 2015. I really hope the Liberals do some soul-searching. They can pick data points and numbers and we can argue about them, but what they cannot argue about is the people in Northumberland—Clarke who are suffering right now.

Just one of those food banks, if I can share a number, has seen a 3,000% increase since 2015. There is a wide cross-section. It has seen a dramatic increase in children, for example, who have to use the food bank. It has seen seniors having to use the food bank. It has seen people who are employed having to use the food bank because of the Liberals' reckless spending, which has driven the cost of living out of control.

The government really needs to do some soul-searching and think about the ways it can reduce costs. I hope it does that in the next budget. I do not think it will, but Canadians desperately need the government to get spending under control so that Canadians can afford to live.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is important to recognize, as the debate winds down, that as much as the Conservatives try to play on the fear of our deficit and debt situation, experts around the world, whether from the monetary associations or credit rating agencies, have recognized that Canada has good financial capacity. Canada has been given, for example, a AAA credit rating. In the G7, that is something that only Germany can also claim.

At the end of the day, we believe that it is important for us to invest in Canadians, in our infrastructure and in so much more. Can the member explain why, as we believe we should be investing, the Conservatives do not recognize the true value of investing?

Mr. Speaker, this comes down to a decades-old, if not centuries-old, debate. Conservatives believe at heart that the best people to spend Canadians' money are Canadians. We do not believe we need the government to control our lives. Ronald Reagan once famously said that Liberals define compassion by how many people the government helps; Conservatives define compassion by how many people the government does not have to help. If we simply restrained spending, parents would be able to feed their children, businesses would be able to thrive and people would have jobs. These are all self-inflicted wounds by the government.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is telling Canadians to just trust him. He wants Canadians to buy fish in the ocean without even seeing them. I think it would be responsible for the Prime Minister to explain that to Canadians, since he is a fantastic economist, and make them understand what he is trying to do.

The government has been borrowing money for the last 11 years non-stop. How long is it going to take the government to realize that what it has been doing is wrong? I would like the hon. member to elaborate on that.

Mr. Speaker, I always at least enjoy the passion brought by the member for Winnipeg North, but he is not the one who came up with some of these economic plans. That was the Prime Minister. In fact, I am so old that I can remember two years ago when the member was arguing for the exact opposite of what the Prime Minister is now saying.
Let us bring the Prime Minister before committee and have him explain why his plan is failing.

Mr. Speaker, the point is that the plan is not failing. It is the Conservatives who are failing Canadians by not recognizing that, whether it is the Progressive Conservatives, and I underline “Progressive”, in some provinces, the New Democrats in other provinces or the Liberals in other provinces, many governments and administrations recognize the value of investing in Canadians. It is only the far-right Conservatives here in Ottawa who seem to oppose it. Why?
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have a tell. Whenever they are losing, they use the phrase “far right”, so we know we are winning on this debate.

I could give members the numbers: the flat GDP per capita, the ever-increasing deficit, the debt at $1.4 trillion and the increase in interest rates. I could go through all that, but I invite the member to come down to Northumberland—Clarke and go with me to the food banks. They will all explain to him the dramatic increase in the use of food banks by children. That is because of his policies, and I—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Saanich—Gulf Islands.

Mr. Speaker, I am inspired by my colleague from Northumberland—Clarke, who thinks that the Liberals are losing when they use the words “far right”. I wonder when we will start calling the current government the “near right”, because I find very little difference between what was found in the Conservative platform and what is being implemented by the new government, which still has the title “Liberal government”.
I wonder if my friend from Northumberland—Clarke notices that there have been quite a number of elements of the Conservative platform implemented recently.
Mr. Speaker, I have heard perhaps the best compliment I have ever heard given to the member for Winnipeg North and the Liberal government.

Although I have heard that before, I do not think it is a reality. Here is the difference. Here is what Conservatives would do. Conservatives would put Canadians back in control of their lives. They would put dollars back in Canadians' pockets, not give them to Liberal government insiders.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise on behalf of the good people of Scarborough Southwest to speak about their stories and, of course, join in debate to discuss our government's plan, which has made targeted and high-impact investments for Canadians while maintaining the fiscal sustainability that is so necessary for our country right now.

I believe I will be able to shed some light on some of the work that we have been doing, and maybe address some of the misconceptions, and the negative energy, frankly, that we hear from the other side every single day. If the Conservatives could just get on board and actually understand the reality of what Canadians are facing every single day, we would be able to work together to actually address some of the challenges that all of us in the House have talked about. We have heard about food banks. Since the pandemic and throughout the last couple of years, we have seen the lines increase at every food bank. In Scarborough, I have seen that myself.

Just recently, when I talk to the food banks, they say they are getting to a point where they are seeing the numbers decrease. We are actually finding solutions. We are actually able to help people. We are helping students who used to line up at those food banks and families who used to line up at those food banks.

I really hope that we are able to have a discussion where we understand that the Conservatives have really highlighted this debate and made it about fiscal responsibility versus economic growth, as a choice. It is one or the other. I want to say that we need both. We need to have fiscal responsibility, and we also need to have economic growth, not one versus the other. We cannot choose one over the other. That is why it is so important that we are being disciplined, controlled in our measures and focused on that fiscal sustainability.

How did our government do that? Let us talk about some of the plans that our government worked on. When we look at our budgets, for example, the way we spend money, something that I have said over the years in my time as a public representative, standing up for the people I represent in my community, is that a budget is a moral document. That means a budget highlights the values that we are focusing on, what we are spending on and what our priorities are. It really is a moral document on how we take care of one another.

When we look at the way we have spent and what our government has been focusing on, the number one priority that I see every single day, that I know is important for my community, is a plan to build housing. I see that as a priority for our government, and we are already working on that. Our plan also builds on major infrastructure to transform and connect our economy. We have had Conservatives in government for years, but one of the things we failed to do in the past was to actually connect our provinces and territories to one another. This government made an intentional effort to make sure that we are able to connect our provinces to one another so that we can actually have an economy that functions in a seamless way. It also means that we diversify our trades with countries across the world, make new friends and build capacity. That is exactly what we have done.

Another thing that we have done is our plan to lower costs to help families get ahead. That means helping families with our groceries benefit and a child care plan, and focusing on a national school food plan that helps in multiple cities. I know in the city of Toronto, that was something that a lot of schools and a lot of parents appreciated.

Canadians expect their government to manage public finances responsibly, and rightly so. Now rising debt servicing costs reinforce that responsibility, because when we look at the rising debt servicing costs, it is about how we are focusing on that responsibility. Fiscal responsibility is not just about balancing a number on the balance sheet, and it is not just about reducing that number and forgetting everything else, which goes back to what I was saying about that choice between fiscal responsibility versus economic growth. It involves making careful choices. It is about making choices today that strengthen our economy for tomorrow. It is about making choices that improve Canada's ability to stand up for the future and for the children of tomorrow.

In our April economic update, the finance minister gave us a clear and transparent account of Canada's economic performance in an increasingly, if I may remind everyone, uncertain world. It has done two things, I would say. One is that it has given transparency to our businesses, not just small and local businesses but all scales of businesses, so they can seize new opportunities and make sure they are able to thrive. It also helped families. It gave families the confidence to plan for their future.

A lot of families were starting to feel that the uncertainties seen around the world were having an impact at home. When we formed government and came into power, within months, families had the confidence to understand how they can move ahead. Yes, it will be tough, and it will get tougher, but we have a plan, and we will work toward making sure we are able to help families move forward.

How did we do that? We remained focused and we were disciplined. We focused on what we can control. That means balancing our day-to-day operating spending with revenues by 2028-29 and maintaining our fiscal anchors. We heard many of my colleagues speak to that in the House. We also looked at every dollar spent. It is not the government's money, but people's hard-earned dollars. We are responsible for people's tax dollars, and we are making sure that people's money is spent on behalf of Canadians to support growth, resilience and their well-being, to make sure they are able to get ahead. We have a responsibility to spend every single dollar in a way that helps Canadians every single day.

This is the approach that is very important for those on the other side to understand, especially for today's debate. Controlling the cost of government while making the investments needed for a stronger economy is what the government has done. It looked at what we could reduce spending on, and we focused on government spending. We looked at how we could build resilience and focus on building a stronger economy for our nation. Our government knows that we cannot just stand still. It is not an option. There cannot be inaction like we have seen in the past. Underinvestment can be detrimental and cost us significantly.

I want to focus on one more thing before I conclude. It is really important for us to understand that we are facing a time when people across the country want us to unite and help them. Canada is a country where we take care of one another, and if we are building resilience and a stronger economy, we must come together and make sure we are building an economy that helps our future generations.
It being 5:15 p.m., it is my duty to interrupt the proceedings and put forthwith every question necessary to dispose of the business of supply. The question is on the motion.

If a member participating in person wishes that the motion be carried or carried on division, or if a member of a recognized party participating in person wishes to request a recorded division, I would invite them to rise and indicate it to the Chair.
Mr. Speaker, I would request a recorded vote, please.
Pursuant to Standing Order 45, the division stands deferred until Wednesday, October 28, at the expiry of the time provided for Oral Questions.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions among the parties, and if you seek it, I believe you will find unanimous consent for the following motion.
I move:

Quote.QuotePara: That, notwithstanding any standing order, special order or usual practice of the House, during the debate pursuant to Standing Order 66 on Motion No. 10 to concur in the tenth report of the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities, later this day, at the end of the time provided for debate or when no member wishes to speak, whichever is earlier, the motion on the previous question shall be deemed adopted on division, and the question on the original motion be deemed put and a recorded division deemed requested and deferred pursuant to Standing Order 66.

Content.ParaText: All those opposed to the parliamentary secretary's moving the motion will please say nay.
Since no one is opposed, it is agreed.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. All those opposed to the motion will please say nay.
Mr. Speaker, I expect that, if you were to canvass the House, you would find unanimous consent to call it 5:30 p.m., so we could begin private members' hour.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Relieving Grieving Parents of an Administrative Burden Act (Evan's Law)

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from May 29 consideration of Bill C-222, An Act to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code (death of a child), as reported (with amendments) from the committee, and of the motions in Group No. 1.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this evening I am speaking to Bill C-222, which seeks to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code. This bill is sponsored by the member for Burnaby North—Seymour, and I want to commend him for introducing this legislation. It is a bill on a sensitive issue that provides for the following:

Quote.QuotePara: ...a person to whom employment insurance benefits are payable to care for a newborn child or a child placed with them for the purpose of adoption remains eligible to receive those benefits even if the child dies during the benefit period.

Content.ParaText: The bill further provides that an employee remains entitled to maternity or parental leave in the event that the employee's newborn child, or a child placed in the employee's care with a view to adoption, dies during the period of leave.

This bill, which is non-partisan and crosses party lines, is compassionate and appropriate, as it seeks to ease the financial and psychological pressure on families who have lost a child. This is a bill that addresses a real problem, and we are confident that Quebeckers and Canadians will benefit from these measures. This is a real game-changer for families dealing with such tragedies. Let us hope that reality will prove the old saying wrong, however, because it is never too late to right the wrongs of the gutting of EI and workers' rights that occurred under Conservative governments.

Let us not forget that, over the past 10 years, minor adjustments have been made without ever addressing the profound injustices against workers and EI recipients. Despite the Liberals' election pledges and commitments, nothing substantial has been tabled in this decade. Labour organizations in Quebec and Canada and the opposition parties, including the Bloc Québécois—which echoed the main criticisms made by the unions—have made many demands over the past decade.

That is why the Bloc Québécois condemns the inaction and obstruction of the Liberals, who voted against Bloc bills and motions to support workers and allow more people to access EI. However, we are persistent and we will once again table a bill for a more comprehensive reform of EI.

Let us get back to the bill before us. As we saw during the committee study of the current bill sponsored by the member for Burnaby North—Seymour, the cabinet and the Prime Minister quickly made a commitment to the Liberal member to offer their support and a promise that his private member's bill would receive the necessary royal recommendations, a crucial step for any private member's bill requiring new public funds.

I will quote a few figures. Infant mortality has remained relatively stable since the early 2000s in Quebec. The Institut de la statistique du Québec has counted approximately 380 child deaths before the age of one. The infant mortality rate for both sexes is 4.9 per 1,000 births. In the rest of Canada, the rate is slightly higher but not statistically significant. Among the countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, or OECD, we have one of the lowest infant mortality rates in the world. Fortunately, this tragic occurrence is pretty rare, as we can see from the figures.

Having seen the Liberals' tendency to cite the state of the public finances whenever they want to justify saying no, whether to a comprehensive reform of the Employment Insurance Act or to old age security benefits for those aged 65 to 74, the low infant mortality rate means that this enhancement to the EI program and the Canada Labour Code should come at very little cost. For those affected by such tragedies, however, a measure such as Bill C-222 would make all the difference and allow claimants to grieve with greater peace of mind, free from financial anxiety.

As we see time and again, Quebec is at the forefront when it comes to socially oriented public policies. Thanks to the Quebec Parental Insurance Plan, or QPIP, Quebeckers already have a social safety net with the same criteria as those set out in Bill C-222. It is understood that a claimant may apply for QPIP benefits even if a child dies after a claim has been initiated. By contacting the plan's customer service department, claimants can receive the information and assistance they need from a representative. As a result, they receive personalized support tailored to their needs. The plan also specifies that the death of a child has no effect on benefit payments, since QPIP provides for a grace period following pregnancy or childbirth. Naturally, this also applies if a parent is grieving the loss of a child.

It is worth noting that, in 1972, Quebec passed the Crime Victims Compensation Act, which allows victims to receive compensation and the care they need to recover. This law sets out a financial compensation regime for any income losses the victim experiences. In December 2007, without specifically addressing the death of a child, the Quebec act respecting labour standards with regard to absences and leave included provisions that provided compensation for employees who are victims of crime, employees who have lost a loved one as a result of a criminal act or suicide and employees whose child goes missing. The Bloc Québécois believes that workers who are employed by a federally regulated businesses should have the same protections. Furthermore, there is a clear parallel between Bill C-222 and Quebec's political action.

It is also worth noting that, when the committee tabled its report in the House on May 29, 2026, the bill's sponsor was particularly proud that his government gave royal recommendation to his bill. That is great. That is the pivotal stage where the executive branch must give its approval when a private member's bill requires a commitment of public funds. It is important to point out that this is the fourth time in the history of Canada that a private member's bill has managed to make it past this legislative step. The member also mentioned that there are approximately 1,600 Canadian families a year who experience the death of a child. According to him, it is unconscionable to ask parents to contact Service Canada every 14 days to justify their need for employment insurance sickness benefits. Bill C-222 seeks to address this cold and callous measure under which parents cease to be eligible for parental benefits.

The amendments presented at report stage were specifically intended to prevent benefits from ending abruptly. They would allow parental benefits to continue, whether under the standard 40-week benefit period or the extended 69-week benefit period, including in cases where benefits have been extended because of a child's hospitalization. If a child tragically dies at the end of a parent's EI benefits period, each parent will be eligible for five additional weeks. In addition, the bill provides for a 17-week extension of bereavement leave with job protection. Lastly, grieving parents will only have to submit an attestation, sparing them the burden of submitting documentation every two weeks.

To achieve this result, the Liberals tried to put forward some amendments to their colleague's bill in committee, but several were ruled out of order by the chair because they required a royal recommendation. Furthermore, the parliamentary secretary had very little understanding of the amendments she was proposing and was of little help. Things were a bit confusing in committee, which significantly slowed down the work. Finally, the Liberals proposed amendments on May 27, 2026. It should be noted that these provisions are very similar to the ones that were rejected by the committee chair because they all involved expenditures and therefore required a royal recommendation from the government.

For example, one amendment sought to add a new ground for extending the benefit period under section 10 of the Employment Insurance Act if a claimant's child dies during the period in which parental benefits may be paid. This amendment would ensure that a claimant can receive up to 26 additional weeks of EI parental benefits after the death of their child. Parents came to testify in committee and their stories were deeply moving. Tears were shed during the committee's proceedings. It was not easy. The parents simply asked us to allow them to grieve in peace and, above all, without having to battle bureaucracy. Honestly, I do not think anyone ever fully recovers from the tragic death of a child. I am thinking of those bereaved parents. The Bloc Québécois is, of course, in favour of this bill, because our political party has always advocated measures that go even further. We have consistently maintained that a 50-week period is appropriate. We have long advocated for this through the “Émilie Sansfaçon” bill. Although different, our proposal was intended to assist claimants facing a serious illness.

Through this motion, the government is proposing to extend this period to 52 weeks. We welcome this measure, having long maintained that a stillbirth, a miscarriage or sudden infant death are profoundly traumatic experiences. We therefore agree that parents should be entitled to a 52-week period of respite to grieve, heal and come to terms with the loss of a child. All that remains is to take action on behalf of seriously ill workers. This is a battle that still needs to be fought, and for which we have already tabled the “Émilie Sansfaçon” bill. We must stop inflicting financial distress on these workers, as it is profoundly unfair.
This is a good start tonight. It is an important step, but it is far from the end of the fight.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise today to speak in support of Bill C-222, an act to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code regarding the death of a child, also known as Evan's law.

I am pleased that all members who spoke during the first hour of debate of report stage expressed their support for the proposed amendments. The revised bill demonstrates that members of Parliament share a deep commitment to Canadian parents and a common understanding that when a parent faces the unimaginable loss of a child, they expect compassion, dignity and care from us.

Nothing in life is as profoundly devastating as the death of a child. It completely turns the parents' life upside down. In such moments, parents are consumed by their grief. Bureaucracy, money and work should not stand in the way of their recovery, yet under the current framework, they often do. This is not intentional and is what Bill C-222 aims to fix.
The hon. member for Burnaby North—Seymour deserves thanks for his leadership and perseverance in seeing this through and for his unwavering support to many parents across Canada.
I would also like to thank the many colleagues, stakeholders, witnesses and advocates who all contributed greatly to the development and improvement of this important bill.
Their voices have been essential in shaping a bill that truly reflects the reality faced by grieving parents.
Our government has long recognized that balancing family and work obligations can be challenging for Canadians raising children, in addition to the financial stress that can come with it.
Every parent's situation is unique, and our support systems should be able to adapt as much as possible.
Over the years, we have taken important steps to modernize EI maternity and parental benefits so that parents have more flexibility.
This includes allowing maternity benefits to begin earlier, up to 12 weeks before the due date, compared to the previous eight weeks, if mothers need to begin receiving benefits earlier.
It also includes offering parents a choice between standard or extended parental benefits and providing more weeks of benefits for parents who share them.
These measures reflect an effort to build an EI system that is responsive, flexible and sustainable and that supports families through major life events.

Grieving the death of a child is a major life event that the current EI system does not provide enough flexibility and compassion for. Losing a child is a tragedy that requires a compassionate and thoughtful response. This is exactly what the amended Bill C-222 aims to fix.

Currently when a child passes away, EI parental benefits stop. If parents do not notify Service Canada, they may unknowingly incur an overpayment and therefore have to repay. Parents can transition to EI sickness benefits, but they are required to report every two weeks. This is an administrative burden that is often overwhelming for grieving parents. This is not the compassion and understanding that Canadians rightly expect from their institutions.

That is why Bill C-222, with the amendments before us, aims to correct the situation. It proposes that parental benefits may continue following the death of a child, alleviating the need for parents to navigate complex administrative processes at a time when they are least able to do so. It would allow EI parental benefits to continue for up to the maximum duration already established, which is up to 40 weeks for those who select standard benefits and up to 69 weeks for those who select extended parental benefits.

More importantly, for parents who would be near the end of their benefits when their child passes away, the amended bill would ensure that eligible parents may receive up to five additional weeks of benefits as bereavement support. This provision would apply to both the standard and the extended benefits that were originally chosen. These additional weeks would be paid at the same income replacement rate selected at the outset, providing continuity and predictability to parents during such a difficult time.

Another important aspect of these amendments is the effort to minimize the administrative burden. While there may be some circumstances where parents would still need to notify the the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, through Service Canada, the bill would introduce a regulation-making authority to make this process simpler and more compassionate. That is a key improvement.

In parallel, these amendments would also ensure that employees in the federally regulated private sector continue to have access to job-protected leave provisions under the Canada Labour Code while they avail themselves of EI parental benefits, including if they receive the additional weeks of up to five weeks.

These include access to the remaining weeks of parental leave. For employees near the end of their leave at the time of the death of the child, they would be allowed to transition to the current eight weeks of bereavement leave for the death of a child, ensuring that parents do not have to choose between grieving and going to work.

These legislative changes are part of a broader effort by the government to strengthen the social safety net and ensure that federal support systems are responsive to the realities that Canadians face.

We have made significant investments in employment insurance and related programs, to provide meaningful assistance where it is most needed. For example, caregiving benefits have long supported Canadians who must step away from work to care for an ill or injured family member, including, of course, a child. In 2022, EI sickness benefits were expanded, extending their duration so individual families facing illness or injury have greater financial security and job protection as they recover. These changes were informed by consultations with Canadians and reflect an understanding of how caregiving responsibilities and health challenges shape people's lives.

Equally important is the work being done to improve how Canadians access these services. Making benefits easier to obtain can provide significant peace of mind, especially during times of crisis. At its peak, the EI system was managing more than one million claims during the COVID-19 pandemic, which is more than five times the usual volume. In response, the government expanded its capacity, streamlined processes and implemented new approaches.

Since then, we have continued our efforts. Between 2022 and 2025, Service Canada employees worked to refine procedures, test new strategies and improve delivery. As a result, backlogs have been significantly reduced, by 73%, as of January of this year. This progress illustrates that government systems can evolve to be more responsive, efficient and compassionate.

When we consider Bill C-222 and the related amendments before us, we must remember that this legislation is about people. It is about ensuring that in the moments darkest for parents, government processes are not an additional source of stress or hardship. By allowing parental benefits to continue, by simplifying requirements and by ensuring that employees in the federally-regulated private sector have access to job-protected leave, these amendments would take steps toward that goal.
For all these reasons, I am pleased to support Bill C-222 with the proposed amendments, and I encourage all members of the House to do the same.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions among the parties, and if you seek it, I think you will find unanimous consent for the following motion:

Quote.QuotePara: That the order made earlier today, pursuant to Standing Order 97.1(3), respecting the deferral of the recorded division on the motion to concur in the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Public Safety and National Security, be discharged and the motion be deemed adopted on division.

It is agreed.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. All those opposed to the motion will please say nay.
It is agreed.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Relieving Grieving Parents of an Administrative Burden Act (Evan's Law)

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-222, An Act to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code (death of a child), as reported (with amendments) from the committee, and of the motions in Group No. 1.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to discuss Private Member's Bill C-222, an act to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code with respect to the death of a child, introduced by the member for Burnaby North—Seymour. I would like to commend the member for taking up such an important issue and for working with all sides of the House to advance this bill through Parliament. I also want to congratulate him for obtaining a royal recommendation from the government, which allows the bill to proceed.

I would also like to acknowledge my Conservative colleague, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan, for his work in collaborating with the member for Burnaby North—Seymour to have the bill move through the various stages, including our own internal caucus review process.

During his intervention in the last session, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan provided members of the House with an excellent summary of the collaborative effort across party lines that it has taken to get to this point, with various members of different parties championing this issue at one time or another, a journey that began over a decade ago with a motion put forward by our colleague from Airdrie—Cochrane that began the conversation in the House on offering more support to parents dealing with loss.

That motion recognized that parents who have paid into a parental leave system and then face the loss of a child should obviously not be forced immediately back to work. It highlighted the need, and it called for a system to be put in place that would allow them to continue to receive benefits that they have paid for, with, as my colleague so eloquently stated, clarity and simplicity and without disruption and red tape.

The member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan is a passionate parliamentarian and carries out his duties as shadow minister for employment effectively and efficiently. I would also like to acknowledge his work to explore the issue of what happens when a parent on leave dies during the benefit period. While it is outside the scope of this bill, I do hope that this issue will also be addressed.

This legislation addresses a topic that many of us do not want to think about. The loss of a child shortly after birth or adoption is an almost unbearable thought, yet it is a reality for so many families. In his speech at second reading, the member for Burnaby North—Seymour mentioned that approximately 1,600 families in Canada are faced with this tragedy each year.

I want to state for the record that I support the bill and am looking forward to its passage through the House. I hope that if it passes here, the other place will take up the legislation quickly so our current laws can be changed to support grieving families. The purpose of the legislation is to support grieving families in two meaningful ways.

First, the legislation would amend the Employment Insurance Act to allow a person who is entitled to employment insurance benefits following the birth or adoption of a child to remain eligible for those same benefits even if the child dies during the benefit period. Practically, what this means is that grieving parents would be able to continue receiving maternity or parental EI benefits for the entire period to which they would have been entitled had the tragic loss not occurred. This change means that parents would not need to apply for a different benefit because their parental EI support ended.

Second, this legislation would also amend the Canada Labour Code to extend the period of bereavement leave to which someone is entitled in the event of the death of a child. The bill would ensure that if a child passes near the end of a parent's leave period, the grieving parent would be entitled to a minimum of five weeks of leave following their loss.

Why are these changes necessary? As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, these proposed changes would potentially benefit 1,600 individuals, or 3,200 when you consider that when a child dies, two parents are impacted, not just the individual who was collecting EI. Additionally, the change would also benefit the families of bereaved parents. There could be other children in the family. There could be grandparents and others. What this change would do is relieve the financial pressure on the grieving couple and their loved ones.

If the bill passes, people would be eligible to remain on parental EI and receive financial support as they experience and work through unexpected grief. Additionally, they would be able to stay on a form of EI that does not require biweekly reporting.

Currently, grieving parents who no longer are eligible to receive parental EI may be able to access other EI supports. However, switching to a different EI stream, such as EI sickness benefits, requires a whole new claim. It requires the applicant to submit medical documentation to support the claim. Additionally, if the application is approved, the new form of EI benefit requires that reports be submitted every two weeks to justify the EI claim. Can members imagine trying to put together a new EI claim at a time when we are already stressed and numb with grief? If we get the new claim submitted and it is approved, can members imagine being asked to relive their grief over and over again by having to articulate the reasoning for their EI claim? The reason for the EI claim does not change from week to week, so it makes no sense to require parents to reapply for EI benefits that they would otherwise be entitled to receive had tragedy not struck their family.

Additionally, it takes a government employee time to process biweekly reports. We do not need to add unnecessary work to the program's administrators or red tape to those seeking these benefits. For those reasons, the proposed legislation is not just compassionate; it is common sense.

In closing, as a mother of four and a grandmother of 11, I am very thankful for the maternal and pediatric health care that we have in the country. We can be grateful that the measures proposed in the bill would not impact the vast majority of Canadians. Not everything we do in this place needs to affect millions of Canadians. It is important that we as parliamentarians recognize and consider the challenges that perhaps a small number of Canadians face.

I believe the changes proposed in the legislation are going to make a huge difference for those who find themselves requiring it. As I mentioned earlier, I do support the bill, and I look forward to voting in favour of it very soon.
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to learn that my colleague is a grandmother of 11.

I rise today at final reading to examine and explore Bill C-222, known as Evan's law, an act to amend the Employment Insurance Act and the Canada Labour Code regarding the death of a child. I speak for the families of Cowichan—Malahat—Langford, from Cowichan Valley to the west shore. I speak for the parents of a Vancouver Island family who welcomed a child into their lives, and who were then asked to bear the unbearable.

I served in uniform and that service brings a different perspective to the value of life. Those who serve and the families who wait for them know how quickly a life can change with one day, one phone call, one sentence that can never be taken back. This is the lens I bring to this bill.

Allow me to explain what the bill would do. When a parent receives employment insurance, maternity or parental benefits, those benefits are tied to a child. Under the current rules, if that child sadly dies, parental benefits end. A parent may switch to sickness benefits, but must report to Service Canada every two weeks to show that they are still grieving. If they do not call within a week of that death, the debt begins to build that the Canada Revenue Agency will later claw back. The Canada Labour Code carries a similar gap, and leave protections may be cut short.

Let us consider what that asks of a family. They are grieving and the system presents them with paperwork. Bill C-222 would correct that, and a parent would keep the claim already in place. They would not file again, and they would not have to learn new rules. They would be given time, and time is the one thing grief demands.

I look forward to collaborating with the government on this. When a sound idea comes from the government benches, the right response is to acknowledge it. I have read this bill, and I have weighed both what it accomplishes and what it leaves undone.

This work did not begin in this Parliament. More than 10 years ago, the member for Airdrie—Cochrane brought forward motion 110, which opened the national conversation on supporting parents who lose a child. This bill rests upon that work. It rests as well upon the courage of families, beginning with the family of Evan, for whom this law is named, who spoke publicly about the hardest day of their lives so that others would not face it alone.
