Young Canadians also keep hearing that they need experience to get their first job. How are they supposed to get experience if they do not get a chance in the first place? The report recommends more student work placements and stable funding for the student work placement program, a program I benefited from when I was in university, in fact. That would help students get experience with an employer while they are still in school so they have something on their résumé when they graduate.

Another recommendation suggests bringing back grants that help apprentices pay for their training. If we need more electricians, carpenters or plumbers, we must ensure that the young people entering those trades can finish the training. However, even with the right training and a job offer, there is another layer of complication, another challenge, which is to find somewhere to live. If a young person is willing to move for work but cannot find a home they can afford, how are they supposed to take the job? The report recommends studying a tax write-off for employers that build housing for their workers.

My children are little, and I do not know where life will take them in terms of their careers, but I want them to know that they can build a good life here in the country we love, Canada. Young Canadians should be able to look forward to their future instead of wondering whether they will ever be able to afford it.

The report gives the government clear recommendations it can act on now to make it easier for businesses to hire, help students get work experience, support apprentices through their training and help workers find housing where the jobs are. Young Canadians should be able to build a future in the country they call home. They are willing to work for it. it is time the government stopped making it harder for them.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, indeed, youth unemployment is a major issue not just in Canada but around the world as well. However, we are talking about Canada, where it is a major issue. We find ourselves in a situation that is rather unique in that there are a lot of young people looking for jobs and a lot of businesses and companies looking for workers. There is a mismatch between people looking for jobs and businesses offering jobs.

In that context, what would my colleague recommend the government do first in order to make sure that the mismatch disappears and that the people looking for jobs can find one that businesses are looking for workers to fulfill?

Mr. Speaker, that is an incredibly important question, and I am a firm believer that we will come up with the best policies when industry and government work close together to find the right policies.

In speaking to young people, they want to be part of the solution. I would encourage every member of the House to create a youth advisory council and get recommendations from youth themselves. In speaking to businesses as well, I have learned that they often find a mismatch for the skills needed for a particular job, which is why training and entry-level experience is important for students.

When we bring both parties, including the people who are part of the solution, to the table to have a discussion, we will have a better outcome in terms of policies. This report actually has some very simple solutions that would help ease the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief comment in response to the question from the Liberal opposite, who quite rightly highlighted the need to work on bridging the gaps that exist between employers and young people in skills development.

One of the critical institutions that does that work in bridging the gap is the vocational institutions that work with employers to offer vocational skills that are highly aligned with the needs of the labour market. This is for young people, and the government is attacking them. In fact, the Minister for Jobs and Families has viciously and aggressively attacked these institutions and suggested they are all fraudulent. One thing the government needs to do is stop demonizing those who are doing this important work of trying to bridge the gap between employers and young people.

I want to thank the member for raising the issue of credential recognition. When skilled professionals trained in other parts of the world are forced to compete with young people for entry-level jobs, that is a big loss to our economy in every sense. How can we do better at addressing this gap in credential recognition so that people who are trained can work in their areas of skill and leave space for young people in entry-level jobs?

Mr. Speaker, in the last election, we were very clear that part of the solution is the blue seal program so highly-trained immigrants could practise in their field of expertise. In speaking to a number of professionals, I have heard nothing but good feedback on that.

On the topic of young Canadians, their first job, that entry-level job they are looking for, their first opportunity, is oftentimes created by small businesses and medium-sized businesses. We need to support them as well.

Mr. Speaker, it was with great pleasure that I heard my colleague mention a program she benefited from in university, because that was when I first had the opportunity to meet her, which was when we were students together.

The country we faced then, a number of years ago, which I will not put on the record for both of our sakes, was very different from the one facing youth now. One of the biggest problems I have seen is that young people cannot get a first job, which means employers are looking at 20-somethings with no experience. Can the member speak to the longer-term consequences of that?
Mr. Speaker, I do thank the member for not mentioning the year we met when we were in university.

That first job is incredibly important. It gives experience, and it is an employer saying, “We believe in you. You can do it. Your contributions are valuable, and we are taking a chance in building your career here in Canada.”

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Earlier on, during questions and comments, when I was answering the question from the member for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, I got carried away a little. I said that the leader of the official opposition would be the next premier of Quebec. I want to make a correction: He will be the future prime minister of Canada.
I thank the member for correcting his comments in the House.
With that being said, we will resume debate with the hon. member for Bowmanville—Oshawa North.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the great people of Bowmanville—Oshawa North to discuss the urgent and important matter of youth unemployment.

There are a lot of statistics that get referred to when we talk about this issue, and those statistics are very important, but I also want to spend some time talking about the people and the lives behind those numbers. To paint a broad picture, as a country, we have lost, in the last two months, 110,000 jobs, and in September, 70% of the jobs lost were lost by young workers. That is 48,000 jobs lost in one month by workers under the age of 25. This number is startling and alarming. It is a reminder that policy makers and legislators here in Ottawa must take this problem seriously and be looking for solutions.

I have the privilege and honour of representing a riding and a community home to two post-secondary schools, Durham College and Ontario Tech University. There are wonderful opportunities for me to not only feel old regularly, because when I speak to students I am reminded of just how much time flies by, but also to be reminded of all the incredible, dynamic, wonderful young people we have in this country.

To give a perspective on the student population of my home community, we have 13,000 full-time students at Durham College, as well as 30,000 part-time and continuing education students. At Ontario Tech University, we have over 14,000 graduate and undergraduate students. I have the opportunity to go to campus and hear how their lives are going, hear how they are experiencing this economy and see from their point of view how the Prime Minister's decisions affect their generation and the prospects they have to build a life, build a career, buy a home one day and move forward with their dreams.

Recently, I was able, with the help of a fantastic professor, Ms. Keri-Ellen Walcer, who is at the faculty of business at Durham College, to bring together a group of student leaders to share their experiences and give me their feedback on how the economy is affecting them, their peers and their families. We got together with heads of the Durham College students' union and the Ontario Tech students' union, as well as the Durham College student business club, the Durham College blogging club and the Durham College makers and shakers club.

What really became clear to me from these conversations is that, if we want to tackle the youth unemployment problem, we have to be cognizant of how the economy is affecting the young entrepreneur. The young entrepreneur is the person who is going to build the economy of the future. The young entrepreneur is going to create jobs for not only himself or herself, but also for his or her peers and the broader community. If we are going to make a dent in these alarming numbers that indicate that job losses are acutely affecting young workers, we are going to have to have a plan for the young entrepreneur to be empowered and supported.

In the feedback that they shared with me, those students raised a number of issues that I think can paint a clear picture for members of the House to better understand how the future leaders of our economy are stressing and struggling with the current affordability crisis and the impact this has on job creation.

I want to start by talking about their concerns over housing. What they made very clear to me was that, because they are just eking by every month to be able to pay rent, and because of how difficult it is for them to make ends meet, it leaves very little time at the end of every day, at the end of every week and at the end of every month to actually work on their businesses, and they have a very broad range of interests, from fashion design to manufacturing and restaurants. They have all sorts of things that they want to be working on, but because of the affordability crisis, they have very little time to access opportunity to work on those things.

We know that in order to grow a business and in order to build an economy, young people need mentorship and they need networking. Especially if they want to start a business, they need mentorship and networking in the field that they want to work in, innovate in, create in and build in, but if someone is eking by every month, struggling just to get by day to day, then they have very little time to do the big picture thinking and planning to actually build those relationships to build that business and grow our local economy.

This paints a very clear and logical picture, so when the government comes out and says, it has a program, and the government and the Prime Minister are very good at announcements, press releases, press conferences and standing at a podium, often with a manufactured design behind them to indicate that they are doing something constructive, it leads to a lot of questions, like, in the middle of an affordability crisis, how much time young people have to access these supposed announcements and programs.

If young people are struggling to get by, where is the time at the end of the day to fill out government paperwork or talk in a government office about a program that is supposed to help their generation build for the future? This is even clearer if someone visits the Durham College campus. There they will see that, like many other campuses across the country, it has started a food bank on campus because of how bad affordability has become for the average student to get by.

This not only paints a picture of a precarious situation for young entrepreneurs to be operating in, but paints a picture of the difficulty in having the time and focus to build the businesses of the future, in accessing mentorship and networking, in accessing programming and in doing the planning necessary to build. It also paints a picture of severe mental health crises. What people will hear if they talk to students, not just at Durham College and Ontario Tech University but at campuses across this country, is that they are dealing with an extreme amount of stress to complete their studies, plan for the future and build a career when they graduate to pay their bills and get by. This leads to very serious mental health concerns for many of their peers, and it leads to a lot of concern about whether there are appropriate resources and supports for young people on campuses and beyond. This is not just clinical support, but community support and the opportunity to build relationships, friendships and fellowship. These things are often lacking in the lives of young people today as they struggle with the affordability crisis.

All in all, if we are to recognize, as I believe we should, that young entrepreneurs are critical to resolving the youth unemployment problem, then we also must understand the circumstances they are growing up in, the circumstances they are studying in and the circumstances they are working in. My belief is that if we are to take this problem seriously, then every time we see a statistic come out in a StatsCan report or a jobs number get released in the news, we should think about young people like the business leaders I mentioned at Durham College and Ontario Tech and the students all across this country who are bearing the brunt of an economy that simply does not work.

I recall that just a couple of years ago, members of an earlier iteration of the Liberal government used to talk a lot about the idea of generational fairness. I remember that buzzword being used very often. However, when we visit students at campuses and hear from them, we hears that the government has not produced generational fairness. In fact, the government has produced a very imbalanced economy where those who already have a home or business and have already made their way do not feel the same consequences as those who dream and strive to have those very same things and who are trying to get those things in an environment where it is much more difficult.

With my remaining time, I would like to highlight a plan that some of my Conservative colleagues have spoken about in the House today. It is a plan that Conservatives have put forward that we believe will make a difference for young workers and young entrepreneurs. It is a plan that will address many of the issues and concerns that I hear when I visit the students at Durham College and Ontario Tech. It is a plan that will address four particular pillars.

The first pillar is unleashing the economy by cutting taxes and reducing red tape. This is economic growth 101, and it is mind-boggling that we even have to argue these points in the House, but we do.

Number two is to fix the immigration system. There are too many people coming into our country. It is skewing the labour market and making the labour market worse for everybody. We have to address that. The only people who benefit from high levels of immigration are the large corporations that would like to see the wages of Canadian workers depressed.

Number three, the Conservative plan mentions the Canada student financial assistance program, to make sure that taxpayer dollars are being marshalled toward supporting students to pursue fields where there are actual jobs and opportunities.

Lastly, that plan is supporting workforce housing, which is very important, because as I mentioned, as young people struggle with affordability and the housing crisis, it makes it harder for them to get ahead and build their careers.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing we can agree on, it is that the Canadian economy is indeed under severe stress. That stress is coming from the trade war. That stress is coming from the pressure of our trusted neighbour, which now wants to make sure that our manufacturing sector goes back to the United States. Of course, that is not going to happen. If we want to increase the creation of jobs for young people, we have to address the elephant in the room, and that is the attack that Canada is under from our trusted neighbour. This is just a comment, not really a question.
Mr. Speaker, it is time for the Liberal government to reflect on the fact that the Canadian people are not falling for this anymore. The Liberals are being held accountable for what they have done.

Premier Eby just lost an election in British Columbia pulling the same shenanigans that the Prime Minister tries to do, which is to blame all of Canada's problems on another country and take no responsibility for his own bad policies. Young people deserve better, and that is why we have put forward the ideas we have. It is so that the government might do its best job possible to do right by our young people.

Mr. Speaker, not all members may know this, but my colleague wrote an excellent book a number of years ago about the challenges young men are facing. Many things in that book are very relevant and very prescient. I know my friend and colleague has spent much of his life and career in this House and long before that trying to address the challenges that young men face.

I am sure he has been hearing, as I have been hearing, about the struggle associated with hitting the initial rungs on the ladder. People want a secure career and a home. Those are the first steps toward being able to build out the life they want. Maybe that means getting married or having children. These things are a bit harder to do when they are living in their parents' home or are not sure where their career is going. These initial milestones are not just about economic well-being. They are also about people being able to realize the goals they have in terms of family, community and so many other things.
I wonder if the member could share, from his experience and the work he has been doing for many years, the particular challenges facing young people today and what we can do about them.

Mr. Speaker, for young people who are facing a whole heap of challenges, as I did growing up, like those who come from a broken home, are dealing with all sorts of economic instability or have trauma that they are processing at a very young age, a job is a life raft of normalcy. It is a pathway to being part of society when they may feel very isolated and pushed away by life circumstances. When we see in report after report that entry-level positions, the kinds of jobs that were the first step for me and a lot of people in my generation, are harder now for young workers to get, it is a denial of that life raft. It is a denial of the normalcy that so many young people crave.

It is not just about the economic opportunity, which is tremendously important, and it is not just about building a career, which is tremendously important. It is about the stability and personal growth that a job offers. I think all young people deserve that.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one of the things that I have been trying to amplify is the fact that there are a number of initiatives the government has taken. It is hard to tell exactly why the Conservatives are in opposition to them. I will give a specific example. With the Red Seal program, youth could benefit from 80,000 to 100,000 potential careers, and that is through a $5,000 incentive to get them to finish the Red Seal program.
I wonder if the member could provide his thoughts on the Conservative Party's position on that program.
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to thank the member opposite for finally asking me a question that is not about the United States. I certainly appreciate it.

When it comes to policies, there are things the government has announced that I think can be very helpful, and there are existing policies of the federal government that can be helpful. The problem is that they are not enough. What we are asking is for the government to take the problem seriously and do more.
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour, as always, to rise on behalf of the people of Elgin—St. Thomas—London South. I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Edmonton Southeast.

I have the great privilege in this role of meeting people all over the communities that I represent, but I love when I get the opportunity to meet with young people. I love when I get the opportunity to speak to classes. I can tell members that whenever I go into a high school class, they are always so enthusiastic. Sometimes they are so overwhelmed by their excitement that they cannot even bring themselves to listen.

I have a great deal of hope for high school students, even if they do not share that hope right now. Whenever I speak to these students, knowing that in any grade 10 class, not everyone is interested in politics, I always try to find issues that connect with them and issues that speak to the experiences they are going through, the lives they are living. Without a doubt, whenever I have asked these classes how many of them are having trouble finding a job, almost every hand goes up.

In fact, a few weeks ago, I was speaking to one grade 10 civics class, and I asked that very question. Students laughed because they view their inability to find a job right now as a punchline. They do not even believe it is within the realm of reality. That is heartbreaking.

We have heard, in the course of the discussion this evening, members talk about the importance of first jobs and the pride one feels having a first job. I remember that my first grown-up job, so to speak, was at the age of 14 working as a busboy at a hotel restaurant. It was an opportunity I had at 14 to develop skills, to earn a bit of income and to do something with my life, however young.

It was interesting. A year into that, for whatever reason, I felt like I wanted to do something else, and I did something that I do not recommend to anyone, certainly not now. I put in my two weeks' notice without having a plan. Within the next two weeks, I had been offered several jobs, at 15 and with one year of work experience. That was the opportunity available to me, available to people my age and certainly available to people in this chamber who are older in years than I am.

It is heartbreaking to me that this is no longer the case. Not only do young people today not face a situation in which they are getting multiple offers, but they are finding themselves applying for dozens or hundreds of jobs and failing to find even one company that will hire them. It is not because they are not passionate. It is not because they are not dedicated or hard-working. It is because the jobs are simply not available to them.

We have seen in the last year, despite the Liberal government's proclamations that things are great in Canada right now, really dismal unemployment numbers. In fact, I remember when youth unemployment reached a record just shy of 15%. How many people in this chamber were sounding the alarm about that? The region I represent has an even worse situation for youth unemployment right now. The London area, which includes St. Thomas and Elgin, has a youth unemployment rate, as of last month, of 19.9%. That means one in five youth looking for work cannot find it.

These numbers are bad enough, but they tell only a portion of the story. They do not show the people who have given up, the people who are not looking for work and the people who have withdrawn from the labour market. That number, when we take all that into consideration, shows an even more grim portrait. When young people cannot find a first job, it means they have a harder time finding a bit of a better job and then a better job than that. What I hear from employers, who are sometimes facing the opportunity to hire someone, is that they are getting applicants who are 20 or 22 years old who do not have any meaningful experience because they have not been able to find jobs where they would normally cut their teeth, where they would normally develop skills and gain experience.

We have now, as the cumulative effect of this, a delayed entry into the workforce, not for lack of desire but for lack of opportunity. There are a number of reasons for this. One of them is the economic climate that businesses and business owners face right now.

This, contrary to what the Liberals, I am sure, are going to say, is not something we can lay at the feet of the United States. This is the consequence of 11 years of Liberal government policy, taxes, regulations, red tape, bureaucracy and high-cost inflation, all of which makes it more difficult, if not impossible, for businesses, especially small and medium-sized businesses, to invest in talent, to hire people. If someone talks to small business owners, they increasingly find themselves working the equivalent of two, three or four full-time jobs because they cannot afford, especially with their margins, to hire. Whenever a decision is made to hire or not to hire, it is often that young entry-level worker who is going to be the one missing out on that opportunity.

They have been doing it recklessly, to the point where now young people are being displaced from job opportunities because of an abundance of temporary foreign workers who are occupying a lot of service positions, because the government said they could. The Liberal government said they could. This is something that everyone sees in this country. Everyone knows that, except for the Liberals, or at least they choose not to acknowledge it. If we do not get rid of this program, we are going to see more and more of what we have been describing tonight take hold. More and more young people will be unable to enter the job market.

We have put forward, as some of my colleagues have shared tonight, a number of concrete steps, things the Liberal government could do right now that would start righting the ship after this disastrous record of theirs over the last 11 years. However, I want to take the opportunity to give a voice to the people who have been the most directly affected by this, young people who have been reaching out to me and continue to reach out to me because of the lives that they are forced to live, because of what is happening.

Then we also have immigration. Now, the Liberals have tried to do this very dishonest thing whenever we raise this issue by saying that we are blaming immigrants for Canada's economic woes, when the reality could not be further from that. We are blaming the Liberal government, which has for 11 years held the keys to the country and decided exactly how many people are permitted to enter the country and work in the country. That is the Liberal government's prerogative as government, and for 11 years the Liberals have been doing this.

Logan writes, “I am at rock bottom. I lost my car due to a weather-related accident. Since then I was forced to quit my job as I was in school. I have not been able to find a job since. Almost every day, I am applying and actively seeking a job. Still with no vehicle, I am running out of time and money. The money I saved lasted me up until now, as I am paying for rent on my own and food.” Benjamin writes, “I cannot find a good job despite multiple degrees.” Tyler writes, “Recently, I've started my last term of schooling to become a licenced plumber. For the last two terms I've been at school, I received a grant at the end of it, which helped me get things to further my career, like tools and textbooks. As of March 2025, the federal government has taken that away from me and all other apprentices.” I am glad the Liberals finally acknowledged that when we talked about the importance of this, because this was so disruptive to students. Tyler continued to write, “Raise this matter in the House. We need Canadian-trained, skilled labour to help build this country.”

We have Candace. I read a little bit of a letter she sent me in question period last week. Despite the minister responsible for jobs saying that she would welcome the opportunity to correspond with Candace, I asked for consent to table the letter and the Liberals shouted it down. Candace, a 25-year-old mother of a 17-month-old daughter at the time she wrote this, was laid off from her job because of the economic downturn and has applied for 500 positions. She says she has tailored multiple versions of her résumé for different industries. She has written personalized cover letters. She has actually made searching for a job her full-time job and has received only a handful of interviews. She has seen companies that she applied to hire temporary foreign workers instead. This is the reality facing young people.

The Liberal government needs to stop being dismissive of this, understand this, listen to this and work with us to deliver the solutions that are going to right this ship, that are going to give these young people who I represent, who all of us in this House represent, the chance at the future that we all had when we were their age.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will say at the outset, I am somewhat concerned about the manner in which the Conservative right today is trying to blame immigrants for problems.
Back in 2012, unemployment amongst youth was over 14%. In 2025, it was under 14%. I do not recall, back in 2012, the opposition criticizing Stephen Harper, saying that immigrants were to blame.

I am wondering if the member was in opposition back then. There were immigrants doing jobs and there were ample examples of youth trying to find jobs. Would the member have been so enthusiastic in trying to paint a negative image of immigrants? Let us think of the harm that is being caused, in terms of racial tension in our communities. It seems to me that we need to be fair in our explanation to the young people of Canada and also be fair to immigrants in terms of explaining the situation.

Mr. Speaker, the disingenuousness of that member is actually disgusting. I was very clear in my comments that this is not the fault of immigrants. I do not blame anyone for wanting to enjoy and embrace the bounty of this country. It is the Liberal government that sets the numbers. This is a mathematical problem.

I get that the Liberals, with their record, are not particularly good at math, but that member should be ashamed of himself for trying to make this about race when it is about opportunity. In fact, immigrants to this country who have done everything right are just as put out by this Liberal government's record. They too are displaced. They too are facing the same issues in the job market that every single person is.

This is not at all about immigrants. This is about the government that has allowed the TFW program to balloon into something where, by the way, even it acknowledges there was a problem. I have no idea where this is coming from.

Mr. Speaker, I want to pick up on this discussion about immigration, because there is a total lack of nuance and seriousness in the discussion on this issue from the Liberals across the way. They are just trying to dodge having an important, substantive and genuinely nuanced conversation about how to get immigration right.

As my colleague spoke about, yes, it is about the numbers, and it is also about categories and skill recognition. When somebody comes here who has specific skills that they could put to use in the economy, and, instead, this government fails to recognize their skills and forces them to compete for entry-level jobs, that is bad for the newcomer, that is bad for the young people they are competing against, and that is also bad for those who could benefit from their skills, if done at a higher level. It is about getting the categories right, it is about recognizing skills and it is about shaping the policy in a nuanced way, rather than this attempt at Liberal demagoguery to avoid being accountable for their own failures.

Mr. Speaker, I agree wholeheartedly with my colleague from Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan. I am so grateful he has been such a stalwart voice on this file, travelling the country and doing the work the Liberal government should be doing to engage these people in the process.

If the Liberals truly believe that they have done right by the country's young people, they need to look at how many of those people have joined the Conservatives because they were sold a bill of goods by the Liberal government. They were sold hope and promised the moon, and now they are seeing that reality is catching up, and they are far worse off than they were led to believe they would be.

Mr. Speaker, just to pick up on an earlier part of the discussion as well, the member and other members have spoken about their first job. The first job that young people get is critically important for developing skills, experiencing what they can contribute to the world and also starting them on that ladder to building a family, to being able to own a home, etc.
These milestones are getting pushed further and further away because of these job problems. I wonder if the member has a comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I do not spend time just speaking to workers, I also speak to employers. One of the issues they have identified is that they cannot find young people with experience because young people have not been given the opportunities to develop those skills. We are seeing long-term consequences here that are going to continue to hurt employers and potential employees alike.

Mr. Speaker, this evening I rise to discuss the issue of youth unemployment, an issue that I know affects many Edmontonians and far more Canadians. I would first like to thank all members of the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities for their hard work over seven meetings to draft this 10th report.

Canada has historically been a country where people build, discover and invest. However, for the last decade, Canada has experienced the opposite. More often, corporations are taking capital investment south of our border and students from our top universities are leaving to work on projects outside the country. Canada needs to do better. As parliamentarians, we must take an active role in shaping the environment for youth to succeed economically. That does not mean planning an economy for them. Rather, it means developing smart, pointed policy aimed at fixing a broken system of brain drain and a major lack of economic opportunities. As they say, the first step to fixing a problem is acknowledging that there is one. The 16 recommendations set forward by this report are an important start and, therefore, should be concurred in by the government.

In Edmonton Southeast, I am hearing more often from parents about their children having difficulty being able to find work, and the data supports these parental concerns. In August of this year, Canada lost 42,000 jobs, including 19,000 jobs for young Canadians aged 15 to 24. Similarly, in September 2026, Canada lost another 68,000 jobs, with youth accounting for 48,000 of those lost positions. In just two months, youth employment declined by 67,000 jobs. That is around 61% of the total decline in employment. These numbers are concerning and call for action.

Conservatives and my hon. colleague from Sherwood Park, Alberta, have offered real solutions. Our four-point plan includes unleashing the economy, fixing training, fixing the system where high-skilled newcomers compete for entry-level jobs and building homes where the work is necessary to create employment opportunities for youth. Conservatives have repeatedly called on the Liberal government to reduce red tape and taxes so that Canada can return to a simple but effective regulatory environment that supports the creation and growth of youth employment.

Multiple witnesses cited in this report conclude that heavy taxation limits the capacity to invest in new technology and expansion. In fact, one witness was even cited as saying that Canada is no longer an attractive place to start a career or business due to our sluggish economic environment. We cannot accept this assertion as fact. We must deliver better for our youth.

Employers must be encouraged to hire, build and keep workers in Canada. Youth are most affected by changing market forces, so entrepreneurs must see Canada as a reliable and predictable market to grow their business. Now, more than ever before, companies can move between countries. It is time for the Liberal government to address these issues by creating a landscape that attracts and retains those companies rather than letting them go somewhere more business-friendly. Furthermore, this report explicitly calls upon the government to acknowledge the importance that resource development and manufacturing play in our economy.

The Liberal government has actively worked to block major resource projects in this country. Announcements are nothing but announcements, and more paperwork does not get Canada back on track. We need faster approvals, shorter timelines and a greater acknowledgement of the people who build our country. Tradespeople are the backbone of Canada. We cannot build our roads and our homes without them.

We need a Canada where skilled trades work is celebrated and honoured. In our economy, these jobs can be some of the highest-paying and most rewarding for youth. There needs to be a shift so the trades are neither looked down upon nor compared to a university education. Each is a unique track that offers positive outcomes. The pipefitter or electrician needs a clear pathway from training to apprenticeship and certification, and they must feel that their work is worthwhile as a career.

The final point I want to mention is the certification of immigrants in Canada. Like many members of the House, I was not born in Canada. However, I always saw Canada as a country of hope, opportunity and prosperity. When I arrived as a young man, I was lucky to be a trained lawyer, and the pathways to credential transfer were clear. This is not the case for most jobs, which is an unfortunate reality that has held Canada back for decades.

The HUMA report finds that this holdup is forcing new Canadians to compete with youth for entry-level jobs. The 2021 census data showed that 25.8% of immigrants with foreign degrees were working in jobs requiring, at most, a high school diploma. This stat reflects Canada's broader productivity problem. Our economy loses out on increased tax revenues from high-wage jobs, and entry-level jobs become unnecessarily competitive for young Canadians. This scenario is all too common and, frankly, benefits no one. Conservatives have been asking for greater pathways for skilled immigrants to gain accreditation and equivalency training. A new framework would benefit the economy as a whole.

It is not a secret that our youth are struggling. Youth without jobs means more lineups at food banks. In March 2026, Food Banks Canada reported that 33% of visitors were under the age of 18. This is more than a 6% increase from the same time a year before. Young Canadians should not have to leave Canada to find opportunity because our economy fails to deliver.

The recommendations set out by this 10th report provides a starting point for addressing these challenges, from reducing barriers to employment to strengthening apprenticeship pathways and improving credential recognition. Concurrence in this report is an opportunity for Parliament to acknowledge the seriousness of youth unemployment and demand meaningful action. The government must now turn these recommendations into results. Young Canadians are waiting.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have good news for the member opposite: Youth do not have to wait, because Canada's summer jobs portal just opened 75,000 jobs every summer, with 340 jobs in my riding of Whitby. I am sure the member opposite can acknowledge that this helps create opportunities for our young people.

We also have 80,000 to 100,000 new skilled trades positions, with training incentives, wage incentives and completion incentives with about $31,000 per Red Seal apprentice. It is significant support for youth that provides opportunities.

We have also cut red tape. We set up a Major Projects Office, and we have Bill C-39 before the House, all of which would remove red tape and get approvals and permitting to speed up, stimulating the economy to make sure we have opportunities for youth. What does the member have to say about that?
Mr. Speaker, the issue is not the temporary numbers. The member talks about summer jobs. Summer jobs are temporary, but the jobs that youth are facing issues with are not just the summer jobs.

It is more than that, and as the committee has recommended, we need to cut red tape. The member just confirmed that they have announced a program that would cut the red tape. It is nothing but announcements yet, so we have to see. We are willing to work, along with the party opposite, to make sure of that. Any positive changes to the current program that can help young people get jobs are welcome.

Mr. Speaker. I have to come back to the issue of completion grants for the trades. Completion grants were started by Prime Minister Harper. It was a very successful policy and strongly supported. The Minister of Jobs and Families came to committee and said that completion grants were not working. It is on the record. The Minister of Jobs and Families said they were not working.

The government cancelled completion grants, then it relaunched them under a new name. It is like the Liberals said, “We came up with this great idea. They are called completion grants, which had been cancelled for a few months.” The minister assured us at committee that we should not worry, as they were going to connect the funding to ensure that nobody lost out in the intervening period.

These are the facts. The government has no new ideas. It is repeatedly celebrating things that have existed in this country for decades, and its approach is failing. It is more announcements, and the government is cancelling and then renaming old Conservative programs.
There is work to do. When will the government get with the program and actually do the work that needs to be done?

Mr. Speaker, I wholeheartedly agree with the member's analysis of the situation right now. The government tries to use our ideas, but then all of a sudden it cuts half of them or applies them half-heartedly. If the government has to apply our programs, let us be honest about it and apply them, so Canadians can have good paying jobs and earn good cheques, and so youth can also be a productive part of society and have well-paying jobs.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member across the way from Saskatchewan was talking about—
Garnett Genuis: Alberta.
Hon. Kevin Lamoureux: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry, it is Alberta. That Saskatchewan name in his riding kind of throws everyone off.

I can say that the member was reflecting on the past. There is one thing I know for sure, because I was in the third-party position when Stephen Harper was here. I know the member opposite actually used to work very closely with Stephen Harper.

The member will recall that they actually cut back on summer programs or summer work for young people, and it was somewhat sad. By the way, that was the same time when unemployment for youth was over 14%. I contrast that to today, or 2025, when it is under 14%. Does the member not agree that it was wrong for the government back—
I have to cut off the parliamentary secretary to give a chance to the member for Edmonton Southeast to respond.

Mr. Speaker, it is really mind-boggling that, after 11 years of government, the member still has to go back to the Harper era or the Harper government. That is because they do not have any concrete figures to rely upon for what they have done in their 11 years.

Mr. Speaker, this has been an excellent debate tonight. The Liberals tried to shut down debate the first time we were discussing youth unemployment, but we have been able to resume it tonight to highlight the Conservative youth jobs plan announced a year ago, a simple plan with concrete, constructive proposals to unleash the economy, fix immigration, fix training and build homes where the jobs are.

We pushed the human resources committee to do a detailed study on youth unemployment. It came up with many very good recommendations reflecting an all-party consensus very much in line with the Conservative youth jobs plan. That was work we started, that the committee continued and that received unanimous support of the committee.

There are great recommendations that the government should follow through on, constructive ideas that it could put in the budget, such as reducing taxes and red tape; recognizing the positive role of natural resource development, manufacturing and other sectors; supporting the alignment of our immigration policies with the needs of the Canadian economy; and punishing companies that hire illegal workers. We heard a bit about that in question period today. There were three questions in English and two more in French asking why the government offered subsidies to companies that hired illegal workers. The government could not provide an answer.

Other recommendations include working to strengthen credential recognition. This is part of fixing immigration. Talented, skilled newcomers who come to this country should be able to put their skills and their training to work rather than competing with young people for entry-level jobs. It would be a double win for our economy to be able to actually deploy newcomers at the skill level they have. This was a central priority for us in the last election, a positive priority about aligning immigration with the needs of our economy.
There is much more in the 10th report. The government should adopt these constructive Conservative ideas in the next budget.
It being 8:24 p.m., it is my duty to interrupt the proceedings.

Pursuant to order made earlier this day, the previous question is deemed carried on division, and the motion to concur in the 10th report of the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities is deemed put and a recorded division deemed requested. Pursuant to Standing Order 66, the recorded division stands deferred until Wednesday, October 28, at the expiry of the time provided for Oral Questions.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 38 deemed to have been moved.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise at this hour in Adjournment Proceedings to pursue a question I asked in question period on May 5.

We were nearly at the anniversary of June 3, 2019, the date of the long-fought-for report. It was such a traumatic experience just to get an inquiry into missing and murdered indigenous women and girls. That inquiry wrapped up, and as I asked my question on May 5, I noted that it was almost seven years ago that the report of the inquiry into missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and two-spirit plus people had been given to the government.

Back then, we hoped. The government of the day said it would do its very best and certainly was committed to achieving all of the calls for justice within the report. There were 231 calls for justice. In other reports, one might just call them recommendations, but I think it was powerful that they were called calls for justice. The horror of the number of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls in this country remains with us, because many of those women and girls are still missing, and many more have gone missing since we got the report back on June 3, 2019.

The response I got from the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations was compassionate, caring and thoughtful, as is she. She did not provide a number of how many of the calls for justice had been achieved. She did, of course, express the concern that justice, as she said, was “not with respect to just one project, but a life we need to continue to live”, and that violence against indigenous people must end. However, it remains the fact that here we are in late October 2026, and we still are dealing with the reality that women are missing and murdered.

I have a lot of friends from all kinds of backgrounds, close friends, but it is only among my indigenous women friends that it is rare to find a friend who is indigenous in this country who has not been beaten up and abused. One of my close friends, I thought I knew about her life until she said, “I never told you about the time I was left for dead in a dumpster.” She said it as if it was a sort of normalized experience for indigenous women and girls, and it is, in fact, far too common.

I tried to find a number for tonight's debate, from Statistics Canada and other sources, as to how many indigenous women and girls have gone missing since we got the recommendations, which have not been fulfilled. It was hard to find a number because Statistics Canada and sources do not necessarily agree, but it is a large number of women and girls from the indigenous communities of this country who have gone missing since the report came out.

I will quote, because it was at least authoritative, the Native Women's Association of Canada, which states, “Despite half a decade passing since the release of the National Action Plan, the implementation of the 231 Calls for Justice has been insufficient.” It states that “many federal commitments remain delayed, fragmented, or difficult to measure in ways that reflect the realities Indigenous communities [face] every day.”

What we are looking at is an ongoing crisis. We have recommendations that were really important and sweeping, such as bringing in a guaranteed livable income, such as ensuring that there is safe and efficient transportation in rural and remote Canada, a recommendation that would serve all parts of society in rural and remote Canada, where people cannot get from A to B unless they own a car, other than hitchhiking and putting themselves at risk.
It is now, with a few seconds left, time to ask again. What is the level of commitment of this government? Will we hear a commitment to achieve these recommendations?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ people continues to affect survivors, families and communities across this country. Of the 231 calls for justice in the final report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, 215 of them call on the federal government in some capacity or other. On June 3, we released the 2025-2026 federal pathway annual progress report, marking the fifth anniversary of “Federal Pathway To Address Missing And Murdered Indigenous Women, Girls And 2SLGBTQQIA+ People”, which is the Government of Canada's contribution to the national action plan.

As it stands now, the Government of Canada has made efforts to advance roughly three-quarters of the federal work outlined in the national inquiry's final report. This year, our government reported progress on 163 of the calls for justice. As I have mentioned, advancing the calls for justice is not a one-time effort or a checklist for one party to fulfill. Many calls for justice require sustained action and an ongoing commitment to collaborate with other governments, organizations and civil society, while continuing to follow the lead of survivors and their families.

On Red Dress Day this year, the Prime Minister was presented with a sacred bundle by the National Family and Survivors Circle. That sacred bundle carries teachings, responsibilities and spirit, reflecting the lived experiences of victims, survivors and their communities from the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls. Receiving that sacred bundle reaffirmed the Government of Canada's commitment to end the national crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

Also, on Red Dress Day we announced an investment of $2.6 million over three years for the National Family and Survivors Circle Inc. to continue its vital work in centring survivors and families in the implementation of the calls for justice. We also announced an additional $300,000 investment to help support the next steps on a red dress alert pilot in Manitoba. We continue to invest in indigenous-led approaches that advance the calls for justice through Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada's supporting indigenous women's and 2SLGBTQI+ organizations program. Twenty-two projects have recently been approved to support indigenous-led solutions and advance indigenous-led priorities.

We also continue to support healing, wellness and community-led responses through the support of the contribution program for the well-being of families and survivors of missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQI+ people. At the same time, Indigenous Services Canada has been expanding access to safe, culturally appropriate spaces through the indigenous shelter and transitional housing initiative, which is part of the $724.1-million comprehensive violence prevention strategy. This investment will have supported the creation of 38 new shelters and 42 transitional homes across Canada, including in northern and urban communities.

There is no doubt that there is lots more work to do on this important call to action and the calls for justice. We look forward to collaborating and to continuing to treat this national crisis with the urgency it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the parliamentary secretary nor any minister would claim that this has been accomplished. I think we can agree that the work is, of necessity, going to be partial, but I am not convinced there is a sufficient level of urgency from the government for the fact that people, especially women and girls, continue to go missing all the time.

There is police training and the kinds of supports required under the calls for justice, including trauma-informed therapists going right away to help a woman who has been assaulted or attacked get through that process. Those kinds of steps were very specific in the report, and they really must be treated with urgency, because every single attack of a woman hitchhiking on a rural road is something that was avoidable, predictable and preventable.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the member opposite that the issue requires urgency and sustained effort. The crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQIA people demands urgent and sustained action, and we remain firmly committed to ending it. Of the 231 calls for justice, 215 are directly related to the federal government in some capacity, and we are acting on that responsibility. As I have said, almost three-quarters have been started and are in progress.

We are making targeted investments that translate into real support, safe places to go, and culturally informed care and services identified by communities themselves. This includes support for indigenous-led organizations, further investments in a red dress alert pilot and expanding shelters and transitional housing across the country. Everything we are doing is built on working together, being accountable and following the leadership of indigenous partners.

Mr. Speaker, I rise again to ask my fellow Manitoban, the Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs, and Manitoba's only voice at the cabinet table, about the complete lack of major projects and development happening in Manitoba under the Liberal government.

The minister's response to my initial question about major projects coming to Manitoba, or the lack thereof, can be described as light at best. Where are the Manitoba Liberals? They are completely missing in action.

Conservatives in Manitoba understand the potential of our great province. We have been pushing opportunities at the Port of Churchill for years, including in multiple campaign platforms. We know that more opportunities exist in expanding our mining industry, and the same is true for the potential in value-added agriculture and processing. As the heart of Canada, Manitoba is geographically positioned to play an even greater role in our national defence industry as well.

Manitoba has all of this potential, yet where is the Liberal government's ambition for its development? On what significant new projects is it working on to bring growth and investment to Manitobans? So far, Manitoba has been a flyover province for the Liberal major projects announcement machine.
Will the minister get up and put on the record what her vision is for expanding major projects happening in friendly Manitoba?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I know I have colleagues on this side from Manitoba who are really fantastic. They work hard and represent some of the ridings in Manitoba quite well.

I will also say that this summer, in the pre-budget consultations, I had the opportunity to meet with Manitoba's finance minister and talk about many of the major projects in Manitoba. Our government is supportive and is serious about working with Manitoba to advance its interests, help grow its economy and take advantage of the significant opportunities that it sees for itself and for Canada as a whole.

Countries around the world are grappling with an affordability crisis, and Canada is no exception. Political unrest and ongoing conflicts on two continents are taking their toll. Here at home, our closest neighbour and largest trading partner has placed tariffs on many Canadian goods entering the U.S. market, placing jobs and prosperity at risk. The cumulative effect of this disruption is higher prices for many essential goods. This is having an impact on Canadians and the businesses that support them.

While the situation originated beyond our borders, our government is standing up for Canadians. We are taking strong, decisive action to address affordability concerns by introducing measures that lower costs and keep more hard-earned dollars in the pockets of Canadians.

One of the most recent of these involves the federal fuel excise tax on gasoline, aviation fuel, diesel fuel and others. In April of this year, we introduced a temporary suspension, lowering the tax per litre for gasoline by 10¢, while the tax on leaded gasoline fell by 11¢ per litre, and the tax on diesel and aviation fuel fell by four cents per litre. This temporary suspension was going to expire on September 7, Labour Day. Before it could end, however, we announced our intention to extend the temporary pause until January 31, 2027, and after that date, regular rates would be reduced by 50% until March 31, fiscal year end.

We have also taken action on grocery prices with the Canada groceries and essentials benefit announced at the beginning of the year. This benefit replaces the GST credit and provides tax-free quarterly payments to individuals and families with low and modest incomes to help manage the rising cost of living. In July 2026, there was a 25% increase to the benefit amount, which will remain for five years. Canadians can expect the amount of this benefit to be recalculated every July based on their adjusted family net income from the previous year.
We have also waived taxes on first-time home purchases at the federal level. That is significant. It is about $50,000 on a $1-million home.

These measures are on top of an income tax cut we announced last year where we lowered the tax rate for the first marginal personal income tax bracket from 15% to 14%, saving over 22 million Canadians money on their taxes. That is $840 for the average dual income family or $420 per individual.

We have cut taxes on income, housing and fuel, and offered a groceries and essentials benefit to help ease the pressures that families are under based on the cost of living. I would say that is progress.
In response to the member opposite's question about Manitoba, we are serious about building all across Canada and working with Manitoba every step of the way.

Mr. Speaker, what an embarrassingly out-of-touch response that was from the parliamentary secretary. I asked about specific, tangible, physical projects that the Liberal government is pursuing for my home province, and all the member had to offer was that he visited it one time and had a 30-minute chat with the finance minister at the provincial level. How typical of the out-of-touch Liberals to forget about the province of Manitoba.

Here are a couple of facts for the member. According to its own website, there are 20 major projects with the Major Projects Office. How many of those 20 major projects are in Manitoba? Not one. The port of Churchill plus is Manitoba's only specifically identified initiative, and the government classifies it as a “transformative strategy”, not a major project, with absolutely zero details listed. Meanwhile, other provinces have eight, three or two projects listed.
When will the Liberal government and the six Liberal MPs prioritize major projects in Manitoba?

Mr. Speaker, Manitoba is without exception a priority for this government, and I am sure it is a priority to the Premier of Manitoba. There are projects and opportunities that we recognize. The Major Projects Office has been set up to advance projects in the national interest that meet the criteria.

Transformative strategies are nothing to be ashamed of. Those are excellent projects as well, and there are quite a number of them. In fact, the projects across Canada that we are advancing, in partnership with first nations and the premiers of each province, are good news for this country's prosperity in the future. We look forward to expediting those projects as soon as the member and his colleagues bring forward more projects that we can advance.

Mr. Speaker, Michael Green, the former CEO of Canada Health Infoway, was fired after overseeing the $300-million PrescribeIT scandal. Despite his massive failure, he was awarded over $1 million in severance benefits, including another performance bonus after he was fired. Apparently, that was not enough for this failed PrescribeIT CEO. Court documents reveal that Mr. Green is now suing Canada Health Infoway for even more money, claiming that his massive payday was not enough.
How many taxpayer dollars are the Liberals allowing Canada Health Infoway to spend on this legal battle with its former CEO?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, just over a month ago, the member opposite posed a nearly identical question during Adjournment Proceedings. I will respond by giving him a nearly identical answer.

As the Minister of Health announced in June, our government believes that Canadians deserve transparency and openness when it comes to how taxpayer dollars are spent. That is to be expected. There were obviously concerns with whether Canadians had received value for money when it comes to Canada Health Infoway, which is why the Minister of Health announced a multiphase review that included both an independent audit and a third party review of the organization's governance and structure.

The member opposite was a member of the health committee when Liberal, Bloc and Conservative MPs unanimously called for the Auditor General to look at the organization in question. What was the Auditor General's response? She said that the reviews announced by the minister are enough for her and that any other work by her would be duplicative and of limited value. Let us allow that work to take place and make sure that the review and the audit show what is working and what is not so that we can be sure that we have modernized health data infrastructure that works best for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am really glad the member mentioned the June story, because in June, the Liberals told The Globe and Mail that they were launching an independent third party audit of Canada Health Infoway after Conservatives exposed the $300-million PrescribeIT scandal. That was over 130 days ago.
Has the government actually hired a third party auditor, and if so, who did it hire?

Mr. Speaker, again, let us review the facts. The member opposite was on HESA when that committee asked for the Auditor General to do an audit. The Auditor General said the work being done by the government to ensure that taxpayers are getting value for their money is enough for her. I trust that the Auditor General knows what she is talking about. It is too bad the member opposite does not have the same level of trust in her.
The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, the House stands adjourned until Wednesday, October 28, at 2 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 24(1).
(The House adjourned at 8:45 p.m.)
